title: AI Everywhere, Results Nowhere: Building the Operating Model for Innovation at Scale
abstract:
This proposed 45-minute interactive session for practitioners addresses one of the most important questions facing business leaders today: Why are organizations investing heavily in AI while so few can point to meaningful, measurable business results? AI is already everywhere. Employees are experimenting, departments are launching pilots, and leadership teams are considering larger investments. But the leading research in the past two years shows clearly that companies who are buying and adopting tools aren't actually seeing an impact to their bottom line - they are stuck in experimentation and scattered adoption. Moving from experimentation to innovation at scale requires more than additional tools. It requires an organization designed to repeatedly identify valuable opportunities, redesign work, manage risk, measure results, and expand what works.

Heather Lenz will draw on her firsthand experience transforming a multi-million-dollar professional services firm into an AI-driven business and ultimately selling it. She will share the threat AI posed to the core business model, what the company initially expected AI to change, what actually had to change, where early efforts stalled, and how the leadership team redesigned workflows, roles, meetings, documentation, quality control, and accountability around the technology. The case study will show how AI value is created not through isolated tasks, but through the deliberate redesign of complete workflows and the operating systems around them.

Heather will connect that experience to the patterns she now sees as Founder and CEO of AI Navigator Collective, where she helps executive teams turn scattered experimentation into practical business value. A professionally trained speaker and experienced facilitator, Heather has spoken nationally and presented to executive and practitioner audiences at AI summits, industry conferences, Chamber of Commerce events, and regional economic development programs. Her recent engagements include workshops at the Wayne County Economic Development Council, Cleveland AI Summit, Culture Matters Conference, and a keynote for the Canton Regional Chamber of Commerce AI Summit. Known for making complex organizational challenges accessible, Heather combines candid business stories, practical frameworks, humor, and active audience participation so attendees stay actively engaged and leave with ideas they can put to work immediately.

Participants will examine the most common reasons AI investments fail to generate meaningful returns: unclear ownership, disconnected experimentation, poorly selected use cases, generalized training without application, and attempts to layer AI onto workflows that were never reconsidered. They will learn how many companies are approaching AI adoption, and what research and practice shows works best. 

The session will introduce a practical method for identifying and prioritizing AI investments across three value categories. Quick wins create immediate efficiencies within existing work. Operational enhancements redesign important workflows to improve speed, quality, capacity, or decision-making. Strategic moves can change how the organization competes, serves customers, uses proprietary data, or delivers products and services. Participants will learn why these opportunities require different levels of investment, governance, measurement, and organizational readiness, and why treating them as interchangeable undermines ROI.

Attendees will also learn to define value before selecting technology. For each AI opportunity, leaders should identify the business outcome, establish a baseline, determine what will change in the workflow, assign ownership, and decide how results will be measured. ROI may include reduced production time, greater capacity, improved quality, faster decisions, lower risk, increased revenue, or entirely new sources of value. This approach gives organizations a disciplined way to decide what to scale, what to revise, and what to stop.

During a guided exercise, participants will identify AI opportunities with the potential to move beyond individual productivity into meaningful operational or strategic value. They will leave with a clearer picture of their organization's readiness, a practical framework for evaluating AI investments, and two or three actions they can take to strengthen ownership, prioritization, workflow design, governance, and measurement.

This is not a technical demonstration or another presentation about which AI tools to buy. It is a candid, highly practical session for executives, business leaders, and transformation practitioners responsible for turning AI activity into measurable results. Attendees will leave understanding that innovation at scale is not one successful pilot replicated across the company. It is the organizational capability to continuously choose the right opportunities, redesign work around them, measure their value, and scale what works as the technology changes.

title: Historical Trends in Job Complexity and Physical Demands: An AI-Automated Cross-Temporal Meta-Analysis
abstract:
For at least the last five decades, diverse theory across economics, human resource management, and organizational behavior has suggested that the nature of work has become more complex and less physical for the typical worker (Autor, 2015; Autor et al., 2003; Fraccaroli et al., 2024). This prevailing account reflects the rise of knowledge work: as mechanization, computerization, and early AI technologies replaced routine tasks, the remaining tasks increasingly required nonroutine knowledge and judgment. Recent advancements in AI seem destined to intensify this historical trend. What novel and complicated work might emerge in a technologically sophisticated world? And yet, for all the technical complexity hidden within AI models and the unprecedented challenges AI might address, recent AI technologies can simplify work or complete challenging work autonomously. Could AI cause a "great reversal" in prevailing trends (Beaudry et al., 2016)? Together, these questions reveal an important gap in work design theory. For all its successes in identifying the consequences of work characteristics, work design research has been far less successful in identifying what causes these characteristics to emerge and change (Parker et al., 2017). Technology is one such distal antecedent, enabling and constraining the tasks, knowledge, and environments that comprise work. Before evaluating whether modern AI represents a continuation or discontinuity, the historical trends must first be established.

I tested the prevailing theory that, over the last five decades, time was (H1a) positively associated with job complexity and (H1b) negatively associated with physical demands and that this trend was intensifying, testing if time had (H2a) a positive nonlinear association with job complexity and (H2b) a negative nonlinear association with physical demands. To test these predictions, I identified all studies that included survey measures aligned with the Work Design Questionnaire's definitions (Morgeson & Humphrey, 2006). Specifically, job complexity is defined as the degree to which work tasks are complicated and difficult to perform, and physical demands is defined as the degree to which work includes physical effort, muscular strength, and muscular endurance. I identified 5,613 potential article titles and abstracts, reviewed 2001 full manuscripts, and ultimately performed a cross-temporal meta-analysis (CTMA) of 121 independent studies (Rudolph et al., 2020; Twenge, 2000; Wegman et al., 2018). The job complexity sample included 72 independent samples and 42,220 subjects; the physical demands sample included 68 independent samples and 62,603 subjects. I directionally aligned study measures, converted study statistics to a common 0-100 percent-of-maximum-possible scale, and weighted study means by inverse variance. I used conventional linear CTMA models and then novel log-linear models, for which constant proportional change implies an exponential trend on the original scale.
All steps of the sample creation and coding procedure were fully AI automated after the initial corpus was assembled from the Web of Science. I built four types of customized tools-a text extractor, a table extractor, table contextualizers, and a symbol mapper-to enhance the performance of a GPT-5.4 Nano API model. A custom prompt engaged with these outputs to read theory, connect construct definitions to operationalizations, apply the inclusion criteria, identify and record study variables, and output the completed CTMA. In this way, the AI performed specialized research work that has heretofore been completed by human meta-analytic coders. To verify this approach, I hand-coded 10% of the initial sample (200 of 2,001 articles). I found over 98% agreement at the code level. In 92% of articles, every human and AI code agreed. 

The overall results indicated that for the typical worker, job complexity increased exponentially over time, whereas physical demands did not change. In support of H1a, time was significantly and positively associated with job complexity (b = .47, SE = .12, R2 = .178, p < .001). Time was not significantly associated with physical demands (b = .10, SE = .16, R2 = .007, p = .510), and H1b was not supported. To test H2a and H2b, I used log-linear models. In support of H2a, time was positively associated with logged job complexity (b = .008, SE = .002, p = .001). Because this coefficient represents constant proportional change, it implies larger absolute increases at later points in time and an exponential increase in job complexity on the original scale. Time was not associated with logged physical demands (b = .004, SE = .005, p = .451), and H2b was not supported. 

These findings both support and challenge prevailing theory on the changing nature of work. The increase in job complexity is consistent with the rise of knowledge work. Yet, the stability of physical demands indicates that work characteristics do not move as a single bundle. That is to say, the decline of some manual occupations does not mean that physical demands have declined within the jobs that remain. Further, routine, simple, and physical work are not interchangeable terms. Time reflects myriad technological, organizational, and societal changes, so these results do not isolate technology as the cause of either trend. Still, my work seeks to reposition technology as an important distal antecedent to work design and provide a historical baseline for evaluating modern AI introductions. Unlike earlier, comparatively deterministic technologies, modern AI can perform complex cognitive work with little human understanding or intervention. This manuscript's AI-automated CTMA is both a contribution to methods and a testament to this potential. Although I carefully reviewed and verified this CTMA, future research using such methods might be conducted without human oversight. If this is the case, the complex work associated with CTMA could be eliminated from the job, leaving only the exceptionally simple task of operating the automated technology.

title: Hedging AI Shocks to Human Capital
abstract:
Human capital constitutes the largest component of wealth for most individuals, yet it is subject to substantial risk arising from technological change and shifting labor demand. These risks may intensify with the diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI), which can rapidly alter the value of specific skills. We study whether equity markets can hedge this form of human capital risk. Departing from the standard approach that models labor income as a single aggregate process, we adopt a granular view of human capital as a portfolio of skills, each generating its own stochastic income stream. This perspective allows us to examine whether innovations in the demand and compensation of individual skills can be partially hedged using traded assets.
Using job postings data from Lightcast covering the United States from 2013 to 2023, we construct monthly time series of labor market outcomes for more than 500 skills. Employing hedonic wage regressions, we estimate skill-level "shadow wages" that control for industry and geographic composition. We combine these with skill posting counts and related measures to capture the labor market value of skills. Innovations in these series-representing unexpected changes in skill demand and remuneration-are extracted using ARIMA and SARIMA models and serve as the targets for hedging.
To hedge these shocks, we construct equity-based projection portfolios designed to capture exposure to technological and broader economic risks. Our primary portfolio captures firms' exposure to AI based on the intensity of AI-related patenting, scaled by market capitalization. We complement this portfolio with market, size, and value projection portfolios following Engle et al. (2020). Using the mimicking portfolio framework of Lamont (2001), we estimate hedge portfolios that offset innovations in skill-level labor market outcomes.
Both in-sample and out-of-sample results indicate economically meaningful hedging performance for a nontrivial subset of skills. Equity portfolios, particularly the AI projection portfolio, explain a meaningful share of the variation in skill wage and demand innovations, and hedge portfolios constructed using rolling estimation windows exhibit significant correlations with future skill shocks.
We evaluate the economic value of these portfolios within a life-cycle consumption-investment framework. Under the empirically estimated skill processes, welfare gains from access to hedge portfolios are modest. However, when we allow for a moderate probability of large skill declines-consistent with potential technological disruptions such as AI adoption-the value of these portfolios increases substantially. Our findings suggest that equity markets can partially hedge human capital risk at the level of individual skills and may provide a mechanism for insuring against labor market disruptions induced by technological change.

title: From AI Activity to Business Performance - Lessons from Scaling AI Inside Large Enterprises
abstract:
Most large companies are now using AI. Far fewer can show it has changed business performance.
Organizations have launched pilots, adopted new tools, stood up governance committees, and invested in data and technology. Many still can't move AI into the workflows and decisions that actually drive revenue, margin, productivity, customer experience, and risk.
This session draws on firsthand experience leading AI, data, and analytics at Kroger and Fidelity Investments, plus current work advising executives across industries. It looks at what separates AI initiatives that scale from initiatives that stay stuck in experimentation.
Scaling AI is an operating and leadership problem more than a technology problem. Value comes from picking the right business problems, redesigning how work gets done, building the organizational conditions for adoption, and putting someone on the hook for the outcome. Technology matters, but it's rarely the reason an initiative succeeds or fails.

Firsthand Lessons from AI at Scale
At Kroger, AI ran across tens of millions of customers, thousands of stores, and a large supply chain, with high-volume decisions being made every day. AI was built into how the business ran, in customer engagement, merchandising, operations, supply chain, and workforce productivity. The AI portfolio became a real contributor to EBITDA, not a side project.
That work also showed the limits of the usual playbook. A technically strong solution didn't automatically produce business value. Use cases had to tie to a real operating need, business leaders had to own the outcome, and adoption had to be built into the process from the start, not bolted on at the end.
At Fidelity Investments, the setting was different but the lessons held. AI and analytics ran inside a highly regulated environment, where trust, risk management, and operational resilience mattered as much as the model itself. Scaling required coordination across business, operations, technology, legal, risk, and compliance, and it required leaders who could tell the difference between an interesting technical possibility and a capability that actually moved decisions, productivity, or performance.
Current advisory work with CEOs, boards, and private equity firms shows the same pattern. Most companies don't lack ideas. They lack a disciplined way to decide which ideas matter, what has to be true for them to work, and how success gets measured. Some have dozens of pilots and no shared view of what any of them are worth. Others start with a vendor or a piece of technology and go looking for a problem afterward. Plenty produce a useful output that never becomes part of how the business actually runs.
That's not a string of implementation failures. It's what happens when AI gets treated as a set of technology projects instead of a change in how the business makes decisions and does work.

Why AI Initiatives Stall
A few problems show up again and again.
Companies measure activity instead of value. Pilot counts, user counts, and licenses show momentum. They don't show business impact.
Ownership stays fuzzy. Technology teams build the capability, but business leaders have to own the result and the changes to how work gets done.
Workflow redesign gets skipped. AI rarely creates value sitting next to an existing process. Someone has to decide how roles, decisions, and handoffs change.
Resources get spread too thin. A handful of consequential use cases, backed by real leadership attention and clear measures, usually beats a wide portfolio of experiments.
Nobody defines what evidence justifies continued investment. Initiatives stay alive because they're promising or because killing them is politically hard. Strong AI portfolios have explicit success measures, decision points, and leaders willing to redirect or kill work that isn't earning its keep.

What Leaders Need to Do Differently
Start with the decisions, workflows, and economics that matter most to the business. Find where AI can meaningfully improve speed, quality, productivity, growth, margin, or risk. Assign clear ownership. Set the measures before you spend the money. Decide what has to change in how the business operates.
Governance should help teams move faster, not just control what they can do. Good governance tells teams where AI can be used, what evidence they need, which risks to manage, and where a human still has to make the call.
Experimentation isn't the enemy. The point is connecting it to a real path toward adoption, operating change, and results you can measure.

Attendee Takeaways
Participants will leave with a practical view of why promising AI initiatives fail to scale, firsthand lessons from running AI inside large, complex companies, a clear line between AI activity and AI value, questions they can use to pressure-test their own initiatives, and a framework connecting use cases, operating change, governance, and financial performance.

Presenter
Todd James is Founder and CEO of Aurora Insights and a former Fortune 25 AI, data, and technology executive. He previously served as Head of AI and Enterprise Data at The Kroger Co. and Chief Data and Technology Officer at 84.51°. Before Kroger, he held senior leadership roles in data, analytics, operations, and strategic transformation during more than 15 years at Fidelity Investments.
Today, he advises boards, CEOs, private equity firms, and senior leadership teams on AI strategy, governance, execution, and value creation.
His perspectives have appeared in Forbes, Fast Company, Harvard Business Review, The Wall Street Journal, and Harvard Data Science Review. He has spoken at the Gartner IT Symposium, the Fast Company Impact Council, The Consumer Goods Forum, the Wells Fargo Consumer & Retail Leadership Forum, and the Özyeğin University AI Platform in Istanbul.
His work focuses on a practical question. How do organizations move AI from pilots and activity into measurable operating and financial results.

title: Publishing to Coordinate: Corporate AI Disclosure and Supply Chain Adoption
abstract: Although large U.S. corporations have systematically withdrawn from scientific research over the past several decades, their AI-related scientific publications have surged in recent years. We explore this phenomenon by proposing that corporate scientific publications serve as a vital coordination mechanism for technology adoption. When AI investments exhibit complementarities, suppliers face uncertainty about others' actions, potentially leading to underinvestment. Scientific publications can resolve this coordination failure by creating common knowledge about a firm's technological commitments-unlike patents, which create exclusionary barriers, or private communication, which cannot coordinate across the supplier network. We find that focal firms' AI publications are positively associated with subsequent supplier AI adoption, with stronger effects under greater coordination challenges: shorter relationship duration, deeper supply chains, greater network centrality, and heavier reliance on foreign suppliers. The publication effect does not extend to competitors. Only publications-not patents-are associated with supplier AI adoption. Our findings identify a novel coordination function of corporate scientific disclosure.

title: AI Exposure, Job Insecurity, and Household Financial Risk-Taking
abstract: We study how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects household financial decisions through labor market insecurity. Exploiting the release of ChatGPT in November 2022 as a plausibly exogenous technological shock, we combine occupation-level and county-level AI exposure measures with individual labor outcomes and household financial data. Workers in more AI-exposed occupations face greater job insecurity: they experience greater layoffs, lower voluntarily quit rates, reduced remote work, and greater resilience on multiple jobs. Households respond by reducing financial risk exposure. In high GenAI exposure counties, households lower equity holdings, especially investments in high-beta stocks, and deleverage by reducing total debt, credit card balances, and mortgage debt. High-exposure counties also experience weaker growth in home-purchase and home-improvement mortgage applications. Together, these findings suggest that AI-driven labor market uncertainty induces conservative financial decisions among exposed households.

title: Your Pecfect Match - Your Date with AI - Setting Boundries with Governance in Business
abstract:
Your Perfect Match: Your Date with AI - Setting Boundaries with Governance in Business
Session Description
AI is the most alluring suitor the business world has seen in decades. It promises efficiency, lightning-fast insights, and unparalleled innovation. But entering a relationship with AI without clear boundaries is a recipe for heartbreak-leading to data leaks, compliance disasters, and algorithmic bias.
How do you move past the honeymoon phase and build a stable, long-term partnership? You introduce Governance.
This session strips away the dry, technical jargon of AI policy and reframes it through a relatable lens: dating. Just like any healthy relationship, a successful business adoption of artificial intelligence requires clear expectations, mutual respect, and firm boundaries. We will explore how a robust AI governance framework serves as the ultimate alignment tool for your business. When every department-from IT and legal to marketing and operations operate under the same set of relationship rules, you eliminate silos, mitigate risk, and ensure that your technology investments directly support your core strategic goals. It's not about playing hard to get; it's about keeping everyone on the same page.
The Format: An Interactive, Dynamic Deep Dive
Forget death-by-PowerPoint. This session is designed to keep you engaged from start to finish using a mix of real-world corporate case studies and interactive scenarios.
• The "Speed Dating" Warm-up: We will quickly analyze different AI tools (Generative AI, predictive analytics, LLMs) and the unique corporate "red flags" each one brings to the table.
• The Alignment Check-In: An interactive exercise mapping out how unauthorized AI usage creates friction between innovation-hungry teams and risk-averse legal departments-and how governance acts as the bridge.
• Audience Live Polls: You will vote on how you would handle tricky compliance, ethics, and data privacy dilemmas in real-time, seeing how your peers handle organizational alignment.
What Attendees Will Experience
When you walk into the room, you will experience an upbeat, high-energy environment that treats AI governance as a strategic enabler rather than a bureaucratic roadblock.
You will be guided through the practical steps of building an AI Governance Playbook that synchronizes your entire workforce. You'll experience what it looks like to achieve organizational harmony, learning how to bridge the gap between executive leadership's strategic vision and the technical realities of front-line staff. Expect lively discussions, highly relatable analogies, and a clear roadmap that transforms disparate departmental goals into a unified corporate action plan. Participants will walk away with a practical playbook to turn abstract AI ethics into concrete corporate action, ensuring your technology investments deliver a stable, long-term partnership.
3 Key Takeaways
• 1. The Red Flag Checklist: How to audit incoming AI tools for compliance, security, and data privacy risks before you integrate them into your workflow.
• 2. An Organizational Alignment Blueprint: Frameworks to establish cross-functional AI steering committees that unite IT, legal, and business units under a shared vision.
• 3. The Long-Term Commitment Strategy: Tools for continuous monitoring and policy updates, ensuring your AI systems remain ethical, unbiased, and permanently aligned with your evolving business objectives.

title: AI as a Research Collaborator: Autonomous and Auditable Hypothesis Discovery in Finance
abstract:
We study whether an AI research multi-agent system can autonomously execute the hypothesis-discovery loop while operating within a rigorous, human-designed scientific environment. We embed a large language model in a research laboratory comprising structured accounting data, a symbolic language of interpretable financial formulas, an automated validation layer, and a fixed empirical evaluation pipeline. Human researchers define the economic ontology, methodological constraints, and standards of evidence; the AI agent system independently generates, tests, and revises hypotheses in response to standardized empirical feedback.

The agent searches for interactions among core economic themes, including profitability, investment, valuation, and quality, and updates its proposals over successive generations. Across eight theme pairs and seven generations, it proposes and evaluates 280 candidate asset-pricing signals in a microcap-excluded universe. Of these, 159 pass a conventional significance screen in the predicted direction, and 38 survive multivariate horse races designed to identify signals with independent predictive content. We then subject the surviving signals to a comprehensive battery of modern asset-pricing tests, including multiple-testing corrections, multi-model factor spanning, and novelty comparisons against 209 published anomalies. A small set continues to provide genuinely incremental information under the strictest filters.

Beyond the specific findings, the project offers a transparent and auditable architecture for human-AI collaboration in scientific discovery. It illustrates a division of labor in which humans design the research environment and govern standards of validity, while AI autonomously explores a large hypothesis space and learns from evidence. The modular architecture can also serve as a foundation for multi-agent research systems in which specialized agents generate theories, critique hypotheses, conduct empirical tests, and synthesize results. More broadly, the study demonstrates how agentic AI can expand the frontier of business research without sacrificing interpretability, empirical discipline, or human judgment.

title: When Machines Think Fast: A Behavioral Economics Test of AI
abstract: We test whether large language models reproduce or correct for fourteen well-documented human behavioral biases. We administer each canonical experiment to ChatGPT and construct a pseudo-panel of responses from each iteration. The biases we examine span belief-formation tasks (anchoring, conjunction fallacy), preference-based tasks (framing effects, prospect-theoretic risk attitudes, present bias, mental accounting, sunk-cost reasoning, the endowment effect, the disposition effect, and naïve diversification), and intertemporal and social-choice problems (myopic loss aversion, save-more-tomorrow commitments, the house money effect, and the ultimatum game). On eight of fourteen tasks, the model behaves in a manner consistent with the rational benchmark. On the remaining six tasks (framing of the Asian disease problem, the conjunction fallacy, mental accounting, the house money effect, naive diversification, and the endowment effect), the model exhibits a directional bias that mirrors the human pattern, but in every case the magnitude of the deviation is smaller than the human benchmark. We interpret these results as evidence that large language models can serve as effective debiasing decision aids in many settings. We show that residual biases inherited from training on human-generated text concentrate predictably in tasks involving valuation, framing, and intuitive judgments about likelihood.

title: Beyond the Virtual Receptionist: Lessons in AI Readiness and Responsible Scale
abstract:
Attendees will learn a five-question readiness test for deciding whether an AI initiative is ready to move from experimentation to responsible scale: outcome, process, data, judgment, and accountability.

The session shares a real client case: a connected virtual-receptionist, customer-response, and lead-management workflow. What worked was treating AI as one piece of a larger system, not an isolated tool, and classifying decisions upfront as AI-supported, human-approved, or human-only. What didn't work initially was assuming the workflow was ready before ownership, data handling, and escalation paths were defined. In hindsight, that groundwork should have come before automation, not after.

Attendees leave with a repeatable way to evaluate their own workflows, plus a one-page Readiness Map they can use to identify risks and next steps before scaling a pilot. The session closes with discussion of how these lessons transfer across industries and organization sizes.

title: When heavy metal meets generative AI: Theoretical promise vs. organizational reality
abstract:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is emerging as a general-purpose technology that is reshaping innovation processes, supporting activities from early-stage discovery to concept prototyping and refinement (Calvino et al., 2025; Füller et al., 2022; Gama & Magistretti, 2025). It is expected to reduce development time and cost, improve innovation quality, and lower barriers to participation in innovation activities (Bilgram & Laarmann, 2023; Wang & Wu, 2025). However, early evidence suggests a gap between these expectations and their systematic realization in practice, particularly within traditional manufacturing industries (Hughes et al., 2026). This shifts attention from whether firms adopt GenAI to where and under what conditions GenAI can effectively be integrated into new product development (NPD). 
We investigate these questions through two in-depth case studies of global manufacturing companies in Finland. Both firms are multinational corporations that depend on R&D for competitive advantage, giving them strong incentives to adopt frontier technologies like GenAI. Yet, their NPD processes span years, involve millions of euros in investment, and carry high costs of error. Their products consist of hundreds of interdependent components, making expert judgment and accumulated historical knowledge essential. This combination of technological ambition and operational complexity makes them a revealing setting for studying how R&D professionals integrate GenAI into innovation work.
We conducted 16 interviews with R&D experts, complemented with observations and documents collected during a years long collaboration between the case companies and the research team. Following Gioia et al. (2013), we conducted an inductive analysis of the material, iteratively discussing first-order codes, grouping them into second-order themes, and arriving at aggregate dimensions. We validated our results with the R&D management teams of the case companies.
Our results show that in these global manufacturing companies, GenAI use is currently concentrated in peripheral, low-risk activities such as editing language and summarizing reports, with limited impact on core innovation outcomes. We explain this pattern as a consequence of socio-technical misalignment between GenAI and the conditions of complex manufacturing NPD. More specifically, we identify four socio-technical conditions that lead to GenAI remaining concentrated in peripheral tasks: organizational arrangements, task structure, user judgments and practices, and technological capabilities and constraints. Internal company policies restrict tool choice and data access; performance metrics prioritize immediate delivery over experimentation; and cross-functional silos limit the availability of structured, reusable knowledge. The GenAI tools themselves are further constrained by fragmented internal data, restricted access to external knowledge sources, and limited integration into engineering and simulation environments.
Our study makes two contributions to knowledge on GenAI use in NPD. First, we highlight the importance of task structure as a boundary condition for GenAI's role in innovation. Existing studies largely focus on innovation tasks that are relatively standalone, where design decisions are easily reversible, and errors have limited downstream consequences. In such contexts, GenAI can readily support exploration, synthesis, and ideation (Bouschery et al., 2023). We show that its integration becomes far more uncertain, when design decisions are tightly interconnected, difficult to reverse, and costly to correct once development has progressed (Thomke, 1998; Ulrich, 1995). In such settings, where innovation outcomes unfold over long time horizons, GenAI's contribution is limited because locally plausible outputs must still be evaluated for their system-wide implications, and current tools do not reliably capture the interdependencies and downstream risks that define complex manufacturing NPD.
Second, we challenge practitioner-oriented accounts that emphasize individual-level capability building, such as prompt engineering and AI literacy, as primary levers for unlocking GenAI value (e.g., Chui et al., 2023). While such efforts are helpful to some degree (Dell'Acqua et al., 2026), they alone do not resolve the constraints identified in this study. We show instead that embedding GenAI into complex NPD is as a socio-technical alignment challenge, where individual use is jointly constrained by organizational structures, tool limitations, and task characteristics. For firms in traditional manufacturing, value-adding integration of GenAI into NPD therefore likely depends less on marginal capability upgrades than broader organizational redesign.

title: The Impact of Generative AI on Skill Demand
abstract:
The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how firms organize work. Unlike earlier forms of artificial intelligence that were typically deployed for specialized prediction or analytical tasks, GenAI can generate and transform text, images, code, and other information through natural-language interfaces. These capabilities make GenAI accessible across a broad range of occupations and functions, extending its influence beyond technical roles. As firms incorporate GenAI into daily operations, a central labor-market question is not only whether employment expands or contracts, but also which worker capabilities become more valuable. Understanding the potential changes in skill demand is crucial, as mismatches between workers' capabilities and firms' requirements may not only compromise workers' employability but also limit the pool of qualified candidates available to firms, creating labor supply-side constraints (Acemoglu and Restrepo 2019).
 To examine how skill requirements evolve in GenAI-enabled work, we use AI literacy as a conceptual framework. Defined as a set of competencies that enable individuals to use, critically evaluate, communicate and collaborate with AI technologies (Long and Magerko 2020), AI literacy encompasses the range of capabilities that are central to harnessing AI's potential (Ng et al. 2021, Chiu et al. 2024). Drawing on the AI literacy framework, we distinguish among three complementary skill domains. Technical skills refer to skills that reflect ability to use AI and digital tools and technical knowledge in AI-enabled workplaces. Evaluative skills reflect ability to assess, interpret and exercise judgment in AI-enabled workplaces. Human skills reflect ability to communicate, coordinate and collaborate effectively in AI-enabled workplace. AI literacy provides a useful lens for our setting because GenAI broadens AI-related work beyond technical tasks to include evaluation, communication, and coordination (Dell'Acqua et al. 2023, Jarrahi et al. 2023). 
 However, the effect of GenAI adoption on these skill domains is ambiguous. On one hand, GenAI's ability to process human instructions may allow firms to automate nonroutine cognitive work that previously depended on human judgment and interpretation. Firms may therefore reduce demand for AI literacy skills when GenAI performs tasks otherwise requiring workers' capabilities. On the other hand, generative models remain prone to hallucinations, inconsistency, and inappropriate outputs, potentially increasing the need for cognitive engagement (Alkaissi and McFarlane 2023, Ferrara 2023). Firms may consequently value evaluative skills for assessing AI outputs and human skills for interpreting, communicating, and integrating them into organizational processes. 
 To examine these changes, we construct a firm-quarter panel of U.S. public firms from 2021 to 2025 by integrating corporate disclosures with labor-market data. We identify technology adoption using 10-K filings and conference call transcripts. Using large language models, we classify firms into three groups: GenAI Adopters, which disclose GenAI adoption; Traditional AI-only Adopters, which disclose traditional AI adoption but not GenAI; and Non-Adopters, which disclose neither type of adoption. We link these classifications to 113 million job postings and construct firm-quarter measures of demand for technical, evaluative, and human skills. Our empirical design uses staggered difference-in-differences estimators that account for variation in adoption timing. We compare GenAI Adopters with Non-Adopters to estimate the overall effect of GenAI adoption and with Traditional AI-only Adopters to isolate changes associated specifically with GenAI.
 Our findings show that GenAI adoption produces a shift in demand toward evaluative and human skills. Relative to Non-Adopters, GenAI Adopters increase the share of job postings requiring evaluative and human skills, indicating that these capabilities become relevant across a broader range of positions. They also increase the average number of evaluative and human skills required within postings, suggesting that firms deepen these requirements at the job level. In contrast, demand for technical skills does not increase significantly along either margin. The same pattern emerges when GenAI Adopters are compared with Traditional AI-only Adopters. The changes therefore do not merely reflect a broader trend toward digitalization or AI adoption. Rather, GenAI introduces a distinct reorientation of skill demand toward capabilities that enable workers to assess, interpret, communicate, and act on AI-generated information. Additional analyses reveal that GenAI adoption also changes how skill domains are combined. Following adoption, firms increasingly seek workers whose positions require technical, evaluative, and human skills together, rather than demanding these capabilities in isolation. GenAI therefore encourages firms to seek integrated skill profiles in which workers can interact with AI tools, evaluate their outputs, and translate those outputs into coordinated organizational action. We further find that postings requiring all three skill domains are associated with wage premiums, indicating that firms place economic value on these complementary capabilities. Heterogeneity analyses show that increases in evaluative and human skill demand are especially pronounced in entry-level positions. Early-career workers may therefore face strong pressure to develop judgment, communication, and coordination capabilities alongside technical familiarity.
 The results remain robust across matched-sample estimations, stricter definitions of GenAI adoption, placebo tests, alternative measures of skill demand, and specifications addressing differences between adopting and non-adopting firms. The conclusion remains consistent: GenAI adoption broadens and deepens demand for evaluative and human capabilities without generating a comparable increase in stand-alone technical skill demand.
 This study contributes to research on AI and the future of work in several ways. First, it extends the task-based view of technological change by showing that GenAI affects not only employment levels or task exposure but also the capabilities firms require from workers. Second, it advances research on AI-related skills by moving beyond a narrow emphasis on technical expertise. As AI becomes easier to access through natural-language interfaces, the complementary value of critical evaluation, judgment, communication, and collaboration increases. Third, by comparing GenAI Adopters with both Non-Adopters and Traditional AI-only Adopters, the study isolates the distinctive implications of GenAI from the effects of earlier AI technologies. Finally, the study provides practical guidance for workforce development. Workers preparing for GenAI-enabled workplaces may benefit less from focusing exclusively on technical proficiency and more from cultivating broader AI literacy that combines technological familiarity with evaluative judgment and human interaction. Firms, policymakers, and educational institutions should therefore design training and curricula that help workers assess AI outputs, solve ambiguous problems, communicate insights, and collaborate effectively in AI-mediated environments.

title: When AI Joins the Crowd: Human Evaluation of AI-Generated Annotations in Crowdchecking
abstract:
Motivation. 
Social media platforms have increasingly adopted crowdsourced fact-checking systems (henceforth crowdchecking) that leverage the collective judgment of platform users to combat misinformation. Following the lead of X's Community Notes program, Meta recently replaced its third-party fact-checking program with its own crowdchecking system, and other major platforms, including YouTube and TikTok, are piloting similar initiatives. At its core, crowdchecking constitutes a multi-stage fact-checking pipeline that begins with note writing, in which contributors identify potentially misleading posts and compose fact-checking annotations (notes). Submitted notes then enter a crowd evaluation stage, where raters assess their accuracy and helpfulness, and a bridge-based algorithm aggregates the ratings to determine whether a note receives sufficient support from raters with diverse perspectives to become public. Note writing, however, is an inherently complex and cognitively demanding task. The writer must gather evidence, appraise the reliability of competing sources, and synthesize the verified material into a high-quality annotation, which has proven difficult for human contributors to sustain. For example, nearly three years after Community Notes' rollout, the system had attracted more than 447,000 note writers, yet each had produced no more than five notes, with productivity declining from more than four notes per quarter to no more than one.

Against this backdrop, X launched the AI Note Writer program, enabling AI-generated fact-checking annotations to enter the crowd evaluation stage alongside human-written ones, with every AI-generated note carrying a visible AI identity label. Yet producing a fact-check is not mere content generation or summarization, but a demanding form of information augmentation, requiring real-time evidence retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and rigorous synthesis-capabilities that remain vulnerable to hallucinations and reasoning errors. Moreover, the AI identity label may distort raters' evaluations irrespective of actual note quality, whether through algorithm aversion that suppresses genuinely helpful notes or algorithm appreciation that allows inaccurate notes to slip through. Therefore, the viability of this AI-assisted approach hinges on how AI-generated notes are evaluated by human evaluators and what drives the evaluation. Accordingly, we ask: How are AI-generated notes evaluated relative to human-written notes, and what mechanisms, quality or identity, drive these evaluation outcomes?

Methodology. 
We leverage X's Community Notes as our research context, monitoring notes composed over a 130-day window and collecting detailed information on note content, rater composition, publication status, and daily metadata on associated tweets and their authors. The resulting dataset comprises 28,612 users, 75,098 tweets, and 93,041 notes. We estimate note-level regressions with a rich set of controls at the note, tweet, and user levels, along with tweet-date and user fixed effects. To address unobserved confounding, we conduct an instrumental variable analysis exploiting the note request feature. Because AI note writers can only compose notes on tweets that have received at least one note request, whereas human writers face no such restriction, and because request information is unavailable to raters during evaluation, note requests provide plausibly exogenous variation in AI authorship. We further validate our findings through entropy balancing, propensity score matching, fractional and conditional logit specifications, and panel analyses.

To disentangle the quality effect from the identity effect and strengthen internal validity, we conduct an IRB-approved randomized field experiment on Community Notes. All experimental notes are generated by a custom-designed agentic AI note-writing system and randomly assigned to either an AILabel condition, submitted through AI note writer accounts and displaying the AI identity label, or a NoLabel condition, submitted through human note writer accounts with no such label. The experiment is deployed in two phases to introduce variation in note quality. Phase 1 reflects the AI's unrestricted performance, while phase 2 constrains output to match human-written notes in length, source link count, and overall fact-checking quality.

Findings. 
AI-generated notes receive average ratings approximately 9.61 percentage points higher than human-written notes, translating to a relative increase of about 15.3% over the sample average. This favorable reception carries through to algorithmic aggregation, where AI-generated notes are 77.1% more likely to become public relative to the baseline mean probability of 0.1. A comprehensive content analysis traces this favorable reception to quality. Specifically, AI-generated notes outperform human-written ones not only in writing quality, such as grammar, readability, lexical diversity, cohesion, and referential clarity, but also in fact-checking quality, including source provision, claim addressiveness, and provision of important context. These patterns are corroborated by raters' optional self-reported quality assessments, yielding convergent evidence from human perspectives.

The experimental results further reveal that within each phase, holding quality constant, differences between the AILabel and NoLabel groups are statistically insignificant for both average ratings and publication likelihood. In contrast, holding the identity label fixed, both outcomes decline significantly from phase 1 to phase 2. Hence, the favorable evaluation outcomes are driven primarily by the higher quality of AI-generated notes, whereas the AI identity label itself exerts no significant effect.

Implications. 
This study provides the first empirical evidence on the integration of generative AI into large-scale, human-in-the-loop fact-checking systems. We find that AI and humans collaborate remarkably well across the entire crowdchecking pipeline. AI can initiate a scalable fact-checking process by drafting high-quality annotations despite the augmentative demands of the task, while human raters prove able to discern and reward these high-quality fact-checks rather than being swayed by AI identity. For platforms, our findings deliver reassuring evidence on both unresolved concerns surrounding AI integration and highlight AI's marked productivity advantage, with each AI writer generating roughly 241 times the notes of its human counterpart. For policymakers navigating intensifying demands for human oversight of AI systems, our study points to an alternative to expert-centric review, namely shifting the evaluation of AI-generated content to a collective decision-making process distributed across a diverse crowd. Overall, this study highlights that AI can be entrusted with producing high-quality fact-checks while a diverse human crowd can reliably screen them on their merits rather than their provenance, thereby offering a scalable model for the upstream human oversight of generative AI in high-stakes domains.

title: Artificial Intelligence or Artificial Hype? Evidence from Corporate Name Changes
abstract: I document AI-themed corporate name changes in U.S. equity markets since 2021 and examine their market and financing consequences. I identify 58 such name changes, of which 35 are non-M&A pure rebrands; the rebranders are markedly younger and smaller than the typical Compustat firm and concentrated in technology-adjacent industries. An event study on the 35 non-M&A rebrands shows that the market reacted positively to the name-change announcement, with statistically significant mean cumulative abnormal returns of 21% to 29% over short announcement windows that are robust to outlier trims, a momentum check, a firm-specific market-model adjustment, and a non-AI name-change control-group adjustment. Relative to non-AI name changers, AI rebranders raise significantly more external capital after the rebrand, concentrated in equity, consistent with using AI rebranding to create a more favorable environment for raising equity capital.

title: Ready, but Wary: How HR Professionals Perceive Prescriptive Analytics and Agentic AI
abstract:
Organizations are rapidly moving from generative AI experimentation toward more advanced systems capable of recommending actions and autonomously executing multistep workplace tasks. Yet scaling AI requires more than technical infrastructure. It also depends on whether employees are prepared to use these systems, critically evaluate their outputs, and recognize when human intervention is necessary. These questions are especially consequential in human resources, where AI-supported recommendations and actions may affect employees and employment-related decisions. This study examines the human and organizational foundations of AI readiness by investigating what shapes HR professionals' intentions to use AI and whether their perceptions change as systems move from decision support toward autonomous action.

The study had two objectives. First, it examined whether established technology-adoption and workplace frameworks explain HR professionals' intentions to use AI. The proposed model integrated constructs from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology and the Job Demands-Resources model with trust, perceptions of ethical AI practices, collaborative AI literacy, and collaborative AI metacognition. Second, the study directly compared HR professionals' perceptions of prescriptive analytics, which recommends courses of action while leaving execution to humans, and agentic AI, which can autonomously plan and execute multistep tasks. The comparison addressed trust, ethical concerns, willingness to use, perceived usefulness, and the need for human oversight.

A cross-sectional survey with a within-person comparative component was administered to HR professionals working in the United States. Following eligibility screening and the removal of incomplete responses, the final sample included 60 participants representing multiple HR roles, industries, and organization sizes. Seventy percent reported that their organizations currently used some form of AI in HR. Established multi-item measures were used to assess technology-acceptance factors, job demands and resources, trust, perceptions of ethical AI practices, collaborative AI literacy, collaborative AI metacognition, and behavioral intention. Multiple regression analysis evaluated the combined and unique relationships between ten predictors and behavioral intention to use AI. One-sample t-tests evaluated whether participants' comparative ratings of prescriptive analytics and agentic AI differed significantly from the scale midpoint of "about the same."

Participants reported a generally strong intention to use AI in their HR work (M = 5.55, SD = 0.89). However, the ten-predictor regression model, based on 54 complete cases, was not statistically significant, F(10, 43) = 1.43, p = .196. Although the model accounted for 25% of the observed variance in behavioral intention, its adjusted R² was .07, indicating limited explanatory power after accounting for the number of predictors. None of the individual predictors reached statistical significance.

Two nonsignificant patterns may nevertheless be useful for hypothesis development and future research. Collaborative AI literacy had a negative coefficient in the behavioral-intention model (estimate = −.30, p = .071), contrary to the hypothesized positive relationship. This pattern raises the possibility that greater understanding of AI could be associated with more critical or cautious adoption orientations rather than greater enthusiasm. Perceptions of ethical AI practices had a positive coefficient (estimate = .27, p = .080), suggesting a potential relationship between employees' perceptions of transparent, accountable, and fair AI practices and their intentions to engage with AI. Because neither relationship reached the prespecified significance threshold, these patterns should not be interpreted as confirmed effects.

The comparison of AI system types revealed a particularly important readiness challenge. Participants perceived agentic AI as raising significantly greater ethical concerns than prescriptive analytics (M = 3.81, SD = 1.03), t(57) = 5.97, p < .001. They also perceived agentic AI as requiring significantly greater human oversight (M = 3.60, SD = 1.14), t(57) = 4.04, p < .001. Nevertheless, participants did not perceive statistically significant differences between the technologies in trust, perceived usefulness, or willingness to use. Thus, HR professionals in this sample recognized the heightened ethical and oversight demands associated with autonomous systems without necessarily viewing those systems as less trustworthy, less useful, or less desirable to use.

These exploratory findings suggest that established technology-acceptance constructs may not, by themselves, fully explain readiness for advanced AI within this sample. As AI becomes more autonomous, adoption may also depend on how employees interpret system autonomy, ethical risk, accountability, and the appropriate boundaries of human control. The findings further complicate the assumption that greater AI literacy necessarily produces greater adoption. Employees who understand AI more deeply may be better positioned to recognize its limitations, question its outputs, and demand appropriate safeguards.

For organizations seeking to scale AI, the findings support governance practices differentiated according to the autonomy and risk of the system rather than a uniform policy for all AI applications. Agentic systems may require stronger human-in-the-loop or human-on-the-loop controls, explicit decision rights, escalation procedures, and documented accountability. Organizations should also move beyond basic tool training toward critical AI literacy that prepares employees to evaluate outputs, calibrate trust, recognize ethical risks, and determine when human judgment must prevail.

The study's cross-sectional design, small convenience sample, reliance on self-reported perceptions, and limited statistical power restrict causal inference and generalizability. Replication using larger and more representative samples, longitudinal designs, and qualitative or mixed-method approaches is needed. Despite these limitations, the study provides early evidence that scaling increasingly autonomous AI is not solely a technology implementation challenge. It is also a human-readiness, governance, and organizational-design challenge.

This research was completed as a graduate thesis through an independent study in the Master of Human Resource Management program at The Ohio State University's Fisher College of Business. Dr. Kate Keeler, Associate Professor of Management and Human Resources, served as the thesis advisor. The study examines HR professionals' perceptions of artificial intelligence, prescriptive analytics, and agentic AI, with particular attention to adoption, trust, ethics, AI literacy, and human oversight.

title: AI-Ready Graduates, AI-Ready Organizations? Lessons from Working Professionals
abstract:
Graduate business programs are under growing pressure to prepare students for an AI-enabled workplace. But many graduate students are already in that workplace. Current and recently graduated Master of Business Administration (MBA) and Master of Human Resource Management (MHRM) students are simultaneously learning about artificial intelligence in the classroom, experimenting with it in their academic work, and applying those capabilities within organizations at very different stages of AI readiness.

This moderated panel brings together current and recently graduated MBA and MHRM students who have transferred AI learning from graduate school into their professional work. Their collective experience spans banking and financial services, food and beverage, public-entity consulting, the federal government, gas and power, technology and software infrastructure, and higher education. Some panelists work in cutting-edge, AI-forward organizations, where they help design and build AI agents and applications for businesses, public entities, and government agencies. Others work in highly regulated environments or organizations that are still establishing their AI strategies, policies, and approved uses.

This range of experience will allow panelists to compare how technical capability, regulation, data sensitivity, risk tolerance, organizational maturity, and workplace culture shape whether and how graduate-level AI learning can be applied at work. Rather than treating AI education as an abstract curriculum question, the panel will examine what happens when working professionals bring newly developed AI capabilities back to their jobs, teams, clients, and organizations.

Panelists will discuss how structured exposure to AI during their MBA or MHRM programs influenced their confidence, judgment, productivity, and approach to problem-solving. They will share specific examples of using AI to support research, analysis, communication, process improvement, decision preparation, learning, and human resource management. Panelists who develop AI solutions will also offer insight into what it takes to move from personally using an AI tool to building AI agents and applications that must operate reliably within businesses and government environments.

The discussion will distinguish between using AI to complete work faster and using it to improve the quality, depth, or creativity of professional thinking. It will also examine the difference between individual AI proficiency and organizational AI readiness. An employee may know how to use AI responsibly but still work within an organization that lacks approved tools, governance structures, technical infrastructure, leadership support, or clear expectations.

The panel will be moderated by Vasiliki Stamouli, a recent MHRM graduate (Class of 2025) and Research Fellow in Applied AI in HR at Experience Management Institute. Her graduate research examines HR professionals' perceptions of artificial intelligence, prescriptive analytics, and agentic AI, including adoption, trust, ethical concerns, AI literacy, and human oversight. She is also a co-author of two peer-reviewed journal articles published in 2026 that examine applied uses of AI and machine learning in education. This research background allows her to connect panelists' experiences to broader questions about applied AI, responsible human-AI collaboration, and organizational readiness.

In her applied work, Stamouli contributed to the development of the Prompt Quality Framework, a proprietary six-pillar methodology informed by AI safety research, human evaluation practices, and educational frameworks. She used the framework to help author and validate a library of more than 1,900 prompts across HR, IT, finance, accounting, grant writing, and leadership communication. She has also designed and delivered evidence-based AI curricula, case studies, workshops, and technical training to more than 200 HR and education professionals.

Her experience extends beyond AI training and prompt development. She has contributed to AI-supported job evaluation, compensation modeling, labor market analysis, public-sector workforce planning, and the development, testing, and quality assurance of AI-powered applications. This combination of peer-reviewed research, AI education, application development, and consulting positions her to facilitate a technically informed discussion while ensuring that each panelist's distinct perspective is fully explored.

The moderated discussion will address questions including:
-How did learning about AI in an MBA or MHRM program change the way panelists use it at work?
-Which classroom experiences transferred most effectively to professional settings?
-Did AI learning primarily improve speed, or did it also improve analysis, creativity, and decision quality?
-How does developing AI agents and applications differ from using existing AI tools?
-What additional safeguards are required when AI solutions are designed for businesses, public entities, or government agencies?
-How do regulation, data sensitivity, organizational mission, and risk tolerance affect AI use across industries?
-What happens when employees' AI capabilities advance more quickly than their organizations' policies and infrastructure?
-How have panelists navigated confidentiality, accuracy, bias, transparency, human oversight, and accountability?
-Has greater AI literacy made panelists more enthusiastic about AI, more cautious, or both?
-What should graduate programs and employers do differently to prepare professionals for responsible human-AI collaboration?

The panel is intentionally designed to surface multiple perspectives rather than promote a single model of AI adoption. Participants include professionals actively developing AI agents and applications, professionals applying AI within their existing roles, and professionals navigating organizations that are still defining acceptable-use boundaries. Their experiences will allow the audience to examine how similar AI capabilities may be developed in one setting, encouraged in another, restricted elsewhere, and governed differently depending on the organization's mission, technical maturity, risk profile, data environment, and level of AI readiness.

Attendees will leave with a cross-industry understanding of how AI learning in MBA and MHRM programs transfers into professional practice; how organizational context enables or constrains that transfer; how building AI agents differs from using existing AI tools; and what universities and employers can do to develop an AI-ready workforce. The discussion will include successful applications, barriers, failed experiments, limitations, and unresolved questions.

The panel will demonstrate that scaling AI is not simply a matter of acquiring technology. It requires professionals who can think critically alongside AI, graduate programs that cultivate responsible and practical AI capabilities, and organizations prepared to support, govern, and learn from employee experimentation and innovation.

title: Bond with Social Bot: A Hidden Markov Model of Parasocial Relationship Dynamics in Human-AI Interaction
abstract: With the advancement of large language models (LLMs), modern AI systems have developed sophisticated conversational and social interaction capabilities. Platforms increasingly deploy these systems not only for functional task completion but also for social engagement, such as providing emotional support and conducting casual conversations with users. This expanding social role raises a critical operational question for platforms: how should AI responses be configured to cultivate relational bonds between users and the bot, and by extension, between users and the platform? We address this question by modeling the dynamic evolution of users' parasocial relationships with an AI bot as a function of the bot's response characteristics, which we treat as controllable operational design parameters. Drawing on the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) framework and parasocial relationship theory, we develop a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) where users' latent parasocial relationship states govern their observed interaction choices and AI response characteristics drive transitions between states. We estimate the model on a longitudinal panel of user interactions with Grok, the built-in AI bot on X (formerly Twitter). We find that greater anthropomorphism and social intelligence in the bot's responses significantly increase the probability that users transition to higher parasocial relationship states, while greater linguistic complexity and a more analytical style significantly reduce it. These effects are most pronounced among users in the low parasocial relationship state, suggesting that the bot's communicative characteristics are especially consequential before meaningful relational bonds have formed. Design simulations identify social intelligence as the most influential operational lever for fostering sustained social engagement. Our findings provide implications for calibrating AI response strategies to cultivate users' relational engagement.

title: Organisational Readiness for Artificial Intelligence in South Africa's Lodging Industry: A Managerial Perspective
abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the hospitality industry by transforming service delivery, operational processes, managerial decision-making, and the nature of work. Despite growing global investment in AI, relatively little is known about how hospitality organisations in emerging economies evaluate their readiness for AI adoption and prepare strategically for its implementation. This study addresses this gap by exploring organisational readiness for AI from the perspectives of senior and middle-level managers within South Africa's lodging industry. Specifically, the study investigates how managers evaluate the strategic value of AI, navigate adoption decisions, identify factors influencing AI adoption, anticipate how AI may transform organisational roles and work tasks, and prepare their workforce through upskilling and reskilling initiatives to support successful AI implementation.
The study is informed by Institutional Theory and Rogers' Diffusion of Innovation Theory. Together, these theoretical perspectives provide a comprehensive lens for understanding how institutional pressures and managerial perceptions shape organisational readiness and influence AI adoption decisions within the hospitality industry. Institutional Theory explains how regulatory, competitive, and normative pressures influence organisational responses to AI, while Diffusion of Innovation Theory provides insight into how managers perceive the relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, and adoption of AI technologies. The integration of these complementary theories offers a richer understanding of the organisational and managerial processes underpinning AI adoption within the lodging sector.
This study employs a generic qualitative research design. Data collection is currently underway through eighteen semi-structured interviews with senior and middle-level managers from hotels, lodges, and Airbnb establishments across South Africa. The data will be analysed using thematic analysis to identify patterns relating to organisational readiness for AI adoption, the strategic value of AI, barriers to implementation, workforce transformation, and the organisational capabilities required to support successful AI integration. As data collection is ongoing, preliminary findings will be presented at the conference.
The anticipated findings are expected to provide context-specific insights into how hospitality managers in an emerging economy evaluate organisational readiness for AI adoption, navigate strategic adoption decisions, respond to barriers to implementation, anticipate shifts in organisational roles and work tasks, and develop workforce upskilling and reskilling strategies in preparation for AI-enabled transformation. The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on AI adoption and within the hospitality industry by providing empirical evidence from an emerging economy and extending current understanding of organisational readiness for AI adoption. By integrating Institutional Theory and Diffusion of Innovation Theory, the study offers both theoretical and practical contributions to the literature on AI adoption, organisation readiness and strategic management. Furthermore, the findings are expected to provide evidence-based guidance for hospitality managers, policymakers, employees, and other industry stakeholders seeking to implement AI responsibly while strengthening organisational preparedness, workforce resilience, and long-term competitive advantage.

title: Testing a Hybrid Sensemaking Framework for Ethical Decision-Making in AI Leadership
abstract:
As organizations increasingly integrate artificial intelligence into products, services, and operational processes, leaders are being asked to make decisions with significant ethical implications in environments characterized by uncertainty, conflicting stakeholder demands, evolving regulation, and incomplete information. Although the AI ethics literature has generated substantial agreement around principles such as transparency, fairness, and non-maleficence, organizations continue to struggle with translating those principles into practical decision-making processes. In many cases, leaders are not constrained by a lack of ethical intentions but by a lack of tools for navigating ambiguity when competing obligations, business pressures, and uncertain consequences collide.

This study addresses that challenge by developing and testing a Hybrid Sensemaking Framework designed to improve ethical decision-making in AI leadership contexts. The framework integrates two complementary streams of scholarship. First, it builds on Weick's theory of organizational sensemaking, which explains how individuals construct meaning under conditions of uncertainty through processes such as retrospection, enactment, social interpretation, cue extraction, and plausible reasoning. Second, it incorporates the leader cognition and ethical decision-making work of Mumford and colleagues, which provides a structured process for problem identification, information gathering, mental model formation, hypothesis generation, implementation, and ongoing evaluation. Together, these perspectives produce a practical framework intended to help leaders move from ethical uncertainty to defensible action.

The resulting model combines the interpretive strengths of sensemaking with a structured decision-making process that can be taught, practiced, and embedded within organizational workflows. Rather than assuming ethical dilemmas can be resolved through fixed rules or compliance checklists, the framework recognizes ambiguity as an inherent condition of contemporary AI development. It therefore seeks to help leaders identify competing stakeholder interests, interpret relevant signals, generate plausible courses of action, evaluate trade-offs, and revise decisions as new information emerges. The framework further emphasizes three foundational ethical principles frequently cited in AI governance literature: transparency, fairness, and non-maleficence.

To evaluate the effectiveness of the framework, this research employed a randomized controlled trial using a difference-in-differences design. A sample of 160 undergraduate business students was randomly assigned to either a control condition or an intervention condition. Participants in the control group received approximately thirty minutes of general leadership training unrelated to ethics or AI. Participants in the intervention group received training on the Hybrid Sensemaking Framework and its application to ethical decision-making in AI product development contexts. Both groups completed pre-training and post-training assessments involving AI-related ethical dilemmas.

The study used a custom-developed Sensemaking Measurement Tool (SMT) to evaluate participant responses. The SMT assessed three dimensions: adherence to the sensemaking process, ethical decision quality, and ambiguity handling. Ethical decision quality was evaluated through the application of transparency, fairness, and non-maleficence principles, while ambiguity handling assessed participants' willingness and ability to engage competing interpretations and navigate uncertainty. Responses were scored using a GPT-based evaluation system calibrated against expert human raters and validated to achieve approximately 95% agreement with human scoring.

Two hypotheses were tested. The first proposed that participants trained on the Hybrid Sensemaking Framework would demonstrate superior ethical decision-making relative to untrained participants when evaluating both high-ambiguity and low-ambiguity AI ethics dilemmas. The second proposed that ambiguity would moderate the framework's effectiveness, with stronger effects expected in highly ambiguous scenarios, and that trained participants would demonstrate greater comfort with ambiguity than control participants.

Results provide strong support for the value of structured sensemaking training in ethical AI leadership. Participants who received the intervention demonstrated statistically significant improvements in overall ethical decision-making performance when evaluating highly ambiguous dilemmas. Difference-in-differences analysis revealed that post-training SMT scores were significantly higher among trained participants relative to the control group, indicating that the intervention produced meaningful gains in ethical reasoning quality and decision process adherence.

For lower-ambiguity dilemmas, trained participants also achieved higher average scores than their control-group counterparts. Although the observed effect did not reach conventional levels of statistical significance, the directional pattern remained consistent with theoretical expectations, suggesting that the framework may provide benefits across multiple decision environments while delivering its greatest value under conditions of elevated ambiguity.

The findings were particularly notable with respect to ambiguity handling. Participants trained in the framework demonstrated significantly greater comfort navigating uncertainty than members of the control group. These effects were observed for both highly ambiguous and lower-ambiguity scenarios, with the strongest gains occurring in the high-ambiguity condition. The results suggest that the framework not only improves ethical decision quality but also develops a cognitive capability that enables decision-makers to engage uncertain situations more confidently and systematically.

This study contributes to three streams of literature. First, it extends sensemaking research by moving beyond descriptive explanations of how individuals construct meaning and demonstrating that sensemaking can be developed through a structured intervention. Second, it contributes to ethical decision-making scholarship by providing empirical evidence that ethical reasoning can be improved through disciplined decision processes rather than ethics principles alone. Third, it advances AI governance research by addressing a persistent gap between ethical guidelines and practical implementation. Rather than offering additional lists of principles, the framework provides a process through which those principles can be translated into action when competing interests and uncertainty make ethical judgment particularly difficult.

Taken together, the findings suggest that ethical AI leadership may depend less on knowing which principles are important and more on possessing a disciplined process for interpreting, negotiating, and acting when those principles conflict. As organizations increasingly confront novel AI-related dilemmas for which precedent is limited and certainty is unattainable, structured sensemaking may represent a scalable and teachable mechanism for improving the quality of ethical decision-making in practice.
