title: [Workshop] The Hidden Governance Problem in AI: Why diverse teams fail when expertise lacks influence
abstract:
Session Type: Interactive Workshop (45 Minutes)

Description

Organizations routinely invest in diverse, cross-functional AI teams because they believe better expertise leads to better decisions. Product managers, engineers, designers, marketers, compliance professionals, legal advisors, and executives are brought together to help organizations identify risks, uncover blind spots, and make more informed choices.

And yet ethical failures continue to emerge.

Despite possessing highly qualified teams and substantial organizational resources, companies regularly release AI products that create foreseeable harms, generate public backlash, undermine trust, and expose organizations to significant reputational, legal, and operational risk. In many cases, the problem is not a lack of expertise. The problem is that critical expertise fails to influence decisions.

This interactive workshop explores a governance challenge that many organizations unknowingly face: the gap between having expertise present at the table and ensuring that expertise meaningfully shapes outcomes.

Drawing on the session leader's more than twenty years of experience leading UX and digital product teams and informed by their ongoing doctoral research examining ethical decision-making within AI development teams, this workshop introduces participants to the concept of Voice Legitimacy and Dissent Protection (VLD): the organizational conditions that determine whether concerns raised by subject matter experts are merely heard or whether they actually influence decisions.

The workshop begins by examining why ethical concerns are sometimes deprioritized in fast-moving AI environments. Participants will explore the competing pressures that routinely shape decision-making, including market expectations, launch deadlines, executive priorities, competitive pressures, unclear governance structures, and organizational incentives. These forces create conditions of ethical ambiguity in which teams must make decisions without complete information, clear precedents, or perfect certainty.

Participants will then engage in a facilitated AI ethics scenario designed to simulate the tensions commonly experienced within modern product development environments. Working in small groups, attendees will evaluate competing priorities, stakeholder perspectives, and risk considerations while attempting to reach a decision. The exercise is intentionally structured to reveal how individuals and organizations interpret ethical concerns differently and why disagreement often emerges even among well-intentioned teams.

Following the simulation, participants will be introduced to the Ethical Improvisation Model (EIM), a practical framework that explains how ethical concerns raised during AI development either translate into meaningful action or disappear during decision-making processes.

The model explores five stages commonly observed in AI development environments:

Ethical ambiguity emerges.
Leadership framing and power structures shape initial interpretation.
Teams engage in collective sensemaking.
Ethical improvisation occurs as stakeholders negotiate tradeoffs and responses.
Decisions are executed and outcomes emerge.

A central premise of the model is that interdisciplinary expertise does not automatically produce stronger ethical outcomes. Rather, expertise creates value only when organizations establish conditions that legitimize dissenting perspectives and protect individuals who raise concerns. Participants will examine how Voice Legitimacy and Dissent Protection functions as a governance mechanism that converts expert concerns into consequential action.

The workshop places particular emphasis on practical application rather than theory. Participants will complete a guided governance assessment designed to help them evaluate whether their own organizations possess structures that encourage meaningful ethical dialogue.

Key assessment questions include:

Who has authority to challenge high-stakes decisions?
How are dissenting viewpoints handled during AI development?
Do subject matter experts possess meaningful influence or merely advisory status?
Are employees protected when raising ethical concerns?
What governance mechanisms exist to ensure ethical concerns receive appropriate attention?
How are tradeoffs between speed, innovation, revenue, and risk negotiated?

Through facilitated discussion and reflection, participants will identify strengths and vulnerabilities within their own decision-making environments and consider practical actions that may strengthen organizational AI governance.

The workshop is particularly relevant for:

AI leaders and managers
Product executives
Digital transformation leaders
Innovation teams
Data science professionals
Governance, risk, and compliance leaders
Human resources leaders
Consultants advising AI initiatives
Researchers interested in AI governance and organizational decision-making

Participants will leave with:

A practical framework for understanding why ethical concerns often fail to influence AI decisions.
A deeper understanding of how governance structures shape ethical outcomes.
Tools for assessing Voice Legitimacy and Dissent Protection within their organizations.
Actionable strategies for strengthening cross-functional decision-making.
A governance-focused perspective on responsible AI deployment and organizational readiness.

As organizations seek to scale AI responsibly, technical expertise alone is not enough. Sustainable AI innovation requires governance systems that ensure expertise, particularly dissenting expertise, has the authority, protection, and influence necessary to shape outcomes. This workshop provides leaders with practical tools to examine those systems, identify hidden vulnerabilities, and strengthen the organizational foundations required for responsible AI adoption at scale.

title: Your AI Works. Why Isn't Your Organization Improving? An Interactive Decision Lab for Scaling AI
abstract:
FORMAT
Industry Track - Creative Format
45-minute interactive decision lab

Rather than a traditional presentation, participants work in small teams as the executive leadership of a simulated 24-site organization tasked with scaling a technically successful AI initiative. Throughout the session, teams make resource-allocation decisions, respond to realistic implementation disruptions, compare approaches with peers, and apply a practical diagnostic to one of their own AI initiatives.

WHAT ATTENDEES WILL EXPERIENCE
Many organizations can build or purchase an accurate AI model. Far fewer translate that model into sustained enterprise value. This session explores why.

Participants become the leadership team of Northstar Health, a simulated 24-site outpatient organization preparing to scale an AI model that accurately predicts avoidable 30-day hospitalizations. The model performed well during a pilot, and the board has mandated enterprise deployment within nine months.

Each team receives a limited implementation budget of 10 investment credits and must allocate them across twelve possible investments, including model improvement, data and interoperability, governance, workflow redesign, workforce adoption, AI literacy, change management, measurement, staged rollout, equity monitoring, and MLOps support. Because resources are intentionally constrained, every investment requires tradeoffs.

After teams commit to an initial implementation portfolio, the facilitator introduces three increasingly realistic scaling disruptions:
• uneven adoption across organizational sites,
• model drift and equity concerns,
• and a pilot-to-enterprise value gap despite continued technical model performance.

Following each disruption, teams may revise only one investment while keeping the same budget. The objective is not to discover a single "correct" solution, but to experience how technical, organizational, governance, and operational decisions interact during AI implementation at scale.

The session concludes with a facilitated debrief that maps participants' decisions onto Six Foundations of Enterprise AI Scale:
• AI Value
• Grounded Data
• Governed Risk
• Workflow Integration
• Workforce & Change
• Measurement & Learning

Participants are then introduced to an AI-enabled learning loop that illustrates how organizations convert AI predictions into governed decisions, operational actions, measurable outcomes, and continuous organizational learning.

Although the simulation is set in healthcare - a high-stakes environment where these tradeoffs are especially visible - the framework is explicitly transferable to finance, operations, marketing, human resources, manufacturing, education, and other industries deploying enterprise AI.

Finally, each participant evaluates one AI initiative from their own organization using a one-page diagnostic and identifies one concrete action they can implement within the next 30 days.

SESSION FLOW
Time Participant experience
0-5 min Scenario introduction and executive challenge
5-12 min Teams build an implementation portfolio using limited resources
12-29 min Three rounds of scaling disruptions and portfolio revisions
29-38 min Debrief and introduction of the Six Foundations of Enterprise AI Scale and AI-enabled learning loop
38-44 min Participants diagnose one of their own AI initiatives and identify a 30-day action
44-45 min Key takeaway and facilitated closing discussion

ATTENDEE TAKEAWAYS
Participants will leave able to:
• Distinguish technical model performance from enterprise AI value.
• Explain why successful AI pilots frequently fail during enterprise scaling.
• Diagnose AI initiatives using six organizational foundations that extend beyond model accuracy.
• Recognize AI scaling as a portfolio of technology, governance, workflow, workforce, and learning decisions rather than a technology deployment alone.
• Apply a practical diagnostic to an existing AI initiative and identify one specific action they can take within 30 days.

The session uses no proprietary data, no vendor product, and no sales presentation. Its purpose is to provide an engaging, transferable decision-making experience that helps participants understand how organizations move from technically successful AI pilots to responsible, scalable, enterprise-wide innovation.

title: Generative AI Search on Content Creation Platform: Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
abstract:
Generative AI Search is an emerging platform-owned search-interface design that places AI-generated content above conventional ranked search results. For eligible queries, it provides users with a synthesized natural-language answer before they inspect or click the underlying sources, shifting the search experience from a retrieval-first, search-and-click model toward an answer-first format. On content creation platforms, where creator-supplied content is itself the informational product users seek, this design may affect both how often users search and how they subsequently consume the underlying content. Using a large-scale randomized field experiment involving 100,000 users on a leading Chinese content creation platform, we examine these two behavioral margins jointly. Treatment-group users received AI-generated content above the conventional ranked user-generated content (UGC) list when a submitted query satisfied the platform's triggering rule for objective or sufficiently standardized experience-based answers, whereas control-group users always saw only the conventional ranked list.

Our results reveal a scale-intensity trade-off in content consumption. Generative AI Search expands the extensive margin of information seeking: users search more frequently, on more days, and across a wider range of content categories and semantic topics. This expansion spans all six substantive search intents, including those less aligned with the platform's triggering rule. On the intensive margin, however, users who search consume less creator-supplied content per session: they browse and click less UGC. Despite this within-session contraction, aggregate UGC browsing and clicking increase, and more search sessions initiate downstream content consumption, which refers to subsequent within-platform content-page clicks after a user opens an initial piece of UGC from the search-results page. An activity-intensity decomposition shows that the expansion in search activity more than offsets the decline in average content consumption per session. Thus, Generative AI Search can reduce the consumption of creator-supplied content within individual sessions while increasing its aggregate consumption, demonstrating why lower per-session consumption need not imply lower overall demand for creator-supplied content.

title: The Meaning Gap: Where Value Moves When AI Scales
abstract:
Organizations are scaling AI faster than they are scaling judgment.

The adoption metrics look good. Output volume rises. Cycle times fall. Teams produce more analysis, more copy, more recommendations, and they produce it faster than any previous generation of knowledge workers could have managed. By every measure most organizations are tracking, AI adoption is working.

And somewhere in the middle of that success, a quieter problem appears. The work starts to converge.

The same models, prompted by similar people, working from similar training data, produce similar first thoughts at scale. Strategy decks begin to rhyme across competitors. Recommendations arrive pre-agreed, because everyone consulted the same source before the meeting. The five options presented to a decision maker turn out to be the same five options presented to a decision maker at a competing firm the same week.

This is the part of AI at scale that no one budgeted for. Not failure, not hallucination, not model risk. Convergence. The competitive differentiation that AI was supposed to deliver quietly erodes, because every competitor deployed the same capability at the same time and asked it the same questions.

This session names that problem, explains where it comes from, and gives participants a practical way to work against it inside their own organizations.

The Argument

There is a widening distance between how fast answers now arrive and how fast people and organizations can make sense of them. That distance is the Meaning Gap.

The gap does not close by adopting more technology. Adding capability to one side of an imbalance does not correct the imbalance. The gap closes, if it closes at all, in a specific place: the space between an answer and a decision. That space is where judgment operates. It is where an answer gets examined, contested, and either owned or discarded. It is also the first thing that speed pressure eliminates, because it is the only part of the process that produces no visible output.

When that space collapses, two things happen at once. Decision quality quietly degrades, because answers are being accepted rather than tested. And differentiation disappears, because a thought that nobody examined is a thought that anybody could have had.

The implication for leaders is counterintuitive. What becomes scarce in an environment of abundant answers is not information, analysis, or output. All of those are now effectively free. What becomes scarce is judgment, divergence, and the ability to arrive somewhere that everyone else did not. Those are the new sources of value, and unlike compute, they cannot be procured. They have to be practiced.

This is not a slower-is-better argument. Organizations cannot opt out of speed, and this session will not suggest they try. The argument is that the space between an answer and a decision can be protected deliberately, cheaply, and at speed, once a team knows it exists and treats it as an asset rather than as latency.

Session Structure

Part One: Framing (approximately 15 minutes)

A short, story-driven framing of the Meaning Gap and the convergence problem. This section establishes why sameness emerges from successful adoption rather than failed adoption, and identifies the specific point in the decision process where value is now created or lost.

No slides of maturity models, no vendor references, no tool comparisons.

Part Two: Live Audience Exercise (approximately 15 minutes)

Every participant arrives carrying a real decision. This part of the session puts that decision to work.

Participants are asked, at the start of the session, to hold a decision they are currently sitting with, one where an obvious answer is already available and waiting to be approved. In this segment they run that decision through a three move practice, live and in real time. Each move is introduced in a sentence and executed in silence:

Out. Approach the decision from a completely different direction than the one already taken.
Wide. Identify who would disagree, and articulate what they would say.
Deep. Ask what is actually happening underneath the situation, and ask it more than once.

The exercise takes a few minutes and produces a result participants can evaluate immediately. Some find their answer changes. Some find it holds. Both outcomes make the point: an answer that has survived examination is a different asset than an answer that was simply accepted, even when the words are identical. One is a first thought. The other is a decision.

The practice is deliberately small enough to be repeated the same afternoon, and it works inside AI workflows rather than requiring participants to step outside of them. The moves can be executed as prompts.

Part Three: Facilitated Discussion (approximately 15 minutes)

Open discussion, structured around three questions:

Where is convergence already visible in your organization, and how would you know if it were happening?
What currently rewards the acceptance of first answers on your teams, in incentives, timelines, or meeting design?
What would it take to protect the space between an answer and a decision without slowing delivery?

This segment is where the session earns its length. Participants hear how peers across industries are encountering the same pattern under different names, which is frequently the most valuable output for practitioners in the room.

What This Session Is Not

A tools session, a vendor demonstration, a maturity model, or a sales pitch. The technology is the occasion for the conversation, not the subject of it. The session is designed to be equally useful to aggressive adopters and to skeptics sitting in the same room, and it does not require participants to share a position on AI to participate in the exercise.

Presenter

Arthur Zards co-founded one of Chicago's first internet service providers in 1992, scaled it, and sold it to a NASDAQ-traded company in 1999

He now works with leaders and organizations on AI adoption, sensemaking, and decision quality, and writes on the Meaning Gap at labz.io/meaning. He founded and ran TEDxNaperville for fifteen years, where he coached hundreds of speakers on shaping an idea for a live audience.

title: AI-generated Summaries in Prediction Markets
abstract: Prediction markets rely on the diversity of participants' private signals to aggregate dispersed information into accurate collective forecasts. To reduce barriers to market participation, leading prediction market platforms have recently begun integrating AI-generated summaries (AIGS) that synthesize contextual information and market-relevant news. Despite their growing adoption, little is known about their broader implications for prediction markets. To address this gap, we leverage Polymarket's introduction of AIGS to examine its impact on individual trading behavior and market forecasting performance. We find that AIGS significantly increases individual participation while inducing an AI herding effect, where individuals rely on AI-provided information rather than their own independent judgment when making trading decisions. Our laboratory evidence shows that AIGS increases trading participation by reducing information acquisition and processing costs while shifting participants' beliefs toward the direction conveyed by the AIGS, providing further support for our proposed mechanism. In addition, at the market level, we find that AIGS reduces prediction accuracy and market efficiency. Taken together, these findings suggest that the introduction of AIGS presents a double-edged sword: while it makes prediction markets more accessible, it may unexpectedly harm the core function of prediction markets by undermining the collective information aggregation. These findings contribute to the emerging literature on generative AI and collective intelligence by revealing how AI-generated information can affect information aggregation on digital platforms.

title: Decision Making using AI: An Examination of Environmental-Oriented Crowdfunding Opportunities with Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Anecdotally, an investment opportunity with an environmental orientation will attract greater interest. While the declaration is entirely voluntary, the effect is likely stronger in a crowdfunding setting. We collected data from Kickstarter, which designated a section for environmental disclosures starting in 2018, and established a baseline on whether a crowdfunding campaign's environmental disclosure affects its funding performance. We then explore the decision-making capability of AI algorithms in such a setting, using semantic-based and LLM-based text analyses to examine the characteristics of the disclosures and to predict the implications on funding performance. Our preliminary findings show that LLM-based evaluation offers greater predictive power for the disclosure effect than semantic-based approaches. However, prompt engineering techniques, such as persona prompting, have limited implications. We also explore the mechanisms behind LLM-based algorithms and receive results that defy our expectations.

title: Prompts as Measurement Instruments: A Theory-Grounded Protocol for Valid LLM Text Classification
abstract:
Research Abstract
Motivation. Marketing scholars and practitioners have unprecedented access to unstructured textual data - social media posts, online reviews, customer-service and sales transcripts - yet converting this text into valid measures of theoretical constructs remains a fundamental bottleneck. Manual human coding, the traditional gold standard, delivers high construct validity because trained coders discern context, irony, and implicit meaning, but it is slow, expensive, and unscalable, and coder consistency degrades over time. Automated alternatives invert the trade-off. Dictionary methods are fast and deterministic but insensitive to context and polysemy, while supervised machine-learning classifiers achieve higher accuracy yet operate as black boxes, require costly labeled datasets, and may exploit spurious correlations unrelated to the construct of interest. Large language models (LLMs) promise to reconcile validity and scale, but early applications reveal a new methodological hazard: LLM outputs are highly sensitive to prompt phrasing, and ad hoc "prompt engineering" - iteratively adjusting wording until results look right - resembles p-hacking, threatening replicability, inviting demand effects, and leaving construct validity unexamined. Prior work shows that small changes in wording or option ordering can shift classification accuracy by ten percentage points. Without a structured prompting framework, LLM-based text analysis defaults to opaque, one-off queries. We argue that progress requires a standardized methodology that embeds established principles of measurement theory into LLM-based classification while achieving human-expert-level performance at machine scale.
Methodology. We develop and validate the Structured Taxonomy AI Measurement Protocol (STAMP), a theory-grounded LLM coding process with three core components. First, STAMP treats the prompt as a structured measurement instrument - a digital codebook - rather than an ad hoc query. Drawing on classical construct-measurement paradigms, the prompt comprises three layers: (1) a literature-grounded construct definition; (2) explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria that operationalize discriminant validity and prevent concept drift; and (3) prototypical examples with chain-of-thought rationales that teach the model not only what the correct label is but why. The layers are delineated with markup-style tags, and the model returns structured output containing both label and rationale, enabling automated auditing. Second, STAMP employs two LLMs of comparable capability from different model families (e.g., OpenAI GPT-4.1 and Google Gemini Flash 2) as independent coders - the methodological analog of dual human coders. Because heterogeneous models differ in architecture, training data, and inductive biases, their convergence provides evidence that classifications reflect the underlying construct rather than model-specific quirks, and the process yields auditable reliability metrics (Krippendorff's alpha). Third, STAMP treats inter-model disagreement as a diagnostic signal rather than noise: a third "summarizer" LLM synthesizes the themes underlying disagreements, a human expert adjudicates flagged cases and refines the codebook, and the cycle repeats until reliability exceeds accepted thresholds (alpha > .67). We validate STAMP in three studies spanning distinct linguistic and conceptual contexts: (1) 1,000 Instagram posts by sales professionals of a global luxury apparel brand, coded for two brand-image constructs (classic luxury style and personalized service) in a high domain-knowledge setting; (2) approximately 600 sentences from Amazon product reviews, coded for customer recommendations in a low domain-knowledge setting; and (3) 1,000 salesperson turns from 50 dyadic chat-based sales negotiations, coded for the value-confirmation sales tactic, where meaning depends on evolving conversational context. Ground truth was established through a two-stage process combining crowd-worker majority votes, an independent trained coder, and senior domain-expert adjudication of all residual disagreements.
Findings. STAMP meets or exceeds human benchmarks on all three evaluation criteria. Inter-LLM reliability: definition-only (zero-shot) prompts produced unacceptable agreement (Krippendorff's alpha of .37-.67 across constructs), while the full STAMP prompt reached .69-.87, comparable to the agreement achieved between human coders on the same tasks. Classification accuracy: STAMP achieved F1 scores above .80 for every construct (up to .92), meeting or exceeding crowd-coder performance (.77-.89). Ablations across prompt layers show the full three-layer prompt achieved the highest F1 in every case, and layer effects differed across models (one model's accuracy temporarily dropped when criteria were added in isolation). These divergences show that prompt sensitivity is model-specific and that dual-model convergence guards against optimizing for a single model's idiosyncrasies. Construct validity: multi-trait multi-method analyses confirmed convergent and discriminant validity in all three studies, with Steiger's Z-tests showing every mono-trait hetero-method correlation significantly exceeding hetero-trait correlations. Robustness checks show classifications are stable within a model family (alpha = .85), across families (two additional flagship models from different providers agreed with STAMP labels at alpha = .93 versus only .62 under definition-only prompting), and for the newest model generation. Bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations) confirms the two LLM coders perform indistinguishably from each other and more reliably than human expert pairs. Cost analyses indicate STAMP operates at roughly 1-2% of the cost of conventional human coding.
Implications. For research methodology, STAMP reframes prompt design as a construct-validity exercise rather than a predictive one, bringing LLM-based coding under the standards applied to new psychometric scales; it converts inter-coder disagreement from noise into a source of theoretical discovery, using contested cases to sharpen construct boundaries; and it formalizes a hybrid human-AI workflow in which LLMs handle routine coding at scale while human expertise is reserved for the ambiguous, contested cases that matter most for theory. Every classification carries a rationale tied to the codebook, producing a glass-box audit trail that supports replication and review. For practice, the protocol is implemented in a no-code web application that handles the underlying technical complexity, enabling brand managers, market researchers, and policy analysts to deploy theory-grounded text classification without programming expertise; a typical classification round on 1,000 texts costs $0.33-$2.75, versus roughly $600 for equivalent crowd coding. More broadly, this research contributes to the measurement of AI effectiveness itself: it provides a template for benchmarking LLM systems against human ground truth on reliability, accuracy, and construct validity jointly. Such joint benchmarking is a requirement for the responsible use of AI in high-stakes business and research applications. Web app: https://tinyurl.com/STAMPTextClassification

title: Your AI Build Has Seven Kinds of Value. Most Teams Measure One.
abstract:
An HR team was hand-editing offer letters across roughly twenty open browser tabs, on airplane wifi, mid-flight. That's the actual moment that got a small automation greenlit inside Cloudflare's People function - a build that cut per-offer-letter editing time from about ten minutes to three, freeing months of FTE work a year. By the ROI conversation most organizations default to, that's the whole story: time saved, capacity created, done.

It isn't the whole story. Around the same time, a different internal AI assistant we shipped hit near-perfect user satisfaction with zero negative feedback in its first weeks. Excellent number. It also had about a dozen users. Judged only on satisfaction, that's a clear win. Judged only on hours saved, it barely registers. Both readings are technically true, and both miss what's actually happening - which is the exact failure mode that makes most AI-ROI conversations unreliable: they collapse everything into whichever single metric is easiest to report, and then either underclaim real value or overclaim weak initiatives.

This session introduces the Value Prism, a six-dimension framework built to replace that single-metric story with an honest, disaggregated one: Scale, Quality, Experience, Risk, and Capability describe how value is created; Financial Impact - the sixth, and only the sixth - asks whether any of it lands on a P&L. I'll score both builds above against all six dimensions live, in front of the room, including where each one honestly scores "not applicable" rather than reaching to claim value that isn't there. That refusal to claim everything is the framework's most important design choice: an initiative that credibly claims three dimensions with real evidence is more useful to a skeptical executive than one that vaguely claims value everywhere.

The framework draws on established scholarship - the Balanced Scorecard's leading/lagging indicator structure, the Kirkpatrick-Phillips model's attribution discipline, the Resource-Based View's account of capability as a strategic asset - adapted for a class of initiative (AI inside people operations) none of those frameworks were originally built to evaluate. But the session is built around the builds, not the citations: attendees watch two real, very different outcomes get scored, and leave with a method they can run on their own next AI initiative in about ninety minutes.

Though every example here comes from an HR context, the six dimensions are function-agnostic - the same scorecard applies to an AI build in finance, ops, or marketing. The takeaway travels with the audience past the session: the next time someone shows up with a single ROI number, the useful question isn't whether the number is right. It's which dimension that number represents, and which five are missing from the story.

title: Configured to Care: How AI Emotional Expression Shapes User Engagement in Mental Health Support
abstract: Conversational agents are becoming an important source of support on online mental health peer-support platforms, where user engagement is a critical pathway through which support value is realized. A distinctive feature of AI supporters is that their emotional expressions are designable rather than incidental. We conceptualize agents' emotional affordance through a valence-elaboration taxonomy that captures both emotional valence and the extent to which emotional expressions reflect a more elaborated form of emotional processing. Using data from a leading online mental health community, we find that negatively valenced expressions, which acknowledge and legitimize users' distress, are more effective than positively valenced expressions in eliciting engagement. In particular, negatively valenced secondary emotional expressions are especially effective, suggesting that users value agents that meaningfully engage with distress and convey more sophisticated emotional understanding. Further analysis shows that these engagement-enhancing strategies are compatible with users' emotional well-being. Our study highlights emotional expression as a key design feature of AI support agents and offers a framework for understanding how agent emotions shape user outcomes in mental health contexts.

title: Agentic Agent, Better Agent: Evidence from Agentic AI in Telemarketing
abstract: Large language models are increasingly being deployed as agentic AI systems that autonomously manage customer interactions, yet their effectiveness in persuasion-intensive telemarketing settings remains largely unknown. We examine whether agentic AI can become a better agent in outbound financial telemarketing through a collaboration with a leading Chinese FinTech firm. The firm deployed three telemarketing agent types in parallel: human agents, a standard LLM-based agentic AI system, and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system grounded in verified internal knowledge. Using a quasi-experimental design and 7.41 million unique customer interactions, we find that standard agentic AI increases the odds of same-day loan initiation by 96.0% relative to human agents, while RAG-enhanced agentic AI increases those odds by 213.9%. RAG-enhanced agentic AI also outperforms the standard system by 39.8%, highlighting the value of grounding agentic AI in verified organizational knowledge. To understand why agentic AI performs so effectively in this context, we draw on the competence-warmth framework to examine the underlying mechanisms. The evidence suggests that agentic AI delivers both greater warmth, reflected in a more positive and more stable emotional tone, and greater competence, reflected in the superior performance of the RAG-enhanced agentic AI, stronger effects among competence-sensitive customers, and a widening AI advantage as human agents accumulate working hours. Although the AI advantage attenuates among customers more likely to recognize the AI identity, it remains economically substantial relative to human agents, suggesting that the effectiveness of agentic AI is robust to AI identity detection. These findings show that agentic AI can outperform human agents in trust-dependent financial sales and demonstrate the business value of retrieval augmentation in customer-facing agentic systems.

title: Fast Forward, Together: Leading Inclusively in the Age of AI
abstract:
Last year a research team set out to answer a simple question: what changes when people get an AI assistant at work? They spent two years analyzing millions of coding activities on GitHub, right after Copilot arrived. The finding sounds harmless at first. Developers with Copilot wrote more code. The real story is just below the surface: AI didn't just change what people worked on. It changed how they worked and who they worked with - if they worked with anyone at all. Junior developers shifted the most. Instead of asking colleagues, they ask the AI, and they miss the early-career moments that build real relationships. Meanwhile Stack Overflow, THE question-and-answer board for the software industry, is turning into a ghost town. Traffic fell 50% from 2022 to 2024. New questions fell 78%. People didn't stop having questions. They stopped asking them where anyone could see.
Software is just where this pattern is showing up first. The same shift is underway in HR, finance, marketing, operations, analytics. This is the question hiding inside AI innovation at scale: when the assistant is everywhere, what happens to the human system around it? And here is the uncomfortable part: working with other people is demanding and complex. If AI makes you more productive without interruptions, misunderstandings, awkward interactions, or judgment, what exactly will motivate you to build the skills an inclusive workplace requires? Inclusion is not just demographics. It is the lived skill of working with people who are not like you. 
I'll open with my five-minute DisruptHR talk on this phenomenon (see here for the talk: https://vimeo.com/1171391170?share=copy&fl=cl&fe=ci). From there the session becomes a blitz workshop. Following the five-minute talk, we go directly into an interactive idea generation for what leaders can do, then five minutes of harvesting and close. 
We warm up with the evidence, briefly. About ten minutes on what field data and controlled experiments actually show about productivity, help-seeking, learning, and the growing sameness of AI-assisted output, and why the gains and losses land differently on junior, expert, and marginalized employees.
The heart of the session is co-creation. In small groups, attendees generate specific moves an inclusive leader could make addressing questions such as: Which friction on your team would you deliberately keep, and which would you happily let AI remove? What would make AI use something people talk about openly rather than hide? What could you reward this quarter that AI cannot standardize? What interaction, ritual, or mentoring moment is quietly disappearing, and how would you design it back in? Groups capture their moves in writing, we harvest them together, and I connect what the room produces to the current research.
We end by assembling the room's moves into a shared playbook, typed up after the session.
I've run this format with an industry audience in April and it went really well. I would love to bring it to this group.

title: Built with AI, Governed by Rules: How Agentic AI Created a Living Rule Engine for Consumers
abstract:
At Scotts Miracle-Gro, we built a system that gives homeowners a personalized, season-aware lawn care plan across our app, CRM, and website. The counterintuitive part, and the heart of this talk, is that the recommendations themselves are not generated by AI at runtime. They are produced by a transparent, auditable rule engine that reasons like an agronomist. AI's job was to build that engine, not to be it. Understanding why we drew that line, and how, is a practical lesson in moving from hype to readiness.

Start with the problem, because it explains the design. Trustworthy lawn advice depends on grass type, geography, season, soil temperature, product availability, and a web of safety and regulatory constraints such as fertilizer blackout dates that vary by state and even zip code. That knowledge is scattered across thousands of product labels and lives in the heads of agronomists. A recommendation that is merely plausible is not good enough when it drives what a consumer buys and applies to their own property. So we set a hard requirement up front: every recommendation must be explainable, reproducible, and reviewable by a human expert. That requirement, more than any model choice, shaped everything that followed, and it is why we kept generative AI out of the decision path and put it to work building the decision system instead.

The build is a four-stage pipeline. The first stage is Extract. Agentic AI agents read our entire product catalog, pulling out grass types, weed lists, application rates, and constraints, and building reference taxonomies from scratch. This is knowledge engineering that would have taken experts months of manual effort, and exactly the high-volume, high-tedium work AI is genuinely good at. The second stage is Structure: we mapped more than a hundred products into forty-eight functional subcategories organized by the job the product does for the homeowner, not by how it sits on a shelf, and we codified expert safety and advisory constraints into a consistent, machine-readable form. The third stage is Reason. This is the runtime engine, and it is deliberately not a neural network. One hundred and twenty-six rules evaluate a forty-eight-field user state vector that blends grass type, region, uploaded photos, weather, and history to produce a plan. Every output is deterministic, traceable, and auditable: for any recommendation, we can show exactly which rules fired and why. The fourth stage is Validate. Subject-matter experts review every rule, agronomists validate the constraints and thresholds, and human-in-the-loop review gates anything before it goes live. AI drafts and structures; humans own correctness.

The real return on all that knowledge engineering is reuse, and this is where the "at scale" part of the story lives. Because the agronomic and product knowledge is now extracted, structured, and machine-readable, it is not a single-app feature; it is a shared intelligence layer the business can point at many surfaces. The same foundation powers the consumer app, where it produces the personalized care plan a homeowner sees. It powers CRM, turning generic campaign blasts into personalized, well-timed outreach grounded in each homeowner's lawn state, region, and season, so the message a customer receives reflects what their lawn actually needs right now. And it powers content generation at scale: because the taxonomies, product mappings, and safety and advisory constraints already exist in machine-readable form, we can generate on-brand, agronomically accurate content far faster than hand-authoring it, with the guardrails the content must respect built in rather than bolted on. One investment in structuring knowledge, many downstream products, is what turns a promising pilot into leverage across the consumer business.

With that architecture and reach in place, the talk turns to the readiness problems that separate hype from production, the ones nobody demos but everybody hits. The first is explainability, which we got largely for free by keeping the decision rule-based, and then reinforced by refusing to let the engine ever silently drop or substitute a recommendation. I will walk through a failure mode where a missing input caused the engine to quietly withhold an entire class of recommendations, and how we redesigned it to surface its assumptions and applied defaults rather than fail invisibly. The lesson generalizes far beyond lawns: in any advisory system, silent suppression is more dangerous than a visible error.

The second is validation at scale. You cannot manually check an engine that spans grass types, regions, and a full calendar year, let alone one feeding multiple surfaces. We built confidence by running large batches of simulated consumer journeys and comparing outputs against expected behavior before shipping, and I will show how that safety net also caught subtle issues, including a case where a testing artifact itself produced misleading results and taught us to validate the validator.

Finally, the operating model, because readiness is as much organizational as technical. Keeping a living rule engine correct over time requires a cross-functional rhythm: an SME and agronomist audit of the rules, documented and reviewed before changes reach production, paired with CI/CD so a small team can evolve the system safely and continuously. AI keeps the knowledge base current as labels and products change; humans keep it trustworthy.

Attendees will leave with a transferable framework built around one provocative idea: the highest-leverage use of AI is often to build the system, not to be the system. Concretely, they will take away how to decide what to make deterministic versus learned, how to use agentic AI to industrialize knowledge engineering, how to design for explainability from day one, how to turn structured knowledge into a shared layer that powers app, CRM, and content generation, how to validate at scale before launch, and how to structure the people and pipeline that keep it dependable. Whether you are building recommendations, personalization, or any AI real customers will touch, the goal is the same: leave the hype behind and get to readiness.

title: Why Accurate AI Fails to Scale: Organizational Translation as the Missing Mechanism
abstract:
Motivation. An AI system can be technically successful and organizationally inconsequential. It may predict accurately, perform well in a pilot, and still fail to alter decisions, routines, outcomes, or enterprise performance. Research on organizational AI readiness identifies organizational prerequisites for adoption (Jöhnk et al., 2021), while IT-business-value research shows that digital investments create value through complementary resources and process change (Melville et al., 2004). Yet these perspectives do not adequately explain the conversion between a model output and durable organizational value. Readiness inventories specify what organizations should possess; they say less about how AI-generated knowledge becomes authorized, routinized, enacted, and revised across an enterprise.

I ask: How do organizations translate technically successful AI outputs into sustained enterprise value, and why does the principal constraint change as scaling unfolds?

Theoretical framing. I define enterprise AI scaling as the replication and adaptation of an AI-enabled capability across organizational units while preserving technical performance, legitimate use, reliable enactment, and measurable value. I conceptualize scaling as a Practice-to-Practice conversion cycle (Practice → Data → Knowledge → Standards → Routines → Practice), a model developed in prior work (Ko et al., forthcoming).

The cycle integrates three insights. Organizational learning becomes consequential when understanding is integrated and institutionalized rather than remaining individual or episodic (Crossan et al., 1999). Knowledge crossing organizational boundaries must often be translated or transformed, not merely transferred (Carlile 2004). Performance arises from systems of complementary choices whose joint value exceeds isolated investments (Milgrom and Roberts 1995). Applied to AI, model performance is only one component of a broader organizational translation system.

Methodology. I use problem-driven integrative theory development. I synthesize research on AI readiness, IT business value, organizational complementarities, organizational learning, knowledge translation, governance, workflow integration, and organizational change. I map recurring constructs onto the Practice-to-Practice cycle and organize them as Six Foundations of Enterprise AI Scale: AI Value, Grounded Data, Governed Risk, Workflow Integration, Workforce and Change, and Measurement and Learning. I stress-test the model against three scaling disruptions: uneven adoption across units; model drift and equity concerns; and a pilot-to-enterprise value gap despite continued technical performance. These disruptions are theoretical probes, not empirical observations.

Findings. The analysis yields four propositions.

Proposition 1: Enterprise AI scale requires completion of the Practice-to-Practice cycle. AI Value defines the consequential problem, decision, and outcome. Grounded Data makes situated work observable and supports credible inference. Governed Risk determines when AI-mediated knowledge is sufficiently valid, accountable, and legitimate to become an organizational standard. Workflow Integration embeds standards in roles, prompts, decision pathways, and escalation rules. Workforce and Change enables actors to enact, adapt, and sustain those routines. Measurement and Learning evaluates consequences and returns evidence to the next cycle. A high-performing model can therefore coexist with enterprise failure when any conversion remains incomplete.

Proposition 2: The six foundations are complementary, not additive. Each addresses a different conversion problem, so excellence in one cannot compensate for absence in another. Better data cannot substitute for decision rights; rigorous governance cannot substitute for an actionable workflow; adoption cannot demonstrate value when outcomes are not measured. Enterprise AI scale is therefore conjunctural: multiple configurations may succeed, but severe weakness at a critical interface becomes a binding constraint.

Proposition 3: Scaling requires configuration migration. Pilot success typically privileges use-case selection, data access, model development, and local champions. Cross-unit diffusion shifts the constraint toward governance, workflow redesign, ownership, workforce capability, and change management. Continued operation elevates monitoring, drift response, equity review, outcome measurement, and routine revision. Organizations enter a pilot trap when they replicate the pilot's technical configuration without developing the institutional configuration required for enterprise use.

Proposition 4: Scaling produces bottleneck migration, and Measurement and Learning serves as a reconfiguration capability. Uneven adoption reveals workflow-workforce misalignment. Drift or subgroup-performance concerns reveal data-governance misalignment. Stable technical performance without enterprise outcomes reveals misalignment among AI Value, operational routines, and measurement. Measurement and Learning is not an end-stage return-on-investment activity. It enables leaders to locate the current bottleneck, revise the implementation portfolio, and decide whether to scale, modify, pause, or retire an AI-enabled routine.

Implications. The model reframes enterprise AI scaling as organizational translation and institutional capability formation. Its process logic identifies where value conversion breaks; its complementarity logic explains why isolated excellence cannot repair a broken cycle; and its dynamic logic explains why scaling requires reconfiguration rather than replication. For research, the model links AI readiness and IT value to organizational learning, knowledge translation, and governance across pilot, diffusion, and adaptation phases. It can be tested through longitudinal cases, process tracing, and configurational analysis. For practice, organizations should manage the completeness and alignment of the learning system, not merely model accuracy and deployment.

(This manuscript provides the academic foundation for the Industry Track decision lab by theorizing the mechanisms underlying participants' resource-allocation choices and observed scaling failures.)

title: Talking to Digital Twins: Selective Disclosure and Belief Measurement in Financial Social Media
abstract: Social media affect financial markets, but public posts by financial media personas are voluntary disclosures. What is not disclosed is therefore usually unobserved. We address this measurement problem by conducting repeated, real-time interviews of ``digital twins'' built from monitored finfluencers' X accounts under a fixed protocol. The interviews recover stock-level public-persona belief proxies even when no public recommendation is made. Because the interviews are generated and archived before the relevant return windows, the design avoids the look-ahead bias that arises when LLMs are queried ex post. The evidence shows that information obtained from these digital-twin interviews predicts the cross section of large-cap stock returns in the expected direction. Repeated real-time interviews therefore show how selective disclosure can be turned into measurable panels of market views.

title: A Simple Solution to Improving Human Supervision of Algorithms: Evidence from Smart Vending
abstract: Organizations increasingly deploy autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems for operational decisions, such as inventory replenishment. Yet fully granting override rights can degrade performance due to human bias and noise, while prohibiting them may overlook valuable private information. This raises a key question: How should override rights be structured to improve human supervision of autonomous AI? We propose a constrained override policy that limits overrides per decision episode to enable selective filtering, thereby prioritizing high-value overrides. We tested it in a randomized field experiment with 553 workers at a major Chinese smart vending machine retailer that manages more than 59,000 machines and 4,000 SKUs. Workers were assigned to no overrides, free overrides, or a two-per-machine limit on downward overrides. Free overrides reduce inventory by 1.95% but also cut sales by 1.19%. Constrained overrides reduce inventory by 1.28% without harming sales, as workers select better SKUs to override, as confirmed by local average treatment effects. Gains are largest for experienced workers, high-incentive SKUs, and growth-stage SKUs. Academics gain novel insights based on the causal effect of discretion design in human-supervised AI, emphasizing selective filtering to enhance decision quality. Managers can benefit from a scalable, low-cost policy for operations such as retail, logistics, and resource planning that reduces excess inventory without sacrificing sales, leverages workers' private information, and requires no algorithmic redesign, information customization, or additional training.

title: Self-Confirming Stigma and Skill-Substituting Technology
abstract:
Evaluators penalize workers who visibly use artificial intelligence, and workers respond by
cutting productive use. This paper shows that the penalty can be correct inference rather
than bias. In recommendation-based work, the technology raises the productivity of weaker
workers by more than that of stronger workers-a property the paper derives rather than
assumes. Visible reliance therefore signals low ability. In the unique refined equilibrium with
a continuum of abilities, every worker above the bottom of the distribution relies on the
tool less than is productive, and the evaluator's penalty confirms itself through selection into
visible use. Rising career stakes push the most able into conspicuous abstention; behavior
at that boundary is stated as a precise open problem. In a two-type version, stigma and full
adoption coexist as equilibria, so the penalty can be a pure coordination failure. Covert use
restores efficiency, because detection reveals nothing when everyone hides, while disclosure
mandates and detection technology destroy it. Calibrated to a recent field experiment using
reliance data alone, the model predicts the experiment's accuracy decline out of sample and
implies that observational comparisons miss two-thirds of the technology's true effect.

title: Should Platforms Replace Search with AI Chat? Evidence from a Live-Events Experiment
abstract:
Online platforms are increasingly integrating conversational AI tools into their search and browsing inter-
faces. To understand how such tools affect user behavior and search outcomes, we run a pre-registered, incentivized
online experiment in which participants search a catalog of several thousand events scraped from a major live-events
platform. We compare three interfaces: a classic, attribute-based filter interface (Filter), a GenAI chat interface (Chat),
and a combined interface offering both (Hybrid). All three operate over the same inventory of events, and the AI output
is restricted via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to only present events from this catalog. Our main result is that,
relative to the other conditions, users in the Chat condition value their chosen event less, spend more time searching
and report lower satisfaction both with the search process and with the chosen event itself. The effect is robust across AI
models, which include both state-of-the-art and legacy models. The performance gap is driven mainly by users who use
open-ended (as opposed to specific artist, venue or sports team) queries. In contrast, there are no significant differences
on any metrics between Filter and Hybrid. We document two mechanisms that explain the results. First, Chat creates
an echo chamber: without a visible menu, users construct queries based on what they think the catalog contains. As a
result, they frequently search for events that are not in the catalog, and they search too narrowly. Second, chat-based
search results in attention displacement: composing queries and waiting for responses consumes a large share of the
session. As a result users spend less effort on inspecting and evaluating the results. Taken together, our results suggest
that AI tools should be used as a complementary tool to existing filter-based search rather than replace it.

title: The Use and Impact of Social Bots among Social Media Users
abstract:
Social media research is mainly focused on influencers, however most users have relatively few followers and receive limited engagement. Among these less-visible users, socializers represent a particularly important but underexamined segment. Socializers actively post and interact with others because they value social connection, yet their small audiences often provide insufficient recognition and reciprocal engagement. Social media platforms have begun deploying social bots-automated agents that respond to users' posts-to increase participation and provide feedback to less-visible users. However, capacity and resource constraints mean that many requests for social bot interaction remain unfulfilled. This creates a potential platform dilemma: the users who most strongly desire algorithmic engagement may also react most negatively when it is unavailable.

Drawing on Attention-Seeking Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this research examines two questions: Which social media users are most likely to request social bot replies, and how do users respond when these requests are unfulfilled? We propose that socializers are more likely than influencers and lurkers to request social bot interaction because of their heightened needs for attention and relatedness. We further propose that these requests become especially likely under conditions that make users' psychological needs more salient, including the use of first-person language and posting later in the day. Finally, we predict that unfulfilled requests will disproportionately reduce socializers' perceptions of and intended actions toward the platform.

Four studies combine large-scale observational data with controlled experiments. Study 1 analyzes 487,015 posts involving CommentRobot, a social bot operating on a major social media platform in China. Weighted logistic regression models examine whether follower count, first-person language, and posting time predict explicit requests for a bot reply. Studies 2-4 use experimental social media scenarios in which participants write a post, decide whether to request a social bot reply, and evaluate the platform following different response outcomes. Study 2 includes 971 participants and compares fulfilled and unfulfilled requests. Study 3 includes 245 participants and distinguishes among fulfilled requests, unexplained nonresponses, and nonresponses accompanied by an explanation. Study 4 includes 289 participants and compares no reply, a human reply, and a social bot reply. Across the experimental studies, participants classify themselves as socializers, lurkers, or influencers and report their needs for attention and relatedness, platform perception and actions.

Study 1 shows that users with fewer followers are substantially more likely to request a social bot reply. This association becomes stronger when posts contain first-person language and when they are published later in the day, suggesting that self-focused expression and temporally heightened relational needs increase demand for bot interaction among less-visible users. The endogeneity analyses provide additional support for this interpretation. Balance tests reveal only minimal differences between fulfilled and unfulfilled requests across follower count, posting time, and first-person language, reducing concerns that the bot selectively responds to particular users or posts. In the control-function analysis, concurrent requests from other users strongly predict bot traffic, while diagnostic tests and the nonsignificant residual term provide no evidence that residual endogeneity explains the main findings. The Study 1 results are also robust to alternative measures of user type. When posting frequency replaces follower count, more frequent posting significantly predicts bot requests. When follower count and posting frequency are entered jointly, follower count remains negatively associated with requesting, while posting frequency remains positively associated with requesting. This pattern is consistent with the proposed distinction between low-activity lurkers, highly active but less-visible socializers, and highly visible influencers.

The experimental studies provide convergent evidence that socializers are the user category most likely to request social bot interaction. In Study 2, 74.4% of socializers requested a bot reply, compared with 53.0% of lurkers. This pattern replicates in Study 3, in which request rates were 80.0% for socializers and 56.1% for lurkers, and in Study 4, in which the corresponding rates were 79.7% and 51.2%. Across the studies, socializers report stronger needs for both attention and relatedness, and mediation analyses show that these psychological needs partially explain their greater likelihood of requesting bot replies. The findings also reveal an important downside of inconsistent bot responsiveness. Among users whose requests go unfulfilled, socializers consistently report the least favorable platform perceptions and the weakest intentions to continue engaging with the platform. This pattern emerges across Studies 2-4. Study 3 further indicates that providing a brief explanation for a nonresponse can attenuate negative reactions, particularly among socializers. Study 4 shows that socializers experience elevated attention and relatedness specifically when receiving a social bot reply; these differences do not emerge after a human reply or no reply. Together, these findings suggest that social bot feedback can carry distinctive psychological value for socializers, while nonresponse can make their unmet needs especially salient.

This research contributes to social media and artificial intelligence scholarship in three ways. First, it redirects attention from highly visible influencers toward socializers, an important group whose active participation helps sustain platform communities despite receiving relatively little recognition. Second, it distinguishes social bots from traditional, transaction-oriented chatbots by demonstrating that social bots can function as an algorithmic form of social feedback capable of addressing users' needs for attention and relatedness. Third, it identifies a potential cost of deploying social bots under capacity constraints: inviting users to request engagement without reliably fulfilling those requests may reduce platform evaluations and continued participation among the users most motivated to connect.

The findings also offer practical guidance for platform design. Platforms should prioritize reliable and contextually appropriate bot responses for users displaying strong engagement needs, carefully manage expectations when responses cannot be guaranteed, and provide transparent explanations when requests go unfulfilled. More broadly, social bots may help platforms make less-visible users feel recognized and connected, but their benefits depend on dependable implementation. Poorly managed social bot systems may not merely fail to increase engagement; they may intensify the dissatisfaction of users who already feel overlooked.

title: Will Human Creatives Survive Generative AI Shocks?
abstract: The rise of generative AI has raised an urgent economic question: will it eventu- ally replace human content creators, and if not, which tasks will survive? This paper develops a flexible modeling framework that yields a sharp answer and helps reconcile mixed empirical evidence. Our baseline result establishes a robust human-AI coexis- tence, analogous to the Grossman and Stiglitz (1980) impossibility of informationally efficient markets: Just as prices cannot fully aggregate private information-otherwise no investor would pay to acquire it, leaving nothing to aggregate-generative AI can- not fully displace human creators-otherwise they would stop producing fresh content, leaving AI to train on a stale corpus, which deteriorates AI performance and creates room for human re-entry. This coexistence is not transitory: it holds even at the theoretical capability limit of current generative AI architecture. We then extend the baseline model to incorporate preference/skill heterogeneity or task complementarity to identify which human tasks will sustain in the generative-AI era. A dynamic extension also provides a microfoundation. The framework generates clean comparative statics and testable predictions for multiple aspects of human-generative AI interactions, and offers actionable guidance for creatives and policymakers navigating the generative AI transition.

title: Steering by Probability: Using AI to build the view leadership actually needed
abstract:
Every executive asks the same question - when will this be done - and most organizations answer with a date somebody made up. At a trucking insurance company, I used the same AI agents that were writing the company's code to build what leadership actually needed: a live picture of what was being delivered, and for every major initiative, the odds it lands by its forecasted date. A probability, not a promise, rebuilt daily from the work teams were genuinely finishing.
 I didn't write the code. I described what leadership needed and directed the agents that built it - the per-team views first, then the portfolio rollup, then the steering page itself. What the agents really gave us was flexibility. Restructuring how the company tracked its work is normally the kind of project nobody wants to start; with agents it took a couple of hours. And because our tracker and our forecasting engine were both wired directly into Claude, getting the numbers out stopped being an integration effort and became something you could simply ask for.
 A forecast is only as good as the data and the system underneath it. The company's own records of when work finished weren't trustworthy, so we rebuilt the measurements from the code itself and cross-checked them independently. Then came the part I didn't expect: the agents turned out to be the easiest way to make the practices stick. Limits on how much work anyone starts at once. Work sized against what the team actually delivers rather than a guess at hours. Rules the agents can't talk their way past, enforced on people and machines alike. Getting teams to hold that discipline is usually the hardest part of my job, and here it was built into the tools they already worked in.
 It changed the conversation. When something slipped, its confidence fell the day it happened instead of surfacing a month later in a status meeting. Leaders stopped asking for commitments and started asking what would move the odds. Teams started managing risk as it appeared rather than explaining it afterward. Over the same period, work that used to sit unfinished for nearly five months was getting done in five days, on a smaller team.
 Not everything landed. We once showed leadership a single combined probability across several initiatives - mathematically correct, and read by executives as failure. We pulled it. That taught me more about scaling this than any success did: the numbers have to survive contact with the people who act on them. What transfers here isn't the tooling. It's the order. Ground the data, enforce the discipline, then automate the view. Reverse it and all you've built is a faster way to be confidently wrong.

title: Response Latency in Asynchronous Care Queues: An Empirical Study of AI-Augmented Measurement and Emergency Department Spillover
abstract:
Patient portals have expanded access to outpatient care, but they also create asynchronous communication
queues where patient-initiated requests for medical advice may remain unanswered while patients continue making decisions
about seeking care. We examine whether unresolved medical-advice requests are associated with subsequent emergency
department use, suggesting that delays in responding through patient portals may spill over into acute care. Using
34 months of patient portal and electronic health records data from a large U.S. health system, we analyze 420,517 patient-initiated
medical-advice threads spanning 2.93 million thread-days. To capture differences in incoming requests, we use
large language models to classify the severity and complexity of each initial patient message. Daily hazard models show
that unresolved requests are associated with a higher likelihood of an emergency department visit. After addressing the
nonrandom timing of clinician responses using a control-function approach based on workload variation, the estimated
effect increases to 1.33 percentage points, suggesting that conventional estimates understate the relationship because
higher-risk requests tend to receive faster attention. Emergency department use is concentrated among a small subset
of requests. Although high-severity messages account for only 5.4% of medical-advice threads, they represent 28.5%
of threads followed by an emergency department visit. Together, these findings show that delays in responding to asynchronous
patient messages can have important downstream consequences and that the content of incoming requests-not
just their volume-should guide how health systems prioritize limited response capacity.
