title: From Academic Evidence to Managerial Insight: The Promise and Peril of Multimodal LLMs
abstract:
This is what makes a new class of tools worth taking seriously. Large language models (LLMs) are deep learning models pretrained on large-scale text corpora to capture broad linguistic and semantic knowledge. Building on this foundation, multimodal large language models extend language capabilities by integrating and reasoning over multiple modalities, such as text, images, audio, and video. As these capabilities have advanced, conversational AI assistants have increasingly incorporated multimodal functionalities, enabling users not only to generate text but also to interpret, synthesize, and transform information across multiple formats. One example is NotebookLM, which allows users to transform a single source document, such as a research article, into complementary outputs including an infographic, an audio overview, and a video (Mehta et al., 2025). Learning science predicts that this should work. The cognitive theory of multimedia learning (CTML) holds that people process verbal and visual information through separate, capacity-limited channels, and that understanding is built by selecting and integrating material across them (Mayer, 2024; Mayer & Moreno, 2003). Drawing this insight, we suggest that splitting a dense research article across multimedia channels with the help of the multimodal LLM interface offloads the verbal bottleneck, frees working memory, and scaffolds an integrated mental model, thereby lowering the accessibility cost that keeps evidence out of practice.
But we also identify its downside: the same machinery that opens the evidence may close the mind that receives it. A research article processed, polished, and delivered in a confident synthetic voice invites the user to stand down their own judgment. People follow AI advice even against contradictory information and their own assessment (Klingbeil et al., 2024), and the more they lean on these tools, the more they offload the cognitive work and the less they think critically for themselves (Gerlich, 2025; Risko & Gilbert, 2016). We call this state unreserved reliance on AI: deference to AI-generated output without critical reservation. Our central claim is that the benefit and the cost are not separate phenomena to be traded off but two faces of one mechanism. The ease that lets a practitioner grasp a research article is the same ease that tempts them to stop interrogating it (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009). 
If the tool is double-edged, the question is whether it can be addressed. The remedy we propose comes from EBMgt's own toolkit. CIMO-logic decomposes a finding into the Context in which it holds, the Intervention it implies, the Mechanism that drives it, and the Outcome it yields; it was built to cast research into prescriptive, transferable form (Denyer et al., 2008). We turn it from a format for writing evidence into a structure for engaging it, prompting users to reconstruct a finding's context, intervention, mechanism, and outcome as they carry it into their own setting: a cognitive nudging function that makes the user think rather than merely receive. This prompting solution cuts two ways at once. Reconstructing a finding in one's own words is generative work that deepens understanding; judging whether it transfers (e.g., does this context match mine, would this mechanism operate here?) is evaluative work that reinstates critical cognitive agency, defined as the active exercise of independent judgment in questioning, contextualizing, and appraising when engaging with a research article. 
We test both edges and the remedy across two experiments, asking whether multimodal LLM interfaces can bridge research and practice, turning "journal language" into "manager language", and whether that bridge can be engineered to inform without inducing unreserved reliance. Study 1 tests whether multimodal translation raises comprehension and unreserved reliance at once. Study 2 holds the multimodal translation interface fixed and pits CIMO-based prompting against a default chat, testing whether structured reflection lifts comprehension and critical cognitive agency together. Study 1 shows that multimodal translation improves comprehension of a research article while simultaneously increasing unreserved reliance on AI. Study 2 shows that prompting users to reflect on the Context, Intervention, Mechanism, and Outcome (CIMO) of a research article enhances both comprehension and critical cognitive agency.

title: Agentic Commerce 101: How AI Is Transforming Retail & eCommerce
abstract:
We've been here before. Every major shift in commerce, mail order, big-box, the internet, has separated companies that read the moment correctly from companies that didn't survive being right too early or too late. Agentic commerce, AI agents that shop, decide, and transact on a customer's behalf, is that kind of shift, and it's moving faster than the internet did.

This talk looks at what actually separated the winners from the losers in past commerce shifts, then applies those lessons to what's happening in retail right now: how AI is already changing how people find and buy things, where this is headed, and what leaders should be doing about it this quarter, not someday.

I lead the AI practice at Aries Solutions, where I work with retailers on exactly these challenges. This talk is based on real world experience, bolstered by research and a bit of storytelling.

Who this is for: retail and eCommerce leaders trying to figure out where agentic AI actually changes their business versus where it's noise, founders and operators building in or around commerce, and anyone whose work touches how people discover, decide on, and buy things.

Format: built for a general, mixed-expertise audience. No AI background required. Retail domain knowledge helpful but not necessary. Runs 30-45 minutes depending on the slot, with room for Q&A.

title: AI and Appropriation Risk
abstract: The capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) depend critically on the data on which it is trained. When AI absorbs a firm's intellectual property during training and subsequently competes against the firm itself, incumbents face a novel source of risk-appropriation risk. I construct a firm-level measure of exposure to appropriation risk from a common AI training corpus, based on how precisely AI can reconstruct each firm's intellectual property. Following the launch of ChatGPT, more-exposed firms experience sharper declines in the market value and number of their patents. The cross section is non-monotonic: patent novelty and long-run cumulative abnormal returns are inverted-U shaped in exposure, peaking at moderately exposed firms. I rationalize these patterns in a model in which AI's productivity depends on absorbed incumbent knowledge and the escape-competition incentive is strongest at intermediate exposure. AI and incumbents are product-market substitutes but, over time, complements in knowledge production.

title: Artificial Intelligence in the Market for Knowledge
abstract:
AI can make answers abundant, yet turn valuable questions into the scarce resource. We study AI in a knowledge economy where firms must not only apply expertise to solve problems but first compete for the opportunities to apply it: client engagements, cases, projects, deals, and other valuable work. AI therefore does more than automate a fixed list of tasks: it changes how much work is found, how firms arrange expertise, and what workers learn. Our study differs from most existing research on AI in one simple yet critical respect: work must be found before it can be done. When AI expands solving capacity faster than the supply of worthwhile problems grows, the bottleneck moves from answers to questions.

This mechanism helps explain an emerging puzzle. Generative AI often delivers its largest productivity gains to inexperienced workers, yet employment losses in exposed occupations appear concentrated among the young. We reconcile these observations in one framework. AI can make each remaining junior more productive while sharply reducing how many juniors a firm needs. It can absorb routine cases, leaving fewer and more knowledgeable experts to handle unusual ones. Displaced workers instead move into finding: they seek clients, originate deals, pitch projects, or work independently. That is a sensible way for each person to cope with automation. But when too many people chase the same opportunities, their efforts duplicate one another. The economy can solve more problems while wasting more resources in a race to determine which problems get worked on. This congestion is our central mechanism.

We build a general-equilibrium model that jointly determines the supply of valuable work (i.e., "problems"), workers' occupations and training, and firms' knowledge hierarchies. People choose between finding and solving, and knowledge is costly to acquire. Free entry and occupational choice connect each firm's organization to the economy-wide race for problems. Junior solvers attempt problems first and pass difficult cases upward, allowing experts to concentrate where their expertise is needed. Finders supply the opportunities on which firms work, but finding is congested: an additional finder can win business partly by taking it from somebody else. Her private reward therefore exceeds the new output she creates. AI has two independent attributes. Its knowledge determines what it can solve; its compute cost determines how cheaply it can be deployed.

We obtain three sets of results. First, knowledge looks up the hierarchy, while cost looks down. AI breaks the human knowledge ladder wherever it enters. Smarter AI changes the hierarchy above it: fewer problems reach managers, so firms need fewer of them, and those who remain acquire more knowledge. Cheaper AI changes the hierarchy below it: workers have less reason to train merely to avoid sending cases to the machine, so they acquire less knowledge and junior layers may disappear. AI that matches an existing human rung can replace it cleanly. AI whose knowledge falls between rungs requires a different surrounding hierarchy and must therefore be cheaper to win adoption. Because alternative organizations can coexist at the same market prices, continuous AI improvements can generate gradual adoption but abrupt changes in firms' training and hierarchy.

Second, AI's welfare effect depends on whether it displaces people, not simply on whether firms adopt it. An adopting firm counts its gains but treats the supply and price of problems as given. When AI-using firms replace human solvers, solving capacity becomes abundant relative to worthwhile problems. Problem prices rise, displaced workers crowd into finding, and part of the technological gain is burned up through duplicated search. The gain is not simply destroyed inside the adopting firm: it is transferred into the price of scarce problems and partly dissipated as people duplicate one another's search. A privately profitable and genuinely productive technology can therefore make workers worse off even while expanding productive capacity. However, once firms converge on the same AI organization, cheaper AI unambiguously raises welfare, as it saves resources and can draw people out of congested finding. Smarter AI remains ambiguous because greater capability may still release workers from solving. When AI finds rather than solves problems, welfare falls while human and AI finders coexist but rises after finding becomes AI-only and problems are supplied more cheaply.

Third, the policy implications are clear but can be surprising. In our model, the first-best response to harmful AI adoption is not an AI tax. It is a tax on income from finding -- the very activity displaced workers use to "cope" with automation. Efficient policy follows displaced workers rather than automatically targeting the technology that displaced them. Set to match the congestion externality, the tax aligns each finder's private reward with the new work she actually creates. Put starkly, if robots displace workers who then crowd into an apparently safer occupation, efficiency may require taxing that refuge rather than protecting it. The model says to tax the human cope, not the machine.

When finding cannot be taxed directly, policy toward AI becomes a second-best tool. But that tool need not be an AI tax. Our model delivers a more surprising possibility: an AI subsidy can also improve efficiency. The relevant test is whether the intervention reduces excessive human finding. An AI tax can help when additional AI use displaces solvers into the congested search for work; an AI subsidy can help when cheaper AI draws people out of finding and back into solving. Displacement therefore does not justify taxing AI forever: a permanent AI tax may preserve the very inefficiency it was intended to cure.

These results change what researchers, firms, and policymakers should measure. The practical test is not only who loses a solving job but where those workers go. Movement into sales, prospecting, business development, independent contracting, and other forms of origination may matter as much as headline employment. Capability benchmarks and job counts are therefore insufficient. Evaluating AI requires tracking training, firm structure, problem origination, and-above all-where displaced workers go. Otherwise, we cannot tell whether AI's private gains become social gains or instead ignite a costlier race for scarce work.

title: Rare Demand, Reliable Access: A Field Experiment on AI-Driven Replenishment in a Retail Pharmacy Chain
abstract:
Retail pharmacies face a replenishment problem that differs fundamentally from ordinary retail. Stockouts can interrupt treatment rather than merely defer a purchase, yet excess stock ties up working capital and increases expiration risk. The problem is especially difficult for slow-moving medicines and geographically remote stores: demand is intermittent, sales are censored when products are unavailable, and delivery opportunities may be infrequent. Although data-driven inventory models promise better decisions, causal evidence from operating retail pharmacies remains limited. We study whether algorithmic replenishment can improve medicine availability and operating efficiency when store-SKU demand is sparse and heterogeneous, and we examine where and why any gains arise.
We develop a quantile-based replenishment system for a pharmacy chain in the Zhoushan archipelago of China. The chain operates stores ranging from dense urban locations to outer islands served by scheduled ferries. In the experimental data, 78.7% of in-stock store-SKU weeks have zero sales, 90% of series average fewer than one unit per week, and the slowest third of SKUs record zero sales in 92.3% of in-stock weeks. Separate forecasting for each store-SKU would therefore be statistically unreliable. The algorithm first removes stockout-censored observations, pools substitutable products into clinically and commercially meaningful groups, and pools information across stores. It then estimates service-level-specific demand quantiles using a two-part global model that separates demand occurrence from positive-demand magnitude. A sparse quantile-regression correction adjusts systematic residual errors, and a stabilized choice model allocates group targets back to individual SKUs without reinforcing past stockouts. The resulting target enters a simple order-up-to policy.
A companion theoretical analysis studies the general global-plus-local architecture. For task \(i\), the estimator combines a pooled nonparametric quantile function with a sparse task-specific linear correction. Under density, complexity, restricted-eigenvalue, boundedness, and sample-splitting conditions, its expected excess pinball risk is bounded, with high probability, by three terms: a global-learning term proportional to \((1/\pi_i+s)\) times the pooled estimation error; a local-correction term of order \(s\log(p/\delta)/n_i\); and an irreducible approximation term determined by residual heterogeneity. Here, \(n_i\) is the local sample size, \(\pi_i=n_i/N\) is its share of the pooled sample, \(s\) is local sparsity, and \(N\) is the chain-wide sample size.
The result clarifies the operational logic of the architecture. Pooling allows the dominant shared component to improve with the full chain-wide sample; sparse correction permits adaptation at a substantially lower local-data cost; and the heterogeneity term identifies the limit of pooling. It also predicts that small or atypical stores, which have small \(\pi_i\), require the most local adjustment. The deployed system uses a pooled service-tier correction, while the theorem establishes the store-specific extension and its finite-sample guarantee.
We evaluate the system in a matched-pair crossover field experiment conducted from January through May 2026. Twenty-seven stores were organized into 11 matched pairs based on revenue, baseline stockouts, island status, and transportation mode. Fifteen stores received algorithmic replenishment in the first 64-day period and manual replenishment in the second; the remaining 12 stores followed the reverse sequence, separated by a 21-day washout. The experiment covered 90 SKUs in six therapeutic categories. Pair-level difference-in-differences removes time-invariant store differences and common seasonal shocks. The design is conservative because the algorithm did not observe warehouse availability or managers' private information and could not substitute across equivalent drugs during execution.
Algorithmic replenishment reduced end-of-day stockouts by 4.7 percentage points (\(p=0.039\)) and controllable stockouts by 4.1 points (\(p=0.041\)). At the same time, turnover improved by 22.3 days (\(p=0.002\)), inventory declined by 0.50 units per SKU (\(p=0.079\)), and gross profit increased by CNY 2.5 per store-day (\(p=0.021\)). Thus, the intervention shifted the service-efficiency frontier rather than moving stores along a conventional availability-inventory trade-off. A fully independent year-over-year design, comparing each store with the same calendar windows in 2025, produced a nearly identical stockout estimate of -4.3 percentage points (\(p=0.020\)).
Mechanism analyses show that the system replenished more frequently in smaller batches, shortened stockout spells from approximately 10-30 days to 4-6 days, and reduced stock age from 125 to 87 days. Gains concentrated in slow-moving products, where managerial attention is most limited, while fast movers changed little. The algorithm also created a chain-wide service floor: the worst-store stockout rate fell from 35.8% under manual ordering to 12.7%, and the number of stores above 15% fell from seven to zero. Because store-level failure is nearly uncorrelated across adjacent years, these findings favor broad deployment over targeting a stable set of "bad" stores.
Geography changed the form, rather than the total amount, of value. Ferry stores did not have materially longer average lead times; instead, manual ordering preserved availability through large, aging buffers. The algorithm widened each delivery from 4.1 to 9.2 distinct SKUs, reduced ferry-store stock age from 133 to 89 days, lowered near-expiry exposure, and increased unit sales. This pattern matters for access because island demand is disproportionately concentrated in chronic medicines. The ferry estimates are based on only two experimental pairs and should therefore be interpreted as mechanism evidence rather than definitive subgroup effects.
Finally, post-experiment monitoring and manager surveys illuminate adoption. Within three weeks of withdrawal, stockouts rose from approximately 5.8% to 9.3%, even though managers ordered more frequently. This monitoring comparison is descriptive, not a separate causal estimate. Managers' perceived benefits were essentially uncorrelated with measured gains, and only three of 27 identified slow movers as the main beneficiaries. Algorithmic replenishment therefore creates value partly through counterfactual events that managers cannot directly observe: stockouts that never occur and long-tail medicines that quietly remain available.
Together, the theoretical and field results show how pooling, quantile learning, and light local adaptation can convert extremely sparse pharmacy data into operationally effective replenishment decisions. The study contributes a finite-sample foundation for global-plus-local quantile prediction, randomized and independently replicated evidence from retail pharmacy operations, and new evidence that remoteness affects freshness and delivery composition more than physical lead time. More broadly, the highest return to automation may arise not in high-volume items that already attract managerial attention, but in the dispersed long tail of decisions for which human monitoring is structurally scarce.

title: (Early) AI Compute Asset Pricing
abstract: Compute (computing power) is a scarce, capital-intensive input at the center of the AI economy. Compute capital expenditure and service flow already exceed 1% of U.S. GDP and are growing rapidly. The price of compute reflects uncertainty over AI adoption. The announced launch of compute futures turns this uncertainty into a tradable risk, raising questions on the pricing of a new asset class. We provide an early asset-pricing framework for compute. We begin by discussing the underlying compute rental market and its indexation. We then turn to pricing: 1) direct no-arbitrage links between futures prices and current spot prices fail due to the non-storable nature of compute, 2) synthetic futures prices from existing term rental contracts are likely upper bounds on true futures prices and, 3) upon financialization, futures prices will be investors' expectations of spot prices at expiration net of a risk premium. Using synthetic futures as stand-ins before the compute futures market launches, we construct the first compute futures return panel sorted by GPU generation and maturity. Our preliminary evidence is consistent with a positive compute risk premium, suggesting hedging pressure on the part of compute providers.

title: How EASE Logistics Embedded Intelligence Into the Core of a Freight Brokerage
abstract:
At EASE Logistics, we didn't set out to experiment with AI. We set out to solve real operational problems - and what we built changed how our entire business operates. This session tells that story honestly, including what worked, what we had to rethink, and what we wish we had known sooner.

AMMI, our proprietary AI platform, was designed to serve two audiences simultaneously: our internal teams and our customers. For our teams, AMMI eliminated the repetitive, time-consuming work that gets in the way of great service - automating quoting, carrier communication, email triage, and compliance check calls, saving an estimated 2,470 hours per month and processing over 4,000 emails daily. For our customers, AMMI delivers a dedicated intelligence layer that provides real-time freight visibility, proactive insights, and the data they need to make faster, more confident supply chain decisions - without waiting on a rep for an answer. The results have been measurable: over $13.5 million in awarded revenue generated through automated spot bid quoting, a 60 percent reduction in inbound carrier call volume, and load progressions handled directly by AMMI growing from 12 percent to 20 to 25 percent in a single quarter.

But the metrics only tell part of the story. I'll walk attendees through how we approached building a platform that people actually use - embedding AI into the systems and workflows our teams already lived in, leading adoption with curiosity rather than mandate, and evolving AMMI from an internal tool into a customer-facing intelligence layer.

We are flexible on session format and happy to work within whatever structure best serves the conference and its attendees - whether that is a standalone case study presentation, a panel alongside other practitioners, or a more collaborative, discussion-based format. The goal is a conversation that leaves attendees with something they can actually use.

Attendees will leave with practical frameworks for scoping an AI build in an operations-heavy environment, strategies for driving adoption without forcing behavioral change, and a realistic picture of what it takes to move from AI experimentation to embedded, measurable impact.

title: Job Architecture Ontology and AI: Rewiring the Operating System for Workforce Design
abstract:
AI innovation matters most when it improves decisions affecting real people, work, and performance. Job architecture is the hidden operating system that shapes how work is defined, how careers progress, and how people are paid. When unclear or outdated, the consequences reach beyond titles and compensation: employees struggle to understand advancement, managers make inconsistent decisions, and organizations lose the clarity needed to match work to capability. Over time, these gaps weaken culture, drive talent away, and leave critical roles unfilled.

When relationships among roles, levels, skills, and compensation are governed, job architecture becomes a trusted workforce ontology. This shared language gives AI a reliable foundation. Rather than reviewing one job description at a time, AI can study the architecture as a connected system. Across thousands of data points, it identifies similarities in duties, surfaces duplicate roles, and reveals career adjacencies difficult to see manually. By analyzing how skills and complexities change between roles, AI helps distinguish natural career pathways from gaps that make stated paths difficult to navigate. AI does not replace expert judgment; it gives leaders a broader evidence base, while humans validate whether those relationships reflect the organization's actual operating model and talent strategy.
In this 45-minute, applied dual-case presentation, we explore what AI innovation at scale looks like when applied to high-stakes workforce challenges. Co-presented by Emily Douglas-McNab (OSU MHRM '07, MBA '09), Co-Founder and Chief of the Experience Management Institute (EXMI) and a Senior Lecturer in Fisher College of Business's graduate programs, and Vasiliki Stamouli (OSU MHRM '25), an EXMI Research Fellow in Applied AI in HR, the session connects human-capital practice with emerging research on responsible AI adoption.

Drawing on two large-scale transformation cases: the post-merger integration of the 8,000-employee Hellenic Telecommunications Organization (HTO Group) and a statewide classification and compensation modernization initiative serving 37,000 public employees, the presentation unpacks the realities of moving AI into governed application. Attendees will learn how a Job Architecture Ontology allows organizations to safely deploy AI to analyze fragmented data, calibrate levels, and modernize systems without abdicating human judgment.

How We Achieved AI Innovation at Scale

1. Untangling legacy data to build a trusted foundation
Scaling AI requires reliable inputs. We examine how AI extracted structured information from a 70-year archive of class specifications that are still being actively used today. The archive included typewritten documents later scanned into digital files and more recent PDFs, reflecting the evolving work of multiple professionals over time. We also show how AI synthesized qualitative interview data across merging entities at HTO Group. Attendees will see how AI accelerates the creation of a reliable fact base for comparing roles while preserving historical context.

2. Building dual-method comparison engines for transparent decision support
Innovation at scale requires transparency. We detail the technical approach used in a statewide Class Specifications Portal. The portal runs two independent comparison methods simultaneously: an LLM-based semantic similarity score (evaluating the meaning of role requirements) and a purely mathematical Jaccard text-overlap score (measuring exact word commonality). Presenting these distinct measures side by side helps human experts make better, more defensible classification decisions.

3. Enforcing a human-in-the-loop governance model
Because job architecture impacts employee livelihoods, organizational maturity is paramount. We share the governance frameworks deployed in both cases to ensure that AI-assisted drafting, synthesis, and comparison remained subject to mandatory expert validation. We discuss how to position AI to augment evidence gathering while ensuring HR and organizational leaders retain full ownership of all final policy, design, and employee-impact decisions.

Five Lessons for Scaling AI Innovation
Based on these implementations, the presentation will devote significant time to five transferable takeaways for practitioners and researchers:

Lesson 1: Anchor AI in a governed architecture, not legacy labels.
AI models are highly sensitive to their inputs. If an organization trains or prompts a model using inflated or inaccurate legacy job titles, the output will institutionalize past mistakes. Scalable AI in HR must be grounded in an objective role taxonomy based on the actual tasks, competencies, and scope of the work.

Lesson 2: Separate the extraction of facts from the judgment of value.
AI is exceptional at extracting structured data from unstructured historical documents, such as 1950s-era class specifications, and synthesizing qualitative interview themes. However, the valuation of that work, including determinations of internal equity and market competitiveness, must remain a human-led, policy-driven exercise.

Lesson 3: Use dual-method validation to build trust.
When introducing AI into high-stakes environments, do not rely on a "black box" score. By pairing an AI semantic-similarity assessment with a transparent, mathematical text-overlap calculation, organizations can give reviewers the confidence to accept AI insights while maintaining their own professional judgment.

Lesson 4: Define what is not changing.
In the HTO Group integration, employees feared that AI-assisted title alignment would result in demotions or pay cuts. Scaling AI requires mature change management. Leaders must clearly communicate the purpose of the technology, the definitions of the new architecture, and, crucially, the protections in place for incumbent employees.

Lesson 5: Treat AI as an input, not a substitute.
The most successful AI implementations in job architecture do not replace compensation analysts or HR business partners; they remove the administrative burden of document management and initial research. The statewide public-sector organization anticipates up to a 60% time savings in managing class specifications, time that will be reallocated to higher-value workforce strategy, internal service, and management of its evolving workforce systems.

Audience Takeaway
Designed for business and HR leaders, technology and workforce practitioners, researchers, faculty members, and graduate students, this session focuses on the practical realities of deploying AI in complex organizational environments. Attendees will leave with a clear understanding of how job architecture functions as a business operating system, and how disciplined, human-governed AI can be used to innovate and scale for the future of work.

title: Advice at Scale: What Happened When a Financial Advisory Practice Put AI Between the Advisor and the Client
abstract:
Financial advisory is a trust business. Clients making exit, succession, and legacy decisions are not evaluating a product - they are deciding whether to hand a stranger the outcome of thirty years of work. That makes it one of the harder places to scale AI, and a useful place to learn from.

This case study walks through what happened when an advisory practice introduced AI into client-facing work: intake and discovery, scenario modeling, meeting synthesis, and follow-up. The honest answer is that the wins and the failures came from different places than expected. AI collapsed the preparation cycle and made the analytical work faster and more consistent. It also produced confident, well-written output that was wrong in ways a client would never catch - and an advisor almost didn't.

Justin Maxwell will cover the foundations that had to exist before any of it could scale: what client data was allowed into a model and what was not, where a human signature was made non-negotiable, how output was reviewed before it reached a client, and the point at which the team stopped asking "can AI do this?" and started asking "should a client ever know AI did this?"

Attendees will leave with:

A practical framework for separating AI-appropriate work (synthesis, modeling, drafting) from relationship work that degrades when automated
A review-and-accountability structure for regulated, high-trust client output - including what to do when the model is fluent and wrong
An honest accounting of what didn't work, what was rolled back, and what would be done differently
The lessons are drawn from professional services but transfer to any organization where AI touches a client relationship that took years to earn and one bad output to lose.

No proprietary client data or trade secrets are disclosed.

title: Friction Discrimination: A Microfoundation of Entrepreneurial Judgment Under AI
abstract:
Motivation. Entrepreneurship theory has long located its central problem in judgment under genuine uncertainty, conditions where outcomes are not merely unknown but unknowable in advance (Knight, 1921). Kirzner's (1973) account of entrepreneurial alertness and Sarasvathy's (2001) effectuation framework both describe an expert logic for acting productively inside that uncertainty: effectual reasoning begins from a founder's actual means, treats surprise as leverageable rather than as deviation to correct, and treats commitment to a provisional position, not resolution of the unknown, as the engine of progress. This logic depends on a founder's willingness to remain inside not-knowing long enough for judgment to form, rather than reaching for the nearest available answer. Generative AI is structurally opposed to that willingness: its basic function is to resolve uncertainty quickly by supplying an answer, and it cannot distinguish a moment where struggle is building judgment (intrinsic, germane cognitive load) from a moment where struggle is merely inefficient (extraneous load; Sweller, 1988; Bjork & Bjork, 2020). Critically, neither can a novice using it, since the capacity to make that distinction is itself part of what the struggle is meant to build. This study introduces friction discrimination, the metacognitive capacity to distinguish productive struggle from non-productive friction, as the mechanism that determines whether a founder's, or a student's, encounter with AI supports or forecloses the development of effectual judgment.

Preliminary evidence. A classroom-embedded pilot in a large undergraduate entrepreneurship course, drawing on the same population and instrumentation as a companion feasibility presentation earlier this year, offers early behavioral evidence that this split is real rather than theoretical. AI-content classification across submissions was distinctly bimodal: one cluster of students sustained engagement with their own reasoning before and after consulting AI, while a second cluster replaced that reasoning outright, more consistent with two discrete strategies for handling uncertainty than with a single continuum of AI reliance. Within this distribution, a subset of students who protected their own reasoning nonetheless received peer feedback that was itself substantially AI-generated, suggesting the discipline effectuation requires, defending a position rather than simply receiving one, can be undercut on the evaluation side of a process even when a student holds it on the production side.

Methodology. Building on this pilot, a confirmatory design tests whether the specific role assigned to AI, functioning as a direct answer-provider versus a Socratic interlocutor restricted to questioning, shapes students' developing tolerance for the kind of unresolved uncertainty entrepreneurial judgment requires. The design uses a two-by-two Latin square crossing academic term and course modality so that AI role is not confounded with either factor, embedded in a required course across a full academic year, N approximately 700. All participants receive an identical, transparent protocol requiring a committed position before AI engagement; only AI's permitted role varies, and that variation is disclosed rather than withheld. A validated intolerance-of-uncertainty measure, operationalizing the Knightian construct this literature treats as foundational, is administered at three points aligned to the course's existing structure, producing a developmental trajectory rather than a single before-after comparison.

Implications. If AI's permitted role shapes the trajectory of students' capacity to tolerate genuine uncertainty, entrepreneurship education faces a specific, previously undertheorized design problem: teaching students to use AI well is not the same task as teaching them to become entrepreneurially capable, and in some configurations the two goals may conflict. Effectuation's founding claim, that expertise is a learnable logic rather than a fixed trait (Sarasvathy, 2001), implies that whether AI builds or erodes this capacity is a design question, not a foregone conclusion. The same mechanism carries a further implication at the organizational level: dynamic-capabilities accounts of competitive advantage assume capability is costly and slow to build, historically a source of protection from imitation (Teece, Pisano, & Shuen, 1997; Helfat & Peteraf, 2003). If friction discrimination is the individual-level capacity standing between AI availability and durable capability, it offers a microfoundational bridge from a classroom-level pedagogical mechanism to a firm-level question about whether capability can still be built and defended once judgment itself can be quietly outsourced.

title: From Frontier Models to Frugal Teams: Harnessing Domain Knowledge for Cost-Efficient Causal Discovery with AI Agents
abstract:
Motivation. Firms increasingly rely on causal structures, formalized as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), to uncover the causes and mechanisms underlying business outcomes, such as the drivers of demand, the sources of operational failures, and the pathways through which risks propagate through supply chain networks. Recovering these structures from observational data, a task known as causal discovery, is particularly difficult when the available observations are limited relative to the number and complexity of the relationships involved. Yet firms often possess substantial proprietary domain knowledge about the meaning, context, and plausible causal roles of the relevant variables. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) create a new opportunity to integrate such knowledge with observational evidence in causal discovery. However, available LLMs differ substantially in both capability and inference cost. Frontier models may reason more reliably about ambiguous or complex relationships, but relying on them throughout the discovery process can be prohibitively expensive at scale, whereas lower-cost models may be sufficient for many steps of the process but less reliable for others. The open question is therefore not whether stronger models improve causal discovery, but where in the process their additional capability is actually needed and worth its cost. We address this question by developing a multi-agent system for causal discovery that uses programmatic falsification tests to determine when a lower-cost model should seek guidance from a stronger model.

Methodology. We introduce CausalCascade, a two-agent AI system that treats model capability as a priced resource. The system operates through an iterative loop. In each iteration, a lower-cost Executor constructs or revises a candidate causal DAG using a structured knowledge base that captures domain context. A programmatic falsification module then tests the candidate DAG against observational data and returns structured feedback. When the feedback indicates a problem for which additional model capability may be valuable, the system invokes a more capable Advisor. The Advisor reads the current DAG, falsification results, and revision history from a shared context and returns a concise set of edge-level recommendations. The Executor uses the falsification feedback and, when available, the Advisor's recommendations to produce the next candidate DAG. The cycle continues until the system reaches the maximum number of iterations, at which point the Executor produces the final DAG. Successive graph versions, falsification results, and Advisor recommendations are logged, creating an auditable record of the discovery process.

We evaluate the system in collaboration with a leading North American telecommunications operator. The firm provided three proprietary causal DAGs (15, 30, and 57 nodes) sourced from its internal supply chain risk assessment. Together, the DAGs capture causal mechanisms at the market, procurement-category, and supplier levels. We treat these proprietary, expert-elicited DAGs as ground truth and generate small observational panels from them, allowing us to evaluate the accuracy of structure recovery while reducing concerns that the results are driven by memorization of public benchmark DAGs. In our implementation, we assign Claude Sonnet 4.6 to the Executor role and Claude Opus 4.8 to the Advisor role. Through controlled experiments, we compare CausalCascade with four classical causal-discovery algorithms (i.e., PC, GES, NOTEARS, and DAGMA), and two single-LLM baselines in which either the Executor model or the Advisor model performs the full discovery process alone.

Findings. CausalCascade and both single-LLM baselines recovered substantially more causal structure than the best classical algorithm across all three DAGs, demonstrating the value of incorporating domain knowledge when observational data is scarce. CausalCascade nearly matched the stronger LLM's average accuracy, achieving a mean F-score of 0.665 compared to 0.669 for the standalone stronger model, while incurring only 53% of its inference cost. CausalCascade achieved the highest F-score on two of the three DAGs. The Advisor's recommendations consistently improved the Executor's graph recovery. Complementary experiments using public benchmark DAGs supported that these results were not an artifact of benchmark memorization by the LLMs. The results also identified an important boundary condition: the Advisor was highly effective at removing or reorienting edges proposed by the Executor, but less reliable at proposing entirely missing edges. Consequently, the system is better suited for tasks where existing domain knowledge can yield a reasonably comprehensive initial graph.

Implications. This research provides a practical, scalable architecture for deploying AI in decision-critical causal discovery. We demonstrate that firms do not necessarily need to rely exclusively on their strongest models throughout the discovery process. By combining selective capability escalation with an auditable decision process, CausalCascade enables firms to manage inference costs efficiently while supporting governance, expert review, and organizational accountability by design. Broadly, this study highlights that organizational AI readiness depends not just on access to frontier models, but on the ability to provide AI agents with the right context and allocate reasoning capabilities where they generate the most value.

title: Reading over 170,000 letters with a machine: an AI-built tracker as a testbed for classification at scale
abstract:
This proposal discusses what happens when an AI assistant does most of the work of a research project and the human keeps the judgment. The setting is a live tracker I built to read the public comment letters on the SEC's semi-annual reporting proposal (File S7-2026-15), filed on May 5, 2026. The proposal would let public companies report twice a year instead of four times, swapping the quarterly 10-Q for a new 10-S. The proposal drew more than 170,000 comment letters, scattered across a docket that almost nobody scrolls to the bottom of. 
The tracker reads them, classifies them, and reports on the docket's sentiment in near real time. The project has contributed input to the public debate over the proposal and has been cited by multiple media outlets. Following that, I prepared two other trackers for two additional proposals.
The project demonstrates how human research skills and capabilities, coupled with AI computational abilities, with embedded controls at every decision point, can produce digital scholarship that is timely and important to the public discourse. 

What the tracker does

The pipeline has two phases, ingestion and classification, with a human decision gate before each.
Ingestion is the mechanical part. Claude (the Opus family, in Cowork) reads the SEC docket index, checks every letter's URL against the ones already processed, and downloads the new ones. De-duplication is the crucial step, because an evolving set of letters is re-ingested several times over the life of the projects. In one case, Claude flagged two letters filed the same day, same last name, with a near-identical four-point argument, where one called the savings "minuscule" and the other a "nothing burger." It judged them related but distinct, proposed keeping both, and asked me to confirm. The machine provides throughput and a first read; the human pilots adjudicate, confirm, or adjust.
Classification is the research problem. Each letter gets three labels: its stance on the proposal, the entity behind the writer, and the rationale for its position. I built the AI raters the way we normally use research assistants. Each letter is read three times for stance, three for entity, and three for rationale, nine reads in all. The three reads are not identical because each follows a different rubric. One reads plainly. One reads as a literalist who credits only what is on the page. One reads as a skeptic hunting for the catch. The majority vote is the label, and because there are three votes, I also report the strength of agreement, from unanimous to split.
The three tasks differ in difficulty, and the disagreement is an honest measure of that. Stance is close to solved: three human experts agree at a kappa of 0.82, and the strong models match the human labels at a Cohen's kappa near 0.85, running as high as 0.92. Entity is harder, because the docket lists a submitter title that often contradicts the letter body. Three retail investors appear on the docket as CEO or CFO, yet each writes as a private individual with no company in the text. The experts fall to 0.67 on entity, the models to between 0.34 and 0.59. Rationale is harder still: I anchor about 20 argument families to the questions the SEC itself raised, a letter can address several at once, and even careful human readers stop agreeing.
Two design choices carry the method. First, the vote decides, and I do not override it, even when a letter comes from someone I recognize. Second, I also ran every letter through 14 different models, adding new ones as they appear, so a label that survives three rubrics, a second unrelated model, and a human spot-check is robust. I also gave 20 letters to human raters and posted the comparison publicly, so the machine can be judged against people on the same letters.
Another important element of the process is creating human-guarded gates. The daily cycle pauses before it downloads a batch, before it classifies, and before it publishes. A version without gates would run faster, but it might drift. Without judgmental checks, the errors would accumulate. 
As of early August, of 159,743 classified letters, 158,977 oppose the proposal and 335 support it, with the rest conditional or taking no position; adding the organized form-letter campaigns pushes the opposition past 210,000. 
An interesting comparison is to a docket for a similar proposal (although not an official one) from 2018. The doc ket there is smaller, and I created a tracker for it as well, containing 89 letters. 

Why it matters

In this project, I develop a tracker of multi-rubric, multi-model AI classification of regulatory comment letters. The data are real, the stakes are public, and the disagreements are on the record. I hope it offers a reusable template for doing careful data work with AI.
The tracker has already contributed to the public debate, drawing coverage from multiple outlets, and the same method now runs two more SEC dockets, on filer-status relief and on the rescission of the climate-disclosure rule. A fuller account of the tracker and the collaboration behind it is on The Dig.

title: Jurisdictional Embeddedness and AI Regulation: Evidence from the EU AI Act
abstract: We study how AI regulation affects firm valuation using the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the world's first comprehensive AI framework. In an event study around the April 2021 proposal, we find firms combining deeper EU presence with faster AI hiring earned higher announcement returns, suggesting markets value "jurisdictional embeddedness'': the depth and durability of a firm's operating presence in the EU jurisdiction is associated with higher market value for AI-intensive firms. The effect is stronger for high-risk AI, for firms with stable and concentrated EU presence, or prior compliance experience, unexplained by size, foreign exposure, or lobbying. EU-embedded, AI-expanding firms increase within-firm EU revenue share more when peers are less embedded.

title: More Than a Label: AI Disclosure Intensity, Justification, and User Responses on a Gaming Platform
abstract:
In the digital era, the entertainment landscape has been radically transformed by the rise of the interactive entertainment industry. Video game industry has evolved into a dominant global economic and cultural force, serving as an important sandbox for examining how emerging technologies reshape product development, platform ecosystems, and user behavior.
Concurrently, the game development process is undergoing a paradigm shift fueled by rapid advancements in Generative AI and LLMs. This technological leap has drastically reduced production cycles and democratized game development. However, this also creates a tension between technological efficiency and user acceptance.
Recognizing the growth of AI content and the demand for transparency, Steam, the leading gaming community and distributing platform, implemented a policy in January 2024, requiring disclosure of AI usage for all games on the platform. Developers are required to disclose whether, and to what extent, AI tools were utilized. These disclosure descriptions are displayed on product store pages. 
This policy shift introduces uncertainty regarding user perception. We still know very little about the influence of AI disclosure on users in highly creative, hedonic digital marketplaces. From online communities to news articles, sentiment regarding AI involvement in artifacts is always highly polarized. However, existing discussions mainly focus on the use of AI in traditional creative content such as fiction, images, and voices, while video game production presents a unique context. Compared with old-fashioned entertainment contents, games always retain a closer relationship with technology innovation and advances. Consequently, players may hold distinct perceptions of AI involvement compared with audiences of more traditional products. Moreover, unlike standardized AI labels, flexible disclosure descriptions provide richer information and enable more nuanced analysis. Therefore, we raise the following research questions: What is the impact of AI usage disclosure on users on Steam gaming platform? How do the heterogeneities of AI disclosure descriptions affect the users?
This paper relates to several streams of literature. First, AI transparency literature, which establishes that revealing algorithmic intervention can be a double-edged sword, frequently triggering algorithmic aversion. Second, research on strategic disclosure decisions, which discusses how corporations make disclosure decisions to manage recipient impressions. Third, research on information disclosure style, examining how communication styles modify user reactions, and how consumers actively evaluate not just what is said, but how it is framed.
We leverage game-week level public data from Steam. The disclosure policy is introduced in 2024. However, we observed that most games did not include AI disclosure immediately when the policy took effect. Rather, the disclosure time varies between games, providing opportunities for a staggered DID setting. 
The treatment group is games with AI disclosures, while treatment time is defined as the disclosure date. To construct a suitable control group, we identified games without AI disclosures that were officially recommended by Steam as similar games on each treated game page. Steam's algorithm considers characteristics such as genre, user behavior, and gameplay similarity, providing a relevant pool of comparable titles. From this pool, we further match the games by PSM on three characteristics: review counts, initial price, and release time. The dependent variable is follower count, an important indicator of user interest on the platform, and highly associated with revenue (Ma, 2025). As robustness check, we also estimated all models using CEM weights and obtained consistent results. 
Additionally, we utilize LLMs to analyze the characteristics of the disclosure descriptions. The style of disclosure varies substantially across games. We focus on two dimensions: AI usage intensity and disclosure language style. We manually labeled a subset of the sample and employed GPT-5.4-mini model to perform Few-Shot Learning classification of the descriptions. The classification accuracies are 75% and 90% for intensity and style, respectively. [CL1.1]
For results, we first examine the overall impact of AI usage disclosure. Both never-treated and not-yet-treated CSDID results indicate that disclosure has a statistically significant negative effect on follower number (effect-size -22%), suggesting that disclosure of AI usage in games is associated with reduced engagement on platform.
We next investigate the heterogeneity effects. Through LLM, disclosure texts are classified into high-intensity and low-intensity AI usage groups. Subgroup DID results indicate that high-intensity games experience a significantly larger decline in followers, while low-intensity games show a much smaller and statistically insignificant effect. This suggests that users distinguish between different levels of AI involvement rather than reacting only to the existence of AI disclosure. Describing AI usage in a more limited capacity appears to mitigate the decline in engagement.
We then examine the impact of linguistic style. Disclosure texts are divided into high-justification and low-justification groups. The results indicate that games using highly justificatory language do not exhibit a statistically significant decline in followers, whereas games with less justification experience a significant reduction. This reveals that justificatory description of AI usage can buffer the negative effects associated with AI disclosure. One possible explanation is that high-justification disclosures typically provide additional context regarding AI usage or reassurance of human involvement, thereby reducing uncertainty and emphasizing human oversight. 
We contribute to literature in following aspects. First, we extend AI transparency research by providing causal evidence from a large-scale digital platform, especially in a novel video games setting. Second, we contribute to research on strategic disclosure decisions and format. We reveal that when disclosure is mandatory, producers retain strategic flexibility through the design of the disclosure itself. Disclosure characteristics can function as informational signals that shape user interpretations beyond the simple presence of AI disclosure.
From a managerial perspective, we demonstrate that platforms should consider not only whether disclosure is required but also how disclosure information is presented. For developers, we reveal that disclosure strategy remains important even under mandatory disclosure policies. Developers should carefully communicate the extent of AI usage and emphasize the continued role of human designers throughout the development process. 
More broadly, the results suggest that producers adopting AI technologies should recognize that users evaluate not only the technology itself but also how it is communicated. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into creative industries, thoughtful disclosures may become an important component of technology governance and user management.

title: When Transparency Meets "AI Slop": The Effects of AI Labeling on Creator and Viewer Behavior on Pinterest
abstract: Generative AI has created new governance challenges for visual content platforms by making synthetic images easier to produce while raising concerns about authenticity, content quality, and user trust. This study examines the behavioral consequences of platform-enforced AI labeling on Pinterest. Using a longitudinal creator-week panel covering 9,706 creators and 1,474,552 Pins from December 2025 to April 2026, we estimate the effects of AI labeling on a propensity score matched sample. Our main approach employs a staggered difference-in-differences design using CSDID, with an interaction-weighted DID estimator as a robustness check. We find that AI labeling significantly reduces creators' weekly content production and follower growth. The main CSDID estimates imply a 16% decline in newly posted Pins and a 16.1% decline in new followers after labeling. In contrast, new comments and likes do not change significantly at the creator or Pin level. However, AI-related and negative AI-related comments increase by 0.3% and 0.2%, respectively, suggesting that the label makes AI somewhat more salient in audience discussion. Heterogeneity analyses show that although posting declines similarly across popularity groups, the follower-growth penalty is larger for more popular creators (18.6% vs. 9.9%). AI labeling also reduces new Pins by 15.5% and new followers by 13.3% among active creators, while estimates for inactive creators are not statistically significant. Potential platform mislabeling, as evaluated through human perception, is associated with significantly fewer subsequent Pins and lower follower growth. We also observe more consistent effects for inspired-to categories and stronger posting effects among creators whose Pins have greater potential for real-life implementation. These findings contribute to research on AI disclosure, platform governance, and creator economies by showing that platform-enforced AI labeling can reshape both audience reactions and creators' productivity.

title: Where Bubbles Hide: Overvaluation and the Term Structure of Disagreement
abstract: We develop model-motivated, closed form empirical predictors of overvaluation persistence and level, above and beyond canonical shorting fees, idiosyncratic volatility, and one-period-ahead analyst dispersion. First, our model predicts that overvaluation correction over any horizon is proportional to the resolution share, the fraction of disputed value resolved within that horizon. Second, our model predicts that overvaluation levels equal disagreement times the present value of disputed cash flows. Bubbles therefore form where disagreement attaches to a large share of firm value, and rationally persist where those disputed cash flows are distant and slow to resolve. Taking these closed-form empirical predictors to the data using a new machine-learning measure of long-horizon disagreement, we find overvaluation persistence is predicted by the resolution share, and that overvaluation levels, as measured by existing mispricing proxies, have 8-12\% of their cross-sectional variation explained by the present value of disputed cash flows. Together, our empirical and theoretical results suggest that it is not only disagreement, nor only duration, that affect overvaluation, but the term structure of disagreement.

title: Substantive vs Symbolic AI Disclosure and Subsequent Safety Risks & Performance: Evidence from US Public Pharmaceutical Firms
abstract:
Pharmaceutical firms talk about artificial intelligence more than almost any other industry, and the claims are large. Industry estimates suggest the AI-in-drug-development market is growing at over 30% annually (Grand View Research, 2023), and consulting analyses project that AI could compress discovery-to-proof-of-concept timelines by 35% to 50% (BCG & Wellcome, 2023). But such projections rest largely on company-reported figures that have yet to be independently verified (Nature, 2023). The reality is less settled. As of first quarter of 2026, no AI-discovered drug has received full FDA approval (Guldvog, 2026) and the most advanced candidate has only recently reported randomized Phase 2a results (Xu et al., 2025). AI-discovered molecules clear Phase I safety testing at unusually high rates, but their Phase II performance, the first real test of efficacy in patients, is not better than historical industry averages (Jayatunga et al., 2024). Separate literature shows that, despite many firms disclosing AI use, it may actually mean little. Because AI disclosure is voluntary, inexpensive, and difficult to verify, firms have incentives to overstate it. Barrios et al. (2025) show that AI disclosures predict operational performance only when backed by credible AI hiring, and Basnet et al. (2025) find markets reward concrete implementation claims but ignore speculative ones. Both studies measure success financially, through stock returns or firm performance. They suggest that AI disclosures fall into two kinds: substantive disclosures backed by actual implementation, and symbolic ones that are not. Whether that difference in AI disclosure predicts safety and regulatory outcomes has not been examined.
We therefore ask two questions. Does AI adoption by pharmaceutical firms change postmarket drug safety, measured by product recalls and adverse-event mortality, and regulatory performance, measured by approval activity and review times? And does any such effect depend on whether a firm's AI disclosure is substantive or symbolic?
We address these questions with a firm-year panel of publicly traded US pharmaceutical firms. The panel covers 2010 to 2024 and currently includes 323 firms and 4,845 firm-year observations. AI disclosure is extracted from SEC 10-K and 8-K filings through the EDGAR API, using a keyword dictionary based on Ferreira and Carneiro (2025). First, we classify each firm's AI disclosures as substantive or symbolic. Substantive disclosures describe a specific implemented application in discovery, clinical development, manufacturing, or pharmacovigilance. Symbolic disclosures are generic, forward-looking, or risk-factor boilerplate. Classification is LLM-assisted and validated against independent human coding of a stratified sample, with inter-rater agreement reported. Then, we tag the stage of AI use following the FDA/CDER lifecycle taxonomy: target identification, molecule design and preclinical work, clinical trials, manufacturing and quality, and postmarket safety.
Our outcome variables come from three public sources merged to the panel. Recall outcomes come from FDA Enforcement Reports (openFDA), covering 911 human drug recall events involving listed firms during the sample period. Mortality outcomes come from FAERS death reports linked to firms. Approval outcomes are drawn from Drugs@FDA: counts of NDA and BLA approvals per firm-year, submission-to-approval review times, and expedited-pathway designations. All outcomes are revenue-normalized.
Our preliminary evidence shows that AI-disclosing firms average 6.99 recalls per firm-year before disclosure, falling to 5.11 afterward, with declines in death reports as well, while non-disclosing firms show no comparable shift. We treat these patterns as descriptive rather than causal. Firms that disclose AI are larger and carry broader product portfolios. The number of firms observed also falls sharply as event time increases. And a firm's disclosure year tells us when it chose to talk about AI, not when it started using it. Reverse causality is also plausible: firms may adopt AI in quality or pharmacovigilance functions precisely because they experienced safety problems.
In the analysis process, we will estimate staggered difference-in-differences models centered on each firm's first AI disclosure year, with planned controls for firm size, R&D intensity, firm age, years since IPO, and therapeutic-area composition. The same design applies to regulatory outcomes in terms of approval counts and review time because AI adoption in discovery and clinical development should plausibly move regulatory throughput even where it does not move safety. The substantive-versus-symbolic classification enters the estimation directly. Rather than analyzing the two groups separately, we include both in a single model and allow the treatment effect to differ by disclosure type. This preserves the full panel, produces an event-study path for each group, and lets us test directly whether the difference between them is statistically significant. Symbolic disclosers face the same incentives to announce AI as substantive ones but have not implemented it, so they serve as a within-treatment comparison group rather than a second set of controls. If the safety improvements we observe reflect AI use, they should appear among substantive disclosers and be absent among symbolic ones. If instead both groups improve, the pattern more likely reflects the kind of firm that talks about AI than AI itself, and this is the result that would most change how we read the preliminary evidence.
The study aims to separate AI hype from AI readiness. Prior work has shown that AI disclosures predict financial performance only when firms actually invest in AI. We explore whether the same holds for drug safety and regulatory outcomes, where the stakes are patient harm rather than share price. The measurement pipeline is built entirely from public data and can be reused, which matters because no registry of AI-enabled drug development currently exists (Jayatunga et al., 2024). The findings will interest the FDA as it develops AI guidance, and the SEC as it looks more closely at AI claims in corporate filings.
