title: A Theoretical Framework for AI-Enabled Digital Twin Orchestration
abstract:
Extended Abstract Proposal

Motivation: 
Digital twins enabled by artificial intelligence (AI) represent a significant trajectory of improvement from static and descriptive presentations of real-world environments into intelligent, dynamic systems capable of supporting continuous adaptation, autonomous decision-making, and efficient human-AI collaboration. As organizations and societies continue integrating AI alongside traditional digital twin technologies, they are met with alarming statistics: 42% of companies lack vision for digital twin deployment, while 70% of digital transformations (including digital twins) fail. The challenges facing digital twins are increasingly extending beyond the techno-centric and domain-specific perspective of coordinating individual technologies to orchestrating human, physical, and computational resources toward shared purpose and unified goals. This transition requires discussions that will advance collective knowledge and understanding about digital twins from a non-techno-centric view and in a domain-independent fashion. These factors have helped expand the intellectual gap between our understanding of heterogeneous digital twin system parts in isolation versus as an operationally valid twin. To help address this gap, this work takes a theoretical approach by borrowing from other fields of knowledge where orchestration is well established to propose an orchestration view of AI-enabled digital twins. 

Theoretical Development: 
AI-enabled digital twins are crucial to explore because organizations of various domains - supply chain, engineering, smart cities, maritime, etc. - either plan to or are currently using them to make critical strategic and operational decisions. However, most organizations still aren't making effective use of the technology after implementation, if at all. For example, 55% of organizations cite poor collaboration and governance as factors leading to digital twin failure. A key critical success factor of digital twin success, especially when enabled by AI is orchestration. The key question this research explores is: "how should the various parts and participants of a digital twin system be intentionally orchestrated and transformed into an AI-enabled digital twin?" 

Based on existing literature, there are four dimensions that can be foundational for discussing AI digital twin orchestration - orchestration infrastructure, orchestration architecture, orchestration governance, and orchestration principles:

• Orchestration Infrastructure: Enabling assets or conditions that must exist before orchestration can occur (e.g., include data, IoT sensors, AI models, data lakes). 

• Orchestration Architecture: The purposeful arrangement and organization of infrastructure to produce the intended outcome (e.g., this would include data stacks, technology stacks, integration stacks, etc.). 

• Orchestration Governance: The vertical hierarchical arrangement of relationships that helps determine roles of authority, scope, and process for making and communicating decisions that will affect the quality of the outcome and outcome itself. 

• Orchestration Principles: The set of universal rules, guidelines, and judgements applied across the entire orchestration framework and helps determine how each level and role should operate to ensure the unified outcome meets goals and objectives. 

While orchestration infrastructure and architecture have been researched extensively, orchestration governance and principles have been studied far less. To help advance our understanding of how digital twins can be managed, this research proposes the AI-Enabled Digital Twin Orchestration Framework - a socio-technical systems orchestration perspective view of digital twins focusing mostly on its orchestration governance and principles, both which are crucial for organizations and societies to understand to design, implement, and manage digital twins that deliver expected results. Orchestration governance levels include institutional governance and computational governance. Institutional governance helps us understand the who, what, why, and how of decisions and authority throughout the digital twin. There are four levels of institutional governance - value, enterprise, domain, twin instance. Computational governance, which includes digital twin-AI harness and technology foundation, is about translating the governance into consistent and functioning controls over technologies serving as digital twin interfaces. While orchestration governance is conceptualized as vertical, the orchestration mega-principles are conceptualized as horizontal, making them essential regardless of the governance level. These principles describe how all parts of an AI digital twin system should coordinate and interact to operate as an adaptive, coherent, and unified system. The framework identifies and discusses six such principles - purposeful orchestration, idiomatic orchestration, coherence is key, data is the lifeblood, adaptive orchestration, and humans-in-the-loop. Lastly, the framework discusses relative usage volume and nature of usage for both generative and agentic AI.

Practical implications and limitations: 
Although the model developed in this work is domain-independent, challenges will still arise when the size, scope, and complexity of an AI-enabled digital twin system increase to the ecosystem or societal levels. The most likely orchestration challenges will be synchronization, interoperability, cyber security, data governance, data sharing policies, gaining stakeholder consensus and commitment, institutional alignment, access to funding, and securing digital twin expertise. In addition, agentic AI will present a fundamental shift in the nature of the human-AI interaction that developed so strongly during the rise of generative AI, and organizations most take care to not underestimate the intricacies of this shift.

Research contributions and future research: 
There are two primary contributions this study makes to existing research. First, in contrast to other views prevalent in digital twin research, this study adopts a socio-technical systems orchestration view of digital twins enabled by AI technologies. Second, the AI-Enabled Digital Twin Orchestration framework is proposed and used to discuss institutional governance, computational governance, and universal orchestration mega-principles as necessary for successful orchestration of AI-enabled digital twins, regardless of domain or scale. 

There are a few paths forward for research as well. First, while there has been expansive research done on traditional digital twins in certain contexts (e.g., supply chain digital twins), there has been little research (theoretical and empirical) conducted on AI orchestration, including within the context of a digital twin. Future studies that introduce new theories and empirically validate factors and challenges of AI orchestration governance and principles will prove beneficial for organizations striving for successful testing and deployment of digital twin systems. Second, the rate of adoption of both generative and agentic AI could mean that digital twins will become a competitive lever. At the same time, industries will see a variety of implementation models. Future research can endeavor to explore the maturity of different models and identify competitive strategies.

title: Automation or Augmentation? Common Knowledge Frictions and Auditor Pipeline Risk
abstract:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping skill-intensive professions, and the audit profession sits at the front of this transformation: major accounting firms are investing heavily in AI tools that can automate document retrieval, anomaly detection, and other junior audit tasks, while simultaneously asserting that AI complements human auditors and raises their productivity. Public narratives diverge sharply between these automation and augmentation views, and the academic evidence is equally split - some studies find AI displaces junior audit tasks and reduces headcount, while others find AI adoption raises demand for human auditors. Against this backdrop, the U.S. audit labor market displays a puzzling combination of facts. Accounting enrollments and CPA exam participation have declined steadily, shrinking the entry-level pipeline. Yet audit firms continue to post stable or growing numbers of junior vacancies, and positions take longer to fill. Standard theory predicts that falling supply against stable demand should push wages up, but auditor wages have barely moved across experience levels for over a decade. Each fact alone is easy to explain; the conjunction is not. A competitive market would bid the wage up until the smaller cohort cleared. Market power, wage norms, menu costs, and cobweb entry lags can each account for one fact, but none can generate declining entry, elevated vacancies, and flat wages together.
This paper proposes and tests one explanation: asymmetric common knowledge about AI's two effects. Everyone - students and firms alike - observes both the automation narrative (AI displaces junior tasks) and the augmentation narrative (AI makes each auditor more valuable). The friction is not disagreement about fundamentals but uncertainty about whether others have absorbed the same information. The automation story travels through public professional media and is close to common knowledge: everyone knows it, and knows that everyone knows it. The augmentation story propagates through decentralized, university-borne experience - courses, pilots, peer discussion - whose reach nobody can verify for anyone else.
We formalize this mechanism in a model in which students enter the qualified-auditor pipeline before firms recruit. Entry decisions reinforce each other: the benefits of joining a profession - specialized instruction, peer learning, firm training, employer recognition - depend on cohort scale, so each student's entry response to a technological effect is amplified by expected peer entry. Because augmentation sits further from common knowledge than automation, its positive effect receives less coordination amplification, and entry contracts even when the technology favors human-AI complementarity. After the cohort is fixed, firms simultaneously post wage scales. Wage posting is itself a coordination game: a firm that raises pay unilaterally mostly poaches applicants from rivals and invites matching, so each posted scale weights rivals' expected scales more than fundamentals. Each shock then passes into wages at its own commonality rate: the wage prices the common automation content, while the unpriced augmentation content accumulates as unfilled positions. The model's sharpest result is that this asymmetry is not merely sufficient but necessary: under any symmetric-information wage-setting friction, rising vacancies and flat junior offers are mutually exclusive, because both reflect the same composite of news. The joint pattern in the data therefore identifies the friction.
Higher-order beliefs cannot be measured at scale, so we test the mechanism through its equilibrium footprints and an exposure design. We use departures of AI faculty from U.S. universities to industry as shocks to the local formation of common knowledge about AI's augmentation value. Universities generate shared curricula, assignments, and seminars that let many students learn the same things and infer that their peers are learning them too; a departure weakens this shared signal without changing AI's technical capabilities, firms' production technology, or the widely publicized automation narrative. Using matched employer-employee data from Revelio Labs, job postings from Burning Glass, and audit outcomes from Audit Analytics, we estimate stacked difference-in-differences models around departure events, comparing treated universities and states with matched local controls and geographically neighboring never-treated states.
Four results line up with the model's predictions. First, entry falls: the share of accounting graduates entering audit careers drops by 2.5 percentage points, a 5.7% decline from baseline, emerging three years after a departure and peaking at six. Second, excess demand appears on both margins: junior auditor postings rise 17.4%, and postings remain open 4.8% longer, concentrated precisely at the junior level where the missing cohort would have arrived. Third, wages do not respond: staff and management auditor wages in treated states are statistically and economically indistinguishable from controls throughout the event window. Fourth, audit quality erodes with a long lag: abnormal accruals rise and modified opinions fall as smaller, less AI-complementary cohorts accumulate within offices.
The findings reframe the auditor pipeline problem. It is not simply automation displacing workers: no agent in our model, or plausibly in the data, is wrong about the technology. It is a coordination failure rooted in beliefs about others, and it identifies universities as upstream information infrastructure. Because universities generate the shared learning environment that makes augmentation knowledge common, they are uniquely positioned to repair the friction. The model also implies a firm-side lever: earlier, credible disclosure of pipeline statistics would rebuild common knowledge among firms and compress the vacancy-wage wedge. The mechanism generalizes to any skilled profession where a technology simultaneously automates routine tasks and augments human judgment, and where the two narratives travel through channels that differ in their distance from common knowledge.

title: Beyond Keywords: Impact of LLM-Powered Search in Online Marketplaces
abstract: Online marketplaces match customers to products through search, yet traditional keyword-based retrieval requires that the words in a query overlap with the words in a product listing. When the search queries and product information do not overlap, relevant products might go undiscovered. We study how augmenting keyword matching with LLM-powered semantic search--retrieval based on meaning rather than word overlap--affects marketplace outcomes. In a randomized field experiment on one of the world's largest online marketplaces (approximately 1.2 million sessions, three arms), we find that semantic search changes behavior across the entire customer journey. Users write longer queries and reformulate less. The products they browse have fewer reviews and come from less prominent sellers. Both models increase conversion, and purchased items are higher-priced and less likely to be cataloged products. These effects arise without changes to the catalog, interface, or information available to the platform, and without customers knowing the system has changed. Our findings establish that how a platform processes existing textual information is a consequential operational lever for marketplace outcomes. They also document behavioral adaptation to invisible back-end AI.

title: Do Non-Competes Slow the Diffusion of AI?
abstract: We investigate whether noncompete agreements (NCAs) slow the diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI). Using state-level NCA events from 2009 to 2024 and individual employment histories from Revelio Labs, we find that stronger enforceability sharply reduces the AI labor mobility. Across firms, AI worker inflows and outflows fall by roughly 23 and 27 percent of their means, and the declines appear for both in-state and cross-state moves, pointing to a broad mobility friction rather than a narrow relocation channel. Downstream, stronger enforceability is followed by 16 to 21 percent fewer AI patent applications and fewer new AI-related firms. Because AI know-how is largely tacit and embodied in scarce human capital, restricting mobility appears to slow AI diffusion rather than merely redistribute its returns.

title: Start Wide, Not Deep: What a Cross-Functional First Cohort Teaches an Institution About Itself
abstract:
When a large organization starts with AI, the instinct is to go deep in one place: pick the department with the clearest use case, run a pilot, prove it, expand. It is an efficient way to learn a great deal about one department.

Cuyahoga Community College - Ohio's first and largest community college, roughly 3,000 faculty and staff across four campuses serving more than 42,000 students - went the other way. Between February and April 2026 it ran its first AI program with fifteen people drawn from fifteen different corners of the institution: faculty across nursing, IT, English and creative arts; deans; IT services; compliance and risk; interactive marketing; executive operations; the corporate training arm; and administrative staff. Each was already curious about AI in their own role. None were sent.

This case study makes the argument for that starting shape, shows what it produced, and is honest about what it did not.

**The core argument.** A first cohort's most valuable output is not the pilot result. It is what the institution learns about itself - which roles take to these tools, which workflows they actually land in, where the friction is real versus rhetorical, and who the credible internal voices turn out to be. A departmental pilot cannot produce that, because it only ever reports on one department. Going wide costs efficiency and buys institutional intelligence, and for an organization deciding how to spend the next three years, that trade is usually correct.

**What attendees will learn:**

1. **A selection logic built on representation and existing interest.** We will cover how the cohort was assembled - breadth across function, campus and seniority, weighted toward people already exploring AI in their own work - and why volunteer curiosity outperformed both mandated participation and technical aptitude as a selection criterion at this stage. The executive sponsor's stated goal was people open enough to explore, not people who already knew the most.

2. **Tailoring the learning to each participant's actual goals, and what that costs.** Rather than a common curriculum with a shared exercise, participants worked their own real problems throughout: a nursing instructor on personalized student feedback, a compliance director on preliminary risk research, an executive operations leader on reporting into a president's office, an IT faculty member on assessment design for a software automation course. We will be concrete about the delivery model that makes this possible - small cohort, in-person core sessions with a virtual option, follow-on 1:1 coaching sessions - and about where it is expensive and where it is fragile.

3. **Cross-pollination as a designed outcome, not a happy accident.** Faculty learning beside compliance, beside marketing, beside IT services produced a shared institutional vocabulary and a pattern of transfer across functions that a departmental cohort structurally forecloses. We will show specific examples of a technique or workflow moving between functions that had no prior reason to talk, and name the conditions that made it possible - including the ones that were uncomfortable.

4. **The executive sponsor as an embedded observer.** The college's CIO did not sponsor from a distance; she participated as a learner alongside her own staff and faculty. That put a senior leader in the room watching, in real time, how fifteen different roles engaged with the same tools and applied them to genuinely different work. We will argue this is one of the most underrated returns on a first cohort - leadership intelligence that no readout, dashboard or vendor report reproduces - and show how it shaped the institution's subsequent planning.

5. **What we measured, and what we would measure differently.** Beyond hours saved (a mean of 8.8 self-reported hours weekly), we tracked *capacity unlock* - 77% agreed AI freed them for important work they previously had no time for - and *new capability*, where 69% reported reaching a quality level they could not before. We also found what we now consider the healthiest governance signal available: concerns training should resolve did (the knowledge gap fell from five participants to zero, plagiarism from eleven to five, misinformation from nine to four), while concerns that should persist for any AI-using professional remained (data privacy held at eleven, accuracy at eleven, overdependence at ten). Participants ended more able to identify AI risk, not less worried about it.

**Honest limits.** Findings draw on a pre-program readiness survey (n=15), a post-program impact survey (n=13, 87% response), twelve matched pairs, and structured retrospectives with the executive sponsor after each phase. Self-reported time savings are self-reported. This cohort was intentionally curated and a second will not resemble it. Our recommendation measure used a 1-5 scale and is not a true NPS. We have no long-horizon follow-up yet showing whether gains held. We will also cover what emerged that we did not design for - including a backlog of unfinished cross-institutional workflows, and early signs that some participants may become credible peer teachers, which was never the program's premise and would require its own design.

**Approach and format.** Roughly two-thirds narrative case, one-third transferable framework, built for a room holding both practitioners deciding what to fund and researchers deciding what to study. The session will incorporate the client's voice through recorded participant and executive-sponsor segments; if scheduling permits, a member of the college's cohort will co-present live, and we will confirm with the program committee as the agenda firms.

**Who this is for.** Leaders responsible for enterprise AI enablement, HR and L&D teams designing internal upskilling, higher-education and executive-education administrators, and researchers studying AI adoption and organizational change. The setting is higher education; the constraints - distributed workforce, no discretionary time, high governance sensitivity, no appetite for a big-bang rollout - are not.

title: Pricing the Physical Constraints of AI: Evidence from U.S. AI-Energy Policy
abstract:
The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is commonly viewed as a technology shock centered on computing, software, and data. Yet AI deployment at scale depends on scarce, location-specific complementary capital, including electricity generation, grid capacity, interconnection, cooling systems, and sites capable of serving large and reliable power loads. Policies intended to support AI deployment may therefore create their most important valuation effects outside the AI sector. This paper studies how equity markets allocate the expected benefits and costs of U.S. AI-energy policy across the infrastructure chain. Our central finding is that these policies are not primarily capitalized as positive shocks to AI firms. Their most systematic valuation effects instead accrue to energy, grid-equipment, and physical-infrastructure firms that supply the constrained inputs required for AI deployment.
We analyze major U.S. policy announcements from April 2025 through March 2026 that address the energy requirements of AI and data-center infrastructure. Although presented as part of a broader AI agenda, these policies concern siting and permitting, electricity generation, grid reliability, large-load interconnection, infrastructure cost allocation, ratepayer protection, and behind-the-meter power. We construct a sample of publicly traded firms positioned along the data-center electricity chain and classify them into AI and cloud infrastructure, power suppliers and utilities, grid equipment, industrial infrastructure, and site-related real estate. Using daily returns, we estimate Fama-French abnormal returns over narrow announcement windows. Consecutive announcements surrounding the July 2025 AI Action Plan are treated as one policy cluster to avoid overlapping windows.
The cross-sectional evidence is substantially more consistent with a complementary-infrastructure interpretation than with a generic technology-support interpretation. Grid-equipment and physical-infrastructure suppliers exhibit the most systematic positive responses to policies that expand generation capacity, facilitate large-load integration, or increase expected investment in the electricity system. These firms provide the equipment, construction capacity, and engineering services needed when AI-driven electricity demand places additional pressure on the grid. Power suppliers and utilities also respond strongly, but the sign depends on the policy margin. They benefit when policy raises the value of generation, reliability, or large-load service, but can lose when announcements constrain cost recovery, protect ratepayers, or encourage alternative arrangements for supplying data-center electricity.
By contrast, AI and cloud firms do not experience uniformly positive announcement returns. Some policies reduce uncertainty about future electricity access and benefit downstream AI firms. Others reveal the scale of the generation, interconnection, and infrastructure investment required for continued data-center expansion, producing weak or negative responses. Site-related effects likewise depend on whether properties combine suitable location with credible access to power. Overall, investors treat AI-energy policy primarily as a shock to the supply and financing of complementary infrastructure, rather than as a general subsidy to AI companies.
We supplement the portfolio evidence with textual measures constructed from earnings calls available strictly before each announcement. The measures capture exposure to data-center demand, load growth, grid and interconnection constraints, power supply and reliability, infrastructure cost allocation, and behind-the-meter generation. Within each event and infrastructure basket, we distinguish exposure to channels directly addressed by the policy from exposure to unmatched channels. For the more fully covered 2025 announcements, firms whose pre-event discussions align with the economic constraint targeted by policy experience stronger returns than firms exposed mainly to unmatched channels. The relationship weakens when later events with more limited transcript coverage are included. We therefore interpret this evidence as supportive of channel-specific pricing, rather than as a definitive mechanism test.
We next examine whether the policy cycle is followed by changes in observable interactions between AI firms and the energy sector. Using Capital IQ Key Developments, we identify targeted contacts involving both an AI firm and an energy-side firm. Energy firms without prior AI-related contact become more likely to enter such interactions after the 2025 policy shift, whereas firms with an existing contact history show little comparable increase. A stricter text screen that excludes conferences and financial transactions and requires substantive cooperation or implementation activity yields the same extensive-margin pattern. The expansion therefore appears to involve the entry of previously unlinked energy and infrastructure firms, rather than merely greater activity among firms already associated with AI.
Announcement returns, however, do not identify which previously unlinked energy firms subsequently enter these interactions. Markets recognize that electricity suppliers, grid-equipment producers, and infrastructure firms as a group become more valuable as AI deployment expands, but are less able to identify the particular firms that later form observable AI-energy links. Complementary firm-year evidence is also consistent with increased physical investment during the 2025 policy period, particularly among utilities. Because this investment evidence attenuates when firm-specific trends are included, we treat it as supporting evidence rather than a causal estimate of policy effects.
The findings contribute to research on technological change and asset prices by showing that value created by a general-purpose technology need not accrue primarily to firms producing that technology. When deployment depends on scarce complementary capital, policy shifts expected rents toward upstream firms that generate, deliver, connect, cool, and finance the required infrastructure. The results also illustrate a limit to price discovery: markets can identify the broad sectors positioned to benefit from an emerging constraint before they can reliably identify the specific firms that will form new commercial links. In the AI setting, the valuation consequences of policy are therefore concentrated not in AI firms themselves, but in the energy and grid companies that relax the physical constraints on AI expansion.

title: Human Interactions with Generative AI in Customer Service
abstract:
Implementing Generative AI technology within product offerings and business workflows has become a priority for many businesses. Leveraging tools like Microsoft Copilot and building agentic AI solutions drives conversations about productivity, efficiency, and elevated user experiences. As businesses work to offer products driven by Generative AI, this project asks how well the technology performs for native and non-native speakers of English. Essentially: do preferences from the model or the human influence the end interaction?

Model preference is defined in this project as models performing better on mainstream or standard American English due to unbalanced training data during model development. Human preference is defined in this project as differences in perceptions of AI conversational partners in comparison to human conversational partners. Preferences include perceptions or judgments related to the conversational partner's personality, trustworthiness, credibility, usefulness, etc.

This project specifically focuses on speech recognition models and voice-enabled agents in a customer service context with the goal of answering two research questions:
RQ1: How well do ASR models perform as AI transcription tools on customer service calls? Does the call center location impact transcription accuracy when one call center is non-US based? 
RQ2: Is a customer service agent perceived differently in terms of competence and dependability, human-likeness, and communicative flexibility depending on whether the listener thinks the agent is AI or a human? Does agent misunderstanding of the customer influence these perceptions? Does being an L1 or L2 English-speaking listener influence these perceptions?

This poster will detail the proposed methods of ongoing dissertation work. Critically, the methods provide a foundation for discussing ways of evaluating current and forward-looking generative AI solutions in a real world context. Questions around how to safely implement and monitor generative AI solutions go beyond traditional computer science methods. In this work specifically, language is the primary interaction of study.

First, automated speech recognition (ASR) models will be tested as transcription tools for customer service data. ASR models will generate transcripts for actual customer service calls from a Fortune 100 insurance company. Transcripts will be analyzed according to word error rate (WER) for calls where the call centers (and subsequently the agents) are US-based and where the agents are Phillipines-based. Results from these methods will answer RQ1. 

Secondly, native and non-native speakers of English will participate in a Matched Guise Task where they will hear a set of customer service calls. Call content will be similar to conversations found in the dataset for Experiment 1. All participants will hear the same set of dialogues. Each dialogue will randomly be assigned to be a conversation including an AI customer service agent, a human customer service agent, or undefined. This per-dialogue information will be randomized for each participant. Participants will then be asked to rate the customer service agent according to 7-point Likert scale ratings for polar elements such as "trustworthy-untrustworthy" or statements such as "I would trust this agent". The goal of this experiment is to see how ratings shift based on if the participant thinks they are listening to an AI agent or a human agent and if those perceptions are influenced by the participant being a native or non-native speaker of English. Results gathered using these methods will answer RQ2.

Both studies aim to showcase nuances in human-AI interactions from the perspective of ASR model and native and non-native English speaker preferences. As these technologies become more easily adoptable by companies, this work contributes to understanding human-AI interaction dynamics from native and non-native English speaker perspectives. Experiment one directly questions preferences within the model that can impact transcript accuracy. Experiment two questions perceptions of customer service agent performance based on if the agent is human or AI and whether the judge is a native or non-native English speaker.

title: Governing Knowledge Across Humans and Machines: How AI Reshapes Organizational Knowledge Management Through Externally Specified and Internally Learned Representations
abstract:
Alongside the relentless scaling of models, data, and computing infrastructure, another defining trend in enterprise AI is the integration of generative models with other knowledge resources. AI capabilities are increasingly realized through hybrid configurations, such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), AI agents that invoke conventional deterministic software, and human-in-the-loop arrangements that retain human judgement and authority. These configurations seek to harness the power of generative AI while improving its reliability and trustworthiness through grounded information, deterministic execution, and human oversight.

Yet existing research on organizational knowledge management lacks a coherent account of what fundamentally differentiates knowledge resources and how they can complement one another in hybrid configurations. Without such an account, hybrid AI innovations are difficult to interpret cumulatively: each appears as an isolated technical advancement rather than an application of more general design principles; moreover, how organizations should design, manage, and govern these configurations remains underdeveloped.

To address this gap, we develop a theoretical framework drawing on research on organizational cognition, knowledge structures, and tacit knowledge, informed by recent advances in neural networks and large language models (LLMs). Specifically, we posit that the distinction between explicit knowledge and tacit skill reflects a fundamental difference in how knowledge is represented: explicit knowledge is encoded and communicated using pre-existing codes, languages, or other representational schemes. For example, a procedure written in natural language uses an established language that others can interpret, use, and share. Tacit skills, by contrast, are acquired through practice, feedback, and repeated experience with task environments. Through this process, the internal representation encoding the skill is itself learned rather than specified using a pre-existing representational scheme. Because this representation emerges through experience rather than deliberate specification, it is not directly observable-even to the person possessing the skill-and the underlying knowledge can be difficult to articulate fully. Tacit skill therefore cannot be fully passed on using shared codes or languages; others must develop their own internal representations experientially.

Traditionally, machines have operated primarily with externally specified representations: their rules, procedures, and task knowledge are encoded in programming languages or computer codes. Advances in neural networks and LLMs have created a machine analogue to human tacit skill acquisition: machines can develop capabilities resembling human tacit skills through internally learned representations formed in large-scale training. This yields a two-by-two framework: knowledge may be acquired and applied by humans or machines, and its representation may be externally specified or internally learned. The framework identifies four modes of organizational knowledge management with distinct strengths, limitations, and implications for how knowledge can be combined and governed.

Our framework reveals implications for how organizational knowledge can be replicated, combined, and governed as organizations seek to scale AI. First, internally learned representations allow machines to acquire capabilities resembling human tacit skills that are difficult or infeasible to reproduce through explicit programming because their fine-grained knowledge cannot be fully articulated using existing codes or languages. Large-scale training instead allows these inarticulable nuances to become encoded in internal representations. However, unlike human tacit skills, which must be developed experientially by each individual, the resulting machine representations can be easily copied and deployed at scale. Internally learned machine knowledge thus combines the acquisition logic of tacit skill with the replicability of explicit knowledge.

Moreover, different knowledge modes can complement and scaffold one another. RAG complements powerful but sometimes unreliable tacit-like capabilities by grounding their application in externally maintained data, while tool use (i.e., allowing AI agents to invoke conventional deterministic software) delegates tasks requiring precision and deterministic execution to software whose rules and procedures must be explicitly specified and coded by humans. These configurations illustrate a broader design principle: limitations of one knowledge mode can be managed by coupling it with the strengths of another.

More fundamentally, AI opens new pathways through which knowledge represented in one mode can guide action in another. Making articulated human knowledge machine-operable historically required labor-intensive recoding by programmers into formal code. Emerging approaches such as Agent Skills now allow explicit knowledge expressed in natural language to directly guide machine action without this recoding step. This both lowers the barrier to articulating task knowledge for machine use and makes previously human-oriented stores of organizational knowledge-such as procedures, policies, manuals, and playbooks-directly operable by machines, potentially unlocking substantial value from knowledge that organizations have already articulated.

Finally, our analysis reframes AI governance around trade-offs among knowledge modes and the pathways connecting them. Externally specified representations are more inspectable, revisable, and controllable, but can be costly or infeasible when knowledge resists articulation; internally learned representations can capture tacit-like nuances but are much less observable and harder to validate and control. Hybrid configurations manage these trade-offs by grounding, constraining, or scaffolding one mode with another. As AI opens more pathways through which knowledge becomes machine-operable, organizations must govern which knowledge artifacts are authorized to guide machine action, how modes are combined, and how outputs are validated before becoming socially actionable.

In conclusion, advances in neural networks and LLMs reveal a machine analogue to human tacit skill acquisition and thereby expose a fundamental representational distinction across the human-machine boundary. Our framework shows how AI unbundles properties of knowledge that organizational theory has historically treated as linked: internally learned machine capabilities retain tacit-like acquisition and opacity yet become readily replicable. This creates an asymmetry: organizations can replicate and deploy tacit-like machine capabilities far faster than they can verify their reliability, making scalability itself a source of governance risk. Organizations have always combined heterogeneous knowledge modes, but AI greatly expands the pathways through which they can be coupled, creating new capabilities alongside new risks and bottlenecks. Scaling AI is therefore fundamentally a knowledge-governance problem: organizations must govern hybrid cognition by configuring how human and machine knowledge modes interact so their complementary strengths can be harnessed reliably and responsibly.

title: Asymmetric Effects of Supplier and Customer AI Focus on Focal Firm Risk
abstract:
Motivation
Artificial intelligence (AI) is commonly portrayed in supply chain management as a technology that improves forecasting, information processing, operational efficiency, and risk management. Most research in this field accordingly asks whether AI adoption or strategic emphasis of a firm improves its own outcomes. Yet firms do not operate in isolation but within interdependent supply chains in which the consequences of AI may extend beyond the organization deploying it. An AI-focused supplier or customer may improve coordination and reduce uncertainty for connected firms, but it may also strengthen its own informational and decision making position alter how value and risk are distributed across organizational boundaries. This study specifically asks whether a focal firm becomes less exposed to risk when a supply chain partner becomes more AI-focused, or whether the partner becomes better positioned to transfer risk toward it.
Theoretical Approach and Methodology
I develop a theory of partner-AI externalities that distinguishes between upstream suppliers and downstream customers and argues that the effect of partner AI focus on focal firm risk depends critically on interfirm dependence. AI focus is conceptualized not as realized AI capability itself, but as the degree to which a firm places strategic and operational emphasis on AI in its public disclosures. This kind of emphasis may accompany greater use of AI-enabled prediction, monitoring, planning, and decision support, creating two competing consequences for exchange partners. The first is an uncertainty reduction effect, in which a partner focused on AI may forecast more accurately, plan operations more effectively, detect disruptions earlier, and coordinate transactions more reliably. The second mechanism involves risk appropriation. Enhanced information and decision advantages may also improve the ability of a partner of the focal firm to negotiate, monitor alternatives, impose adjustments, or shift uncertainty related to transaction toward a more dependent counterpart.
To explain when each mechanism dominates, the study integrates transaction cost economics with a power and dependence perspective. Transaction cost economics explains how AI related organizational emphasis can alter information availability and exchange, monitoring, coordination, and uncertainty within interorganizational exchanges while recognizing the possibility of opportunistic behavior. Power-dependence reasoning explains why the benefits generated by these improvements need not be shared symmetrically because the party that is less dependent on the relationship is better positioned to appropriate value and resist the transfer of risk.
The framework produces different predictions for supplier and customer relationships. On the upstream side, supplier AI focus may reduce risk for the focal firm when dependence on that supplier is relatively low because the focal firm can benefit from improvements while retaining sufficient flexibility and switching options. As supplier dependence increases, the focal firm becomes less able to appropriate those benefits and more exposed to the enhanced informational and bargaining position of the supplier. The effect of supplier AI focus on risk reduction should therefore weaken and may eventually reverse as supplier dependence rises.
On the downstream side, customer AI focus can similarly improve demand prediction and coordination, but high dependence on a major customer creates a different type of exposure. A customer with a strong focus on AI may possess better information about demand, pricing, alternatives, and market conditions, while a dependent focal firm has limited ability to resist changes in purchasing terms, inventory expectations, volume commitments, or supplier substitution. As a result, customer AI focus is expected to become increasingly risk enhancing as dependence of the focal firm on that customer rises. More broadly, the framework suggests that AI does not have an intrinsically beneficial or harmful interorganizational effect, because its consequences depend on who possesses the advantage related to AI and on the structural dependence surrounding the exchange.
The framework also offers a clear path for empirical operationalization in longitudinal supply chain settings. Partner focus on AI can be captured through the strategic and operational emphasis on AI within public corporate disclosures and investor communications of firms, including annual regulatory filings and earnings call transcripts. Supplier and customer dependence can be represented through the purchasing concentration of the focal firm with major suppliers and revenue concentration with major customers, respectively. Risk for the focal firm can be operationalized through idiosyncratic equity return volatility, with accounting based earnings volatility providing a complementary perspective. Together, these measures provide an empirically tractable foundation for examining the framework's predictions across publicly listed firms and their major supply-chain relationships.
Theoretical Findings
The study yields three theoretical findings. First, AI in supply chains should be understood not only as a source of capability creation but also as a potential mechanism of risk redistribution across firm boundaries. Second, the effect of partner focus on AI is inherently conditional, where dependence of the focal firm determines whether uncertainty reduction benefits or risk appropriation pressures will dominate. Third, upstream and downstream partner AI may generate different patterns of exposure because supplier and customer relationships differ in how operational benefits, information advantages, and economic dependence are translated into bargaining leverage.
Implications
These arguments contribute to AI and supply chain research by shifting attention from the firm adopting AI to the firms economically connected to that adopter. The study introduces risk allocation, rather than risk reduction alone, as an important consequence of AI in interorganizational settings and explains why technologically sophisticated partners may simultaneously represent operational resources and sources of exposure. For managers, the framework suggests that evaluating the value of AI in supply chains requires looking beyond whether a supplier or customer is technologically advanced. Firms must also consider how dependent they are on that partner and whether AI-enabled information and decision advantages are likely to improve joint coordination or reshape the distribution of risk within the relationship.

title: When GAI Writes: Generative AI Disclosure and Analyst Forecasts
abstract:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is reshaping the world since ChatGPT was released available to the public on November 30, 2022. Recent evidence also shows GAI produces a detectable share of new text in disclosures, for example, financial reporting (Blankespoor et al., 2025). However, there is limited evidence on its impact on financial markets (Cao et al, 2026). As corporate disclosures rarely travel directly from firms to prices, they pass first through a layer of professional intermediaries whose business is to process them. Sell-side analysts read firms' filings, press releases, and conference call remarks, and transform them into the forecasts that anchor market expectations.

Therefore, we examine how the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in financial reporting affects the behaviors of sell-side financial analysts. Using report-level measures of GAI usage from Blankespoor et al. (2026), we identify likely GAI users based on the standardized change in GAI usage around the release of ChatGPT. Specifically, for each firm, we compute the difference between post-ChatGPT and pre-ChatGPT GAI usage in MD&A, scaled by the cross-sectional standard deviation of GAI usage. Firms with larger standardized increases are more likely to have adopted GAI. We validate this classification by showing that likely GENAI users experience a significant increase in GENAI usage in their financial reporting after the launch of ChatGPT. Then we examine the difference between likely GAI users and non- likely GAI users on analyst forecast behaviors around ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, mainly one-quarter-ahead forecasts. The results show that GAI usage in financial reporting writing is associated with better, not worse, forecast outcomes. Analyst's earnings forecast errors are smaller for likely GAI users after the release of ChatGPT, and forecast dispersion is lower. Additionally, the forecast consensus and analyst coverage are higher for likely GAI users. We find no evidence of reduced analyst effort, proxied by forecast revision activity. Taken together, our findings are inconsistent with the concern that machine-written disclosure has impaired the professional processing of firm information.

In the further analysis, we explore whether there is any difference in linguistic characteristics between the GAI users and non-likely GAI users, which might drive the results. We find that filings with higher GAI usage are more positive, shorter, and more specific. The results are consistent with Blankespoor et al. (2026), who use within-report analyses to contrast the linguistic properties of content that is the least versus most likely to use GAI and find that GAI content of MD&A tends to be more positively toned, more readable, and more specific. The above results lend support to our underlying mechanisms, as readability and specificity reduce analysts' processing costs (Lehavy et al., 2022; Hope et al., 2016) and positive sentiment is associated with positive forecasts. 

Additionally, we find that the relationship is more prominent for firms with lower risk proxied by lower leverage in fiscal year 2021, and firms with more analysts following in year 2021. We conclude with a battery of robustness tests that corroborate our findings. We re-estimate our main specification using alternative cutoffs for classifying likely GAI users, a shorter sample window that begins in 2008, clustering standard errors at the firm level, and re-estimate the results using annual forecast sample. These inferences are consistent with our main findings. 

We contribute to the literature on information processing by providing early evidence on how the automation of disclosure production affects the output of professional information intermediaries. A growing literature examines how analysts and investors use AI to consume information (Bradshaw et al. 2025; Christ et al. 2025; Cheng et al. 2025; Bertomeu et al. 2025; Kim, Muhn, and Nikolaev 2024). We ask the complementary, supply-side question: what happens to forecast quality when the documents analysts process are themselves machine-written? We thereby answer a question explicitly posed by Blankespoor et al. (2025), who document GAI usage but leave its consequences for information processing open. We also complement concurrent work relating AI-like disclosure language to market outcomes, e.g. aggregate trading outcomes and investor reactions (Irons 2024; Plate et al., 2024) by opening the intermediation channel through which such aggregate effects arise. Our evidence suggests one reason markets appear to have absorbed machine-written disclosure without disruption: the professionals who stand between firms and investors process it efficiently. To sum up, our findings suggest that concerns about generative AI degrading the quality of corporate disclosure may be overstated, and inform ongoing regulatory discussions about whether firms' use of AI in financial reporting warrants disclosure or oversight.
session_title: AI Disclosure & Labeling: Platforms and Firms

title: AI for 1.4 Billion: The Effects of the World's Largest Tax Analytics Experiment on Firms
abstract:
We see evidence throughout the world that organizations such as firms and governmental agencies are increasingly reliant on artificial intelligence (AI) for activities that previously required human involvement or intervention. According to Raisch & Krakowski (2021), AI involves machines performing cognitive functions that are usually associated with human minds, including complex processes such as learning, interacting, and problem solving. This is accomplished through the conversion of data into an electronic format that AI can interpret based on mathematical rules and algorithms. In doing so, AI is generally thought of as a means to create greater organizational efficiency through reduced need to handle and store physical documents, saving time and manpower, increasing accuracy, and transforming data in meaningful ways.
 
 While the overriding assumption is that the adoption of AI will invariably lead to positive outcomes for organizations, there may in fact be unintended negative consequences from AI, particularly for firms. A key driver of firms' competitive advantage is their intangible resources (Barney, 1991), consisting of highly tacit knowledge that is embedded in routines, processes and path-dependent learning (Nelson & Winter, 1982). A firm's intangible resources serve as the foundation of its unique innovative capabilities, value chain configuration, marketing prowess, and organizational culture, which distinguish it from other firms. Yet, much of this knowledge is not meaningful transformed into mathematical rules nor conducive to algorithmic analysis. Undue reliance on AI where intangible resources are involved may lead to incorrect analyses that can harm the firm. Given the critical role of firms' intangible resources for their competitive advantage, the purpose of this research is to examine firms' intangible resources affect the use of AI.
 
To systematically examine the effects of AI with respect to firms' intangible resources, it is important to hold the adoption of AI constant across firms. Comparability is reduced when firm adoption of AI is piecemeal or varied in type and scope. To overcome this issue, we use a natural experiment involving publicly listed Indian firms in the years before and after the 2007 adoption of an AI based tax system in India, a system referred to as state-of-the-art and a model for other countries by worldwide accounting firms such as PwC and Deloitte. Since 2007, firms in India have been subject to the same AI-based scrutiny of their reported accounting and financial data, reducing concerns about non-comparability. While such data can encompass both tangible and intangible elements, we expect that it is the more intangible features of these data that will trip up AI-based tax assessments. Misinterpretation of key firm data will cause firms to dispute significantly more of their taxes after the institution of the AI-based tax system than before such a system was in place. 
 
 We develop a set of hypotheses that highlight the intangible features of accounting and financial data typically included in tax returns, including price-cost margins, sales variance, leverage, contingent liabilities, foreign ownership and business group membership. We suggest that flaws in interpreting these intangible features by the AI-based system will lead to higher disputes on the part of firms. Our findings offer significant support for our arguments, demonstrating that the majority of these variables are associated with more tax disputes. In fact, tax disputes continue to grow in the nearly two decades after adoption of the AI system. We support our analyses with a number of robust tests.

This research offers important insights on AI's ability to interface with firms' intangible resources. By taking advantage of the natural experiment offered by India's large-scale adoption of a state-of-the-art AI based tax system, we were able to study how AI handles the more embedded and tacit elements of resources across a wide range of firms. Despite important benefits from using AI in terms of efficiency and cost, the fact that all AI systems are modeled on quantifiable and historical data may not allow them to adequately capture the evolving nuances of firm decisions. Firms with greater operational complexity based on a more opaque set of intangible assets are less conducive to algorithmic analysis. Given that firms derive important competitive advantage from the more innovative and unique aspects of their strategy, AI may provide incorrect solutions to problems based on an over-simplification of how the firm operates and manages its knowledge. This research helps to answer the call by Anindya Ghose, made in his keynote address at the inaugural AI conference at OSU last year, for scholars turn their attention to the shortcomings and mistakes in the use of AI.

title: Too Neat to Be True? AI-Generated Review Summary Discrepancies and Consumer Response
abstract:
Research Motivation
Online reviews affect sales (Chevalier and Mayzlin, 2006), and generative AI is rapidly becoming part of the interface through which consumers encounter them. Platforms increasingly use large language models to interpret those reviews and present their own condensed assessments. AI-generated summaries (AIGS) are meant to help consumers understand a large and heterogeneous review record. Existing work treats the AIGS, once introduced, as given (Kim et al., 2024; Su et al., 2024). Its discrepancy from the contemporaneous review record has received little attention.
The convenience of this summarization layer, however, creates a new information problem. An AIGS may not agree with the human reviews displayed alongside it. An average rating stands in a transparent relationship to the ratings beneath it. An AIGS is produced through an opaque process of selecting, weighting, and compressing review content. It may emphasize unrepresentative opinions or remain anchored in an earlier review record as new reviews accumulate. When the two sources conflict, consumers must determine which one better represents the service. AIGS-review discrepancy therefore bears on trust and purchase decisions.
The consequences of such disagreement differ by direction and by attribute. An AIGS that is more favorable than recent human reviews may appear overly promotional or misleading. One that is less favorable may be interpreted as cautious or conservative. Hotel attributes also differ substantially in their pre-purchase verifiability, consistent with the search-experience distinction (Nelson, 1970, 1974; Huang et al., 2009). A prospective guest can compare a claim about location with maps and transit times before booking. Service, cleanliness, and noise are learned primarily through the stay itself. Disagreement may therefore be more salient for attributes a guest can check in advance. We ask how the magnitude, direction, and attribute of a discrepancy relate to hotel demand.
Data and Methodology
We monitored Tripadvisor hotel pages in 31 major tourist and business cities in North America, Europe, and Asia over 2025, observing three waves of updates. The update interval rarely falls below two months, so we treat each two-month window with an unchanged AIGS as one period. This yielded 11,220 hotel-period observations for 4,389 hotels and review histories of 1,536,730 human reviews.
To place the two texts on a common scale, we label both with a single large language model procedure. Instructions, prompts, and parsing rules are held fixed across the corpus. For each text, the procedure identifies references to eight hotel attributes (location, atmosphere, rooms, value, noise, cleanliness, service, and amenities) and to overall emotional tone. Each mentioned item receives a score from 0 to 10; unmentioned items remain missing. The signed discrepancy is the AIGS score minus the median score among human reviews posted in the preceding 30 days. Its mean across non-missing dimensions gives the hotel-period discrepancy, whose absolute value is our main explanatory variable.
Purchase intent is not directly observable, so we impute demand from review counts in review-equivalent units. Reviews observed in period t are generated by demand in period t and in earlier periods. The review series is therefore a distributed lag of latent demand, and inverting this system recovers demand. The lag, calibrated from Tripadvisor view-to-booking and auxiliary Expedia booking-to-review data, places 68.5% of eventual reviews in the period of the initial view. We regress imputed demand on the absolute discrepancy with hotel fixed effects, add period fixed effects, and estimate direction-specific slopes, clustering by hotel. These specifications use 8,619 hotel-periods from 3,230 hotels. Each attribute is estimated separately.
Findings
Discrepancy magnitude is negatively associated with contemporaneous imputed demand within hotels (−0.964). The pattern remains when period fixed effects enter the specification (−1.002; both p < 0.01). The direction-specific estimates sharpen the result. The negative association is concentrated in periods of overstatement, in which the AIGS portrays the hotel more favorably than recent human reviews (−1.280, p < 0.01). Understatement does not lower imputed demand. The direction of a discrepancy therefore carries information that its magnitude alone leaves out.
Attribute by attribute, the overstatement slope is negative for seven of the eight hotel attributes and statistically significant for all seven. The ordering follows pre-purchase verifiability. Location carries the largest estimate (−1.432). Atmosphere (−1.338) and amenities (−1.264), which a listing and its photographs verify in part, follow. Rooms, service, cleanliness, and value come next at smaller magnitudes (−0.909 to −0.656). Noise does not exhibit the same pattern.
Implications
For research on platform information design, these results turn a feature usually treated as fixed into a variable. The discrepancy between an AIGS and the record beneath it varies within a property over time and is associated with imputed demand. The search-experience distinction was developed for product categories. It is informative at the attribute level inside one service category, where location and service occupy different points of one spectrum on a single page.
A platform can compute the discrepancy from material it already holds, namely the summary text and the review record. This comparison can therefore run continuously. A monitoring series records a discrepancy's magnitude, direction, and attributes. For a hotel, the AIGS belongs to a storefront the platform composes, and the attribute breakdown shows where a discrepancy concentrates. Tracing the feedback among summaries, bookings, and later reviews is the natural next step.
References
