Huang, P., Lurie, N.H. and Mitra, S. (2009) 'Searching for experience on the web: an empirical examination of consumer behavior for search and experience goods', Journal of Marketing, 73(2), pp. 55-69.
Kim, A., Lu, Y., Ma, T. and Tan, Y. (2024) 'Less is more? Impact of AI-generated summaries on user engagement of video-sharing platforms'. Available at SSRN 5020305.
Nelson, P. (1970) 'Information and consumer behavior', Journal of Political Economy, 78(2), pp. 311-329.
Nelson, P. (1974) 'Advertising as information', Journal of Political Economy, 82(4), pp. 729-754.
Su, Y., Wang, Q., Qiu, L. and Chen, R. (2024) 'Navigating the sea of reviews: unveiling the effects of introducing AI-generated summaries in e-commerce'. Available at SSRN 4872205.

title: AI Scales-but Can It Deliver in High-Stakes Finance?
abstract:
The question financial institutions face when they scale AI 

AI has diffused rapidly through financial institutions. In a 2026 survey of 628 organizations across 151 jurisdictions, 81% reported AI adoption and 40% reported advanced adoption. Yet 55% of respondents-and 76% of large institutions-struggled to measure deployment value (Cambridge CCAF, 2026). The gap reflects a deeper distinction: output is easier to count than reliable delivery. Financial workflows bundle routine production with judgment-intensive verification. AI can scale routine production, but judgment determines whether its output becomes decision-ready. When verification remains the bottleneck, faster intermediate work need not shorten delivery. End-to-end productivity is therefore decision-ready work per unit of expert time at fixed assurance-not intermediate output. The question is whether AI improves that outcome after human judgment and verification. 

Existing evidence rarely answers this question. Firm-level studies infer aggregate effects without isolating routine from judgment-intensive work. Field experiments observe task output but mostly on bounded tasks-writing, support, coding, and consulting-where errors do not expose professionals to a live decision's full consequences. Such studies show whether AI accelerates a task, not whether it reduces the expert effort required to deliver the workflow. 

Standard AI evaluation datasets are further from production: exam questions are self-contained and scored against documented answers; real cases require deciding what evidence matters, what to rule out, and what risk remains. We call work high-stakes when error can cause substantial downstream harm and an identifiable person or firm remains professionally or legally accountable. That accountability cannot be delegated: any model output entering the decision must be reviewed by the human who answers for the outcome. 

A rare view into a high-stakes financial workflow 

Evidence from high-stakes work is usually out of reach: real inputs paired with expert judgments are confidential. Cryptocurrency offers a rare exception. In decentralized finance (DeFi), smart contracts - code that automatically holds and moves users' crypto assets - replace traditional financial intermediaries. Before such code goes live, professional auditors read it and report flaws. Both the code and the paid audit reports are unusually public. Our data link code and reports for roughly 8,000 DeFi projects in a market that has held 200 billion dollars and lost 7.6 billions to documented attacks.

The setting combines three rarely observed features. First, it is genuinely high-stakes: the protocol team decides whether to deploy, and the audit firm attaches its name to disclosed findings. Credible assurance combines routine code inspection with judgment about protocol economics and plausible attack paths. Second, for each protocol, we observe code the auditor reviewed and findings a paid firm published. Reports are professional judgments, not infallible ground truth. Our primary test is report-relative recall: whether AI recovers disclosed findings. We label model-only findings as report-relative false positives for benchmarking; because reports may omit genuine findings, that label denotes disagreement, not necessarily factual error. Third, standardized model evaluations across thousands of matched protocols reveal benchmark-relative misses, additional flags, and performance variation. 

Framework: why reliability thresholds-not average accuracy-govern adoption 

We model AI assistance where a human remains accountable for the final judgment. The primary empirical constraint is report-relative false negatives-disclosed findings the model fails to recover. Many such misses mean the model does not reproduce the professional benchmark; when a missed finding is genuine, deployed funds may face difficult-to-reverse losses. Model-only flags create a secondary cost because each requires adjudication, although some may be genuine auditor omissions. 

The economic question is whether AI improves the whole workflow, not whether it generates useful output. High report-relative miss rates do not justify reducing independent checking; excessive additional flags increase the verification burden. Reliability cannot be reduced to average accuracy: the primary requirement is a sufficiently low miss rate, especially on severe cases; the secondary requirement is manageable additional-flag volume. Because we do not observe expert time directly, these error profiles identify necessary-but not sufficient-conditions for labor savings; they do not measure productivity. 

Findings 

Against this standard, none of the frontier models we evaluate-GPT-5.5, Claude Fable, or Gemini 3.5 Pro-meets the reliability conditions required for end-to-end productivity. More strikingly, even the best-performing configuration recovers only 59% of disclosed findings and 41% of severe findings, with no model satisfying both reliability thresholds. Scaffolding, retrieval, and multi-pass review improve recall by no more than 10 percentage points. This does not mean LLMs add no value: reasoning models identify contextual findings beyond predefined rules or pattern matching. But outperforming conventional automation does not clear the reliability bar. A model can matter without being dependable enough for accountable work. 

To locate the shortfall, we compare model and auditor findings by vulnerability type, severity, protocol complexity, and pattern frequency. Two patterns emerge. First, report-relative misses concentrate in attack types infrequent in our sample, so average performance conceals long-tail shortfalls where reliable coverage matters most. Second, performance declines with reasoning depth: models handle familiar patterns more reliably but struggle with multi-step, counterfactual reasoning about interactions between code and economic incentives. Higher capability does not eliminate this gap. The binding weakness is uneven reliability on long-tail, reasoning-intensive cases where professional judgment is hardest to substitute. 

The division of labor is therefore specific. AI's most plausible near-term role is the mechanical layer-screening known vulnerability patterns, checking standards, and triaging code. Human auditors retain economic judgment: interpreting incentives, tracing novel attacks, and adjudicating flags; accountable protocol decision-makers own deployment. AI can scale expert assistance before it can scale accountable delivery. 

Contribution and fit with "AI Innovation at Scale" 

To our knowledge, this is the first task-level evidence on AI in a high-stakes financial workflow, measuring benchmark-relative reliability against observed professional judgments rather than adoption proxies or generic benchmarks. Our portable design pairs observable inputs with disclosed professional outputs and maps report-relative misses and additional flags into necessary-but not sufficient-conditions for labor savings. Scaling routine production is not end-to-end delivery: the models we test do not yet meet the reliability conditions required for an accountable human to do less without sacrificing assurance.

title: AI Human Capital, Real Outcomes, and Management Forecast Accuracy: Evidence from Clinical Trials
abstract:
Motivation. 
Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely heralded as transformative, yet its returns are strikingly uneven: one recent report finds that 95 percent of organizations see no return on their in-house AI investment. This unevenness raises two questions of first-order importance to managers and investors: when does AI create value, and through which workers? We address these questions in the pharmaceutical industry, where AI is increasingly deployed across the drug-development process and where clinical trials generate granular, verifiable, project-level records of a firm's core operating activity. Clinical trials are also a unique setting to study disclosure and forecast quality: sponsors must register an expected completion date and update it over the trial's life, producing a mandatory, verifiable, non-financial management forecast that is ultimately settled against a realized date.

Data and methodology. 
We measure AI human capital at the worker level using online professional-profile data from Revelio Labs, classifying positions as AI-related and, crucially, distinguishing AI-skilled professionals with pharmaceutical domain expertise (clinical and research roles, and data scientists holding a life-science degree) from those with a primarily technical, computer-science or infrastructure background. We link these measures to roughly 12,000 interventional trials sponsored by 392 U.S.-listed pharmaceutical firms over 2010-2022, drawn from ClinicalTrials.gov. Because AI staffing is not randomly assigned, we identify its effects from variation within a firm's own workforce: all models include firm fixed effects and phase-by-disease-by-year fixed effects, and we complement this design with entropy balancing and a leads-and-lags falsification test. We study three trial-level outcomes that together reveal whether, and how, AI creates value: (i) trial completion, a verifiable operating milestone; (ii) the stock-market reaction to the completion announcement, which captures investors' revised valuation of the firm; and (iii) the accuracy of the firm's completion-date forecast, which captures its ability to plan and deliver the trial on schedule.

Findings. 
First, AI human capital raises the probability that a trial is completed; a one-standard-deviation increase raises completion by about 4.4 percent, identified entirely within firm. This effect is delivered by domain experts: the per-standard-deviation effect for domain workers (about 3.4 percent) is roughly double that for non-domain technical workers (about 1.6 percent), and it is concentrated among senior domain staff. Examining the mechanism, AI reduces terminations for strategic and safety reasons (avoidable failures) but not terminations for lack of efficacy, indicating that AI helps firms run and triage trials more effectively rather than making drugs work. Second, the market prices these completions: a one-standard-deviation increase in AI is associated with a completion abnormal return about 33 basis points higher, and this reaction concentrates in firms with a less transparent information environment (low analyst coverage, high illiquidity), where completions are most informative. The reaction is more pronounced for firms richer in domain experts (over 38 basis points), reinforcing the value of integrating AI skills with domain knowledge. Third, AI does not improve completion-forecast accuracy on average, but it sharply improves it where forecasting is hard: among the most analytically complex trials, a one-standard-deviation increase in AI reduces the delay between the promised and realized completion date by about 2.4 months and cuts the probability of a twelve-month-plus slip by roughly a third. Decomposing the forecast miss into the promised horizon and the realized duration shows that high-AI firms finish complex trials sooner, shortening realized duration about twice as much as they shorten their promises, so more accurate forecasts arise from more efficient execution rather than from more conservative reporting.

Implications. 
The returns to AI are context-specific and depend on who inside the firm does the work: value resides in experienced, domain-expert employees rather than in generic technical headcount. For managers and investors, realizing AI's potential in complex, knowledge-intensive settings therefore requires pairing AI capability with deep domain expertise. The study contributes to (i) the economics of AI and firm productivity, by providing direct, project-level evidence of AI's operating effects and identifying domain expertise as the key complement; (ii) the accounting literature using clinical trials, by linking AI human capital to trial completion and to the accuracy of mandatory management forecasts; and (iii) research on management-forecast quality and real decisions, by exploiting a setting in which promised and realized outcomes are both observed to show that AI improves forecasts by changing operations, not reporting.

title: Order to Cash Without Adding Headcount: What Actually Ships When a Mid-Market Distributor Puts AI Into Operations
abstract:
Mid-market distributors and e-commerce operators rarely fail at AI because the models are weak. They fail at the seam between a model and an operation that already runs. A pilot is scoped by a vendor, it demos well against clean data, and then it meets a real order path where the quote, the pick, the invoice, the shipment and the ledger entry are held together by people who improvise. Nobody owns that seam, so the pilot is quietly abandoned and the company concludes AI is not ready.

This session describes an operating model built from the inside of companies in the five to fifty million dollar revenue band, run by a practitioner who owns the production systems rather than advising on them. The method is narrow on purpose. Find the leak, which is the one step in the order to cash path where work is redone, delayed or re-keyed. Build a system for that step alone and put it into production behind the process that already exists. Hold it, meaning someone is accountable for it on the days it degrades. Then repeat, instead of buying a platform that promises the whole path at once.

The talk works through where this holds and where it does not, using the operational surfaces that carry real volume in distribution and e-commerce: warehouse and inventory movement, invoicing, shipping documentation, bookkeeping reconciliation and the CRM record that everything else keys off. It covers what changes in the operating model itself: how work gets specified when the builder is also the operator, what governance looks like without an internal data team, why the retirement decision matters more than the launch decision, and how to tell within weeks whether a deployment is earning or being carried.

The session is aimed at practitioners deciding where to place a first or second AI system, and at researchers studying adoption in firms too small to staff an AI function and too large to run the process by hand. It offers a candid account of what survives contact with an operation and what does not, including deployments that were shut down after they were measured.

title: AI Automation and Effort Allocation: Evidence from Sophisticated Investors
abstract:
In the asset management industry, too much focus has been placed on the direct investment implications of AI. In this solo-authored paper, "AI Automation and Effort Allocation: Evidence from Sophisticated Investors," I ask a related but different question: how do investors make complementary use of AI? Specifically, I examine how AI complements fund managers via its labor-saving capacity. I show that not all (fundamental) hedge funds adopt AI, but for those that do, they increase earnings call participation (with more call appearances and more questions on an average call) after AI adoption.
Artificial intelligence can do more than automate work: it can redirect skilled workers toward the tasks where human judgment matters most. My research asks whether, in the AI era, high-skilled workers devote more effort to human-intensive tasks, and I study this question in the hedge fund industry. Hedge funds are sophisticated investors who manage clients' money by developing informational advantages. They build these advantages by gathering information from two main sources: digital corporate filings and earnings conference calls. The difference is important: conference calls require real-time human interaction, while corporate filings do not.
Before adopting AI, it was extraordinarily difficult for humans to download and process the enormous volume of corporate filings in a timely way. AI makes that task feasible and performs it much more effectively. I show that when hedge funds adopt AI to automatically handle corporate filings, they reallocate time and effort toward earnings call participation. After adopting AI, hedge funds attend more earnings calls and ask more questions. In other words, AI shifts effort across information-acquisition tasks rather than simply replacing labor.
This shift has important consequences. I show hedge funds that adopt AI and then participate in earnings calls make better investment decisions, executing more profitable stock trades and achieving higher returns. The broader message of this research is that the power of AI lies not only in substitution, but also in redirection. We often focus on automation's disruptive side, such as robots replacing delivery workers. But that is only part of the story. My research proposes and tests a different view of the human-machine relationship: AI does not just replace human effort; it also increases effort in non-AI tasks that humans do best.
The central insight of my study is that AI frees up human effort for hedge funds to focus more on information acquisition activities that require human interactions. I combine two unique datasets to investigate my hypothesis. First, I identify each hedge fund's participation in the universe of virtual and in-person US conference calls over 2006-2017. Second, I use IP addresses and their retrieval speed and volume in SEC EDGAR log files to identify which funds adopt AI to automate the collection of machine-based information. Third, I document that this shift in information acquisition effort translates into better investment performance-hedge funds' post-automation call participation is associated with greater stock trade performance.
I examine two core empirical relations: the automation-participation relation, where left-hand-side earnings call participation is regressed on right-hand-side AI adoption (in the previous quarter/year); and the participation-performance relation where I explore the stock trade performance effect of post-automation earnings call participation. To this end, I hypothesize that hedge funds tend to increase earnings call participation following AI adoption in the first participation hypothesis, and that hedge funds will achieve better investment performance by extracting value-relevant information from earnings calls after automating SEC downloading in the second performance hypothesis.
To examine the first participation hypothesis, I first use a dynamic difference-in-differences empirical setup to provide descriptive evidence on hedge funds' earnings call participation behavior around AI adoption as a baseline. Additionally, I find stronger participation effects for larger, older, lower-portfolio-turnover funds, consistent with larger funds being more flexible with human capital redeployment, older funds being more informationally advantaged, and lower-portfolio-turnover funds relying more on a fundamental-investing approach. To further corroborate the causal interpretation of the automation-participation relation, I use a technology salience instrument to pin down a causal relation between AI adoption and earnings call participation. The basic idea is to use fundamental hedge funds' technology salience induced by local quants' initial 13-F filings to instrument for their AI adoption decisions. The IV test results confirm the positive and significant automation-participation relation in the baseline and indicate that the relation is likely causal.
To examine the second performance hypothesis, I construct a long-short portfolio that consists of stocks purchased minus sold by post-automation call participating HFs. The positive return spread speaks to profitable trades associated with post-automation call participation, consistent with human-interaction-based information extracted from earnings calls being value-relevant. I further find that the trade performance effect is concentrated in hard-to-research stocks, consistent with the marginal benefit of information acquisition being largest for informationally opaque stocks.
My empirical findings have implications for revisiting the productivity effects of automation technologies in the task-based framework. Prior studies focus on either new task creation or existing task substitution. In the former case, automation creates new tasks that require human effort, reflecting pure task complementarity, whereas in the latter case automation replaces human effort at some existing tasks, reflecting pure task substitution. 
What is missing in the empirical literature is a third case that lies between the two extremes, where task complementarity is embedded in existing task substitution. To shed light on this gap, I empirically identify a novel effort-reallocation mechanism through which automation raises productivity for high-skilled workers performing partially automatable tasks. The empirical effort-reallocation channel in my study also echoes the theory evidence on the time allocation mechanism in a contemporaneous paper by Gans and Goldfarb (2026), where the authors extend a classic production model with the case in which machines replace tasks of a given quality, and time is reallocated across the remaining manual tasks.
Another major twist in this paper is exhibited in contrast to the common replacement narrative associated with robotics automation: I show that AI automation does not just replace human effort, it also increases the amount of effort that high-skilled knowledge workers devote to human-centered tasks.

title: Racing or Partnering? Adoption Timing and Collaboration Strategies of Generative AI in the Creator Markets
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is transforming creator markets, yet little is known about how creators should use it once the technology becomes widely accessible. Prior research has largely asked whether firms or individuals should employ GenAI by comparing AI-generated and human-generated output. As GenAI becomes embedded in organizational workflows and individual practice, however, the more consequential question is when to adopt and how much of the creative process to delegate. Drawing on diffusion of innovation theory, we extend diffusion thinking to two-sided creator markets and argue that adoption timing shapes the content value available from a maturing technological and normative environment, whereas collaboration mode shapes how much of that value audiences attribute to the human creator. Using data from Wattpad, we find that later GenAI adoption is associated with higher audience engagement, whereas more AI-dominant collaboration is associated with lower engagement. The timing advantage is stronger for speculative content, and the AI-dominant penalty is stronger for experienced creators. Timing and mode further operate as substitutes, with later adoption producing the greatest engagement premium when creators preserve human-dominant production. Simulation analyses translate these findings into a strategic matrix based on content type and creator experience. The results challenge the industry view that creators should use GenAI early and extensively, showing instead that audience engagement depends on matching adoption timing and collaboration mode to creators' audience relationships and creative domains.

title: The Pilot Was Never the Product
abstract:
If your organization already has someone directing AI agents, that person ships faster than your staffed teams. Probably not as fast as they could, though: directing agents well is its own skill, and few people have it yet. The question that follows is the same: how do we get more of that speed. That is the wrong question. The right one is what the work left behind. The most valuable thing that person produced is not the software, and most organizations are about to throw it away. Speed is the part everyone sees; the handoff decides whether any of it was real. You're already feeling a version of this: a mandate from above to show AI results, a compliance function beside you that says no by default, and a pilot nobody can evaluate.

I was that person. In three months, working alone inside a regulated federal healthcare operation, I built a platform and, on it, a product identifying other health insurance coverage, built to drive cost avoidance and recovery. It hasn't reached production yet: the rollout is deliberately careful, which means deliberately slow. One person directed a set of AI agents organized like a team, with defined roles and handoffs. Karna's governance process certified the work PHI-free before real data was involved; an independent review is scheduled before production.

I designed the system to document everything, on purpose. What I underestimated was how much that discipline would end up mattering.

An agent cannot infer what a colleague infers. A new engineer reads half a design document, fills in the rest from experience, asks three questions in the hallway. An agent has no hallway, nothing to fill in from. So the architecture, coding philosophy, control mechanisms, and workflow had to be explicit before any code existed. Because the work does not proceed otherwise.

A staffed team can revise a plan as the work slowly reveals its gaps. Agents move too fast for that: by the time a planning gap shows up, it is already built. So the planning has to be right before anything starts, not adjusted as you go.

Most organizations have spent years trying to get engineers to write that material before code: review gates, templates, definitions of done. It does not hold: for people, documentation is optional. This is the first arrangement I have worked in where it is not.

Then the same thing happened again, one level up. Before anyone else could join, the rules had to exist on paper: a risk assessment, a tiered access model, a certification path people complete before they earn access. All of it was drafted and submitted for committee review before most of the people it governs went through it. My manager and I cleared the same checkpoint; a third colleague has since started the path. The readiness material existed before the readiness question did.

That's the finding, and like any single case, it has real limits.

What transferred is the system. What has not been tested is the role. The speed came from absence: no division of work to negotiate, no onboarding, nobody to bring along. Those are not efficiency gains, they are the defining conditions of a pilot. It also came from skill: extensive personal practice directing these systems. The agents gave back the specification, not a second person who can direct them.

That is what we will be measuring. A technical lead directs people who infer intent, push back, and correct them. Directing agents is specification under total literalism, with none of that return signal. Our correction is designed rather than proven: put a second operator on the work from week one, directing alongside, rather than reading documentation after the fact. One colleague is the first test of it.

One open question a single case can't fully settle: how much of this came from the agents, and how much just from working alone. I've worked mostly solo before, across earlier technical roles, and documentation was never this heavy. That's suggestive, not proof.

Here is why that should matter most to the most constrained people in this room. Agents and auditors want the same artifact: intent written down before action. The regulated organizations everyone assumes will adopt agents last are already fluent in the only discipline that makes agents safe.

The generalizable claim is about evaluation and staffing, not technology. Assess an agent-accelerated pilot: speed tells you little, artifacts tell you a great deal. Ask what the pilot produced besides working software. A pilot run by one operator has to produce a full specification, an asset most organizations don't credit. Then ask who runs this next, not who maintains it. If one person and their agents produced this, you can't hire your way to more of it: that skill isn't on the job market yet. You grow it in someone, the way the certification path above does; you don't recruit it.

I am a Data Science Program Manager at Karna, a healthcare and regulated-industry analytics consultancy, forward deployed into the client's operation. Fifteen years in operations where being wrong has consequences: experimental physics, critical infrastructure, utility and grid analytics, and federal healthcare data. PhD in physics with a CERN publication, MBA from Fisher, two patents, and the person who introduced agentic AI development at Karna.

The most valuable thing the agents produced was never in the codebase. It was the written rules that let the next person start, and we had them before we knew who that person would be.

title: Kingmaking: How Venture Capitalists Pick Artificial Intelligence Winners
abstract:
Motivation. The cost of training a competitive general purpose model has risen by roughly two orders of magnitude. A venture intending to compete at the frontier must now raise several hundred million dollars before it has a product, a customer, or evidence that its approach works. This changes the shape of the financing problem, not only its scale. The capital must arrive early and in one piece, and the information that would justify it arrives only after it has been spent.

The consequence for market structure is arithmetic rather than behavioural. A fund observing the customary diversification covenant of about twelve percent of committed capital needs roughly three and a third billion dollars under management to place four hundred million into a single company. Very few venture partnerships clear that bar, so the set of investors able to finance a frontier entrant is small for reasons unrelated to the merits of any team. Because that set decides before the product market can express any preference, the competitive map of the sector is drawn by a few general partners. This paper calls that act kingmaking and asks when it produces a better set of firms than the alternative.

The obvious answer is not clearly right. Concentration is normally treated as a distortion, on the reasoning that more independent participants explore more of the opportunity set. That depends on participants being wrong in different directions. In artificial intelligence they read the same benchmark tables, hire from the same laboratories and attend the same conferences, which is a consequential deviation from what the argument requires.

Methodology. The paper is theoretical, with a calibrated numerical illustration and a measurement design built on existing data. Candidate ventures require an indivisible fixed outlay representing the first informative trial, and fund sizes follow a Pareto upper tail. Participation requires that a fund's diversification covenant permit a cheque of the required size, which yields a closed form for the number of qualifying allocators.

Allocation is modelled as competition in a common value environment, since a frontier venture is worth roughly the same to any investor able to finance it. Price decomposes into three components: the rational bid, which conditions on the informational content of winning; a premium from the fund's contractual deployment clock, grounded in the literature on fee structures and implicit compensation through future fundraising; and an error term for incomplete correction of adverse selection, formalised through cursed equilibrium.

Selection quality is analysed by splitting each investor's assessment into a component common to everyone evaluating a venture and a genuinely private one. Standard aggregation results give the effective number of independent screens as a function of headcount and belief correlation. Welfare separates pecuniary transfers between entrepreneurs and limited partners from real resource allocation. All propositions are proved formally, and parameters come from customary covenant terms, typical syndicate sizes and standard characterisations of private capital concentration.

Findings. The number of investors able to finance an entrant alone falls as the fixed cost raised to the power of minus the tail exponent of the fund size distribution. With an exponent near one and a half, doubling the fixed cost removes about two thirds of the possible backers and a tenfold increase removes more than ninety five percent. Syndication shifts the schedule outward without changing its slope, because coordination is costly and bounded in the number of parties. Under representative parameters the count falls from effectively unconstrained at application layer costs to single figures at frontier costs, or roughly forty with generous syndication.

The second result concerns price. Rational bidders shade downward as competition rises, because winning against more rivals is worse news, while the deployment clock and cursedness push the other way. Since the three components respond differently to the number of bidders, the sign of the price response to competition identifies which dominates. Practitioners report that competition raises prices and auction theory says rational bidders lower them. That disagreement is usually treated as a puzzle. Here it is the measurement.

The third result concerns the quality of the funded set. Belief correlation caps the number of independent views at the reciprocal of the correlation coefficient, however many investors participate, so a diffuse market delivers far less exploration than its headcount suggests. Concentration improves the funded set when the skill advantage of the few outweighs the information lost through fewer independent views, and the required advantage falls sharply as correlation rises. The framework therefore does not conclude that concentration is harmful. It concludes that the diffuse alternative is worth less than assumed, and that the case for concentration rests on whether the few allocators genuinely screen better.

The fourth result moves inside the funded firm. Deployment pressure delivers capital in larger tranches than milestones justify, and the excess converts mechanically into irreversible commitment, since a venture that raises more than it needs signs a compute contract rather than holding cash. Such ventures should pivot less, fail later and fail larger, which differs from failing more often and is testable without return data. Welfare turns on two channels of opposite sign, and the conditions under which concentration dominates hold at the frontier and fail in the application layer, yielding a split within the sector rather than a verdict on large funds.

Implications. For founders, modest reductions in initial compute requirements may widen the financing set by more than they cost in capability, and terms depend on where a prospective backer sits in its investment period. For limited partners, the analysis points at the fee base rather than the carry structure, and at staggering investment periods across a portfolio to decorrelate deployment clocks. For incumbents, the entrant set in any segment can be forecast from the cost of a first trial, without firm level information. For competition authorities, access to compute is competition policy, since anything reducing that cost widens the entrant set with a large multiplier without intervening in capital markets. The paper closes with three indicators constructible from existing data, and with predictions that would falsify the framework.

title: The AI Bullwhip Effect: Operations in AI Model Marketplace
abstract: The rapid growth of generative artificial intelligence has given rise to AI model marketplaces that facilitate the development, sharing, and adoption of fine-tuned models. We study whether these platforms generate an AI bullwhip effect, whereby fluctuations in downstream engagement are amplified into upstream model production. Using a panel dataset from a leading AI model marketplace, we link model releases and adoption to image-level engagement and estimate a structural model of fine-tuner development decisions. Demand expectations follow a Martingale Model of Forecast Evolution, allowing us to separate responses to anticipated demand from responses to unexpected demand news. We find that fine-tuners respond strongly to positive demand shocks and that adjustment frictions create persistence in development activity. Together, these forces transform short-lived engagement shocks into larger, delayed, and more persistent fluctuations in model supply. As model development consumes substantial computational and energy resources, such amplification can lead to redundant development and excess compute use. Our findings highlight platform information design as a potential lever for mitigating supply-side volatility while preserving incentives for innovation.

title: Escaping the Nash Trap: Structural Estimation and Alignment of Strategic Reasoning in Large Language Models
abstract:
As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as decision-making agents in competitive and strategic environments, their performance depends critically on how they model human counterparts. Yet little is known about the implicit assumptions LLMs make about human rationality. 

Drawing on level-k thinking, we design normal-form games and develop a structural estimator that infers, from observed choices, the reasoning depth an LLM appears to attribute to its opponent. Across models, we find a systematic strategic mismatch: LLM agents overwhelmingly assume humans to be Nash-type players, i.e., fully rational strategic optimizers, and respond with equilibrium play. However, human subjects in our online experiments exhibit substantial heterogeneity, spanning Random through Nash reasoning types. 

This mismatch can help or hurt. An LLM may outsmart a boundedly rational human, but overestimating human sophistication can also create a Nash trap, in which equilibrium play is not the payoff-maximizing response to observed human behavior. We address this problem with two supervised fine-tuning approaches that translate human behavior into payoff-relevant targets. Direct SFT learns a single policy across trap and non-trap games, targeting the human-calibrated best response in traps and the Nash action otherwise. Trap-Aware SFT (TA-SFT) fine-tunes only on trap games and selectively activates the adapted policy, retaining equilibrium play elsewhere. On held-out price games, both methods improve payoff performance against the empirical human-choice distribution. Conditional on correct trap identification, TA-SFT achieves higher target-action accuracy while preserving equilibrium behavior in non-trap games. Effective human-AI strategic interaction therefore requires not only strong reasoning, but also calibrated expectations about human behavior.

title: Integrating AI in Teaching Business Stats / Analytics To Elevate Critical Thinking, Personalized Learning, and Engagement.
abstract:
The advancement of AI is rapidly reshaping the landscape across all sectors. We are living in an era where almost everyone has access to AI in their pockets. In academia, the key question is: How do we use AI ethically in ways that enhance critical thinking, personalized learning, and student engagement?

AI offers several opportunities to improve course design and assignment development in Business Statistics and Analytics classrooms. At the same time, it presents significant challenges, particularly when students use AI as an answer machine for take-home assignments, projects, and online exams. Despite the use of lockdown browsers and honorlock systems, significant number of students are finding ways to use AI to achieve near-perfect scores without developing a meaningful understanding of statistical concepts, tools, and outputs. As a result, they may lack the ability to explain and interpret results or make appropriate decisions and conclusions based on their analyses.
These challenges require educators to rethink how learning is designed and assessed. In this talk, I will discuss practical approaches for integrating AI into teaching while maintaining statistical rigor and fostering genuine student learning and understanding.

I hope attendees will leave with practical strategies and examples for designing AI-integrated activities that promote critical thinking, learning, and engagement in Business Statistics and Analytics classrooms.

title: Artificial Intelligence Investments and Expertise Erosion
abstract: We study the feedback between automation and expertise accumulation. Building on Autor and Thompson's (2025) "expertise framework", we develop an overlapping- generations model with endogenous on-the-job learning. Automation reduces learning in entry-level tasks, slowing expertise acquisition and worsening the economy's exper- tise distribution. Yet we show that pre-existing automation decreases firms' willingness to pay for improvements in automation: such improvements benefit occupations requir- ing high human expertise, while the supply of high-expertise workers declines with prior automation. This weakens the dynamic complementarity between automation and expertise-substituting technologies. We then endogenize automation and show that no degree of competition among AI producers eliminates the erosion externality. When the depreciation rate is sufficiently high, the optimal policy taxes their investment.

title: Making the Product, or Making It Seen? Generative AI and Where Value Comes From on Digital Platforms
abstract:
Introduction
Studies on generative AI (GenAI) ask whether AI raises productivity, improves output quality, or substitutes for skilled labor, and value is presumed to flow from building a better or cheaper product (Berg et al., 2023; Noy & Zhang, 2023). However, as a general-purpose technology with its wide applications, GenAI not only shapes how the product is built (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025; Heshmati & Wang, 2026); it also shapes how the product is presented. The same tool that writes a game's dialogue also draws its store banner. Firms can deploy generative AI in product development or in product representation. Representation is not simply decoration, but the mechanism through which demand is allocated (Zhang et al., 2022). 
In creative industries, consumer demand is largely shaped by the product's representation. While using AI may improve the product or productivity, the use of AI in creation, decision-making, and intellectual tasks may trigger algorithm aversion (Raj et al., 2026; Vanneste & Puranam, 2024; Yang et al., 2026). Such tension became especially acute, in contexts such as digital games that are distributed primarily through online platforms. In such a setting, a store page that presents the game is the only thing most buyers ever see before deciding (Bakos, 1997; Marchand & Hennig-Thurau, 2013).
A parallel line of studies asks whether audiences reward or punish firms that disclose the AI use (Wang & Liang, 2026). The answer is consistently punishment in that labeled creative work is rated lower (Bellaiche et al., 2023; Granulo et al., 2021), disclosing crowdfunding campaigns attract 31 percent fewer backers (Heshmati & Wang, 2026), and disclosing games are evaluated more harshly after play (LI, 2026). However, extant studies on AI disclosure do not distinguish the actual use of AI and treat AI adoption as a binary choice.
Neither literature asks the question that matters for strategy: does generative AI create value by improving the product that a firm sells, or by improving how the product is presented? The two are observationally identical wherever adoption is a binary choice; however, their performance implications may entirely differ. Whereas product improvement raises what buyers get (Brandenburger & Stuart Jr, 1996), presentation improvement may raise the number of buyers, and may leave the product and the buyers worse matched with the product (Kovács & Sharkey, 2014; Li & Hitt, 2008; Rietveld & Ploog, 2022).
In this study, we ask: when firms adopt generative AI, does the performance gain come from changes to product improvement or from changes to how the product is presented, and how does it affect heterogeneous producers?
Context
Steam's January 2024 disclosure mandate applies retroactively to games already on sale, so the same product is observed before and after its AI use becomes declared, and developers must state what the AI produced in their own words. Reading all 354 disclosure texts yields a clean separation: 28 percent describe AI used only on storefront assets such as capsule images, banners, achievement icons and trading cards, several stating explicitly that the game contains none; 51 percent describe AI inside the game as textures, character art, music or voice.
This distinction does the analytical work. Games in the first group cannot have improved as products. If they nonetheless gain sales, the gain must come from presentation. Identification uses coarsened exact matching on release timing, genre, and pre-shock sales level and growth, then two-way fixed effects difference-in-differences with game and quarter fixed effects, clustered by game, against roughly 13,600 matched controls.
Preliminary Results
We find that games in which GenAI was only used in product representation gain 36.3 percent in units and 44.7 percent in revenue with no change in engagement. Games with AI going into the product gain engagement and reviews and no sales. Presentation sells the game; content keeps players playing.

Heterogeneity
Subsample analyses show that the performance gain concentrates entirely among low-visibility games, at +0.37 against roughly zero for established titles. Every per-buyer measure is flat, so more people arrived rather than each getting more. A placebo using the non-AI games of the same developers returns nothing, so the effect attaches to the listing rather than the studio. Storefront AI in a low-visibility game moves every outcome, including revenue by 70.2 percent. The identical intervention in an already-visible game moves nothing, while still incurring a significant 3.7-point rating penalty. And AI placed inside the product moves nothing measurable in either group. If generative AI created value through some general productivity or quality channel, the in-game panel would carry the result and high-visibility adopters would gain too. Neither happens.
Read together, the two panels say that what matters is not that a firm adopted AI, nor even what it produced with it, but whether the firm faced a visibility constraint that better presentation could relax. 

Contribution and implications
We contribute to the literature by testing whether the source of value creation for generative AI comes from better representation of the product or better product in the online game context. Value here flows almost entirely through representation rather than production, which no technology-adoption framework predicts and which is invisible to any design coding adoption as binary. 

Limitations
Adoption timing appears staggered, with effects emerging in the fourth quarter after the mandate, so recovering per-game disclosure dates and re-estimating with a heterogeneity-robust estimator is the immediate next step.

title: Narrowing the Extraversion Advantage: AI-Assisted Upward Voice and Supervisor-Rated Communication Competence
abstract:
Extraversion confers a small but persistent workplace advantage, particularly in interpersonal and performance-related domains (Wilmot et al., 2019). At the same time, artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming part of human-to-human communication. AI-mediated communication allows a computational agent to modify, augment, or generate messages to help a communicator accomplish interpersonal goals (Hancock et al., 2020). Recent theory further suggests that AI can reshape both what people say and how they say it through affordances such as co-creation and adaptability (Zhu et al., 2026). We develop a compensatory communication scaffold argument. Specifically, AI may be especially useful for employees lower in extraversion when they prepare to speak up to supervisors because it can provide private assistance with wording, framing, timing, and situational fit. This possibility is consequential because managers evaluate not only how often employees speak up, but also how effectively they communicate their ideas, and higher-quality voice is associated with more favorable managerial evaluations (Brykman & Raver, 2021).
We examine this argument across two complementary field studies. Study 1 used time-lagged employee data (N = 164) to test a broader compensatory pathway. AI-mediated communication use positively predicted AI competence (β = .479, p < .001), and the interaction between AI communication use and extraversion was negative (β = −.135, p = .029), indicating that the relationship between AI communication use and competence became stronger as extraversion decreased. AI competence, in turn, positively predicted later AI-enabled innovative work behavior (β = .627, p < .001). The index of moderated mediation was significant (index = −.085, 95% CI [−.163, −.005]). Because the competence construct in this study captures broader AI competence rather than interpersonal communication competence, we treat Study 1 as converging evidence for the compensatory logic rather than as an exact test of the focal upward-communication mechanism.
Study 2 provides a more direct, multisource test using matched employee-supervisor data. We focus on a four-item measure of AI-assisted upward voice preparation, capturing employees' use of AI before sharing new ideas, making recommendations, expressing work-related opinions, and suggesting procedural changes to their supervisor. In the focal sample (N = 90), AI voice communication use interacted with supervisor-rated employee extraversion to predict supervisor-rated communication competence, b = −.290, p = .005. The interaction remained significant using HC3 robust standard errors, p = .033. The relationship between AI voice use and communication competence became more favorable as employee extraversion decreased. Supervisor-rated communication competence was also positively associated with supervisor-rated innovative behavior. Supplemental analyses further indicated that communication competence was positively associated with leadership-promotion potential. Because these downstream supervisor evaluations were collected from the same source at the same time, however, we treat them as consequential correlates rather than as strong causal evidence.
Together, the studies suggest that the consequences of workplace AI use depend not only on what task AI performs, but also on who uses it and for what interpersonal purpose. This extends research showing heterogeneous returns to AI. Generative AI can compress performance differences in some work settings, whereas other evidence suggests stronger augmentation among already higher-skilled employees (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2024). Our findings identify a different source of heterogeneity, employee extraversion, and shift attention from task productivity toward interpersonal evaluation. The contribution is therefore not simply that AI improves communication. Rather, AI may alter how personality translates into socially consequential workplace perceptions by providing a private scaffold before upward voice occurs. Practically, AI-based communication support may broaden whose ideas can be expressed effectively to supervisors. A follow-up multi-wave dyadic study is designed to separate employee-reported AI voice use from later supervisor evaluations and to account for baseline communication competence and actual voice behavior, providing a stronger confirmatory test of the proposed compensatory mechanism.

title: Reference Dependence and Risk Management: Evidence from Human and AI Crypto Traders
abstract: Risk management often requires traders to reduce exposure precisely when doing so is psychologically most costly: when a position is already below the reference point and adverse risk is rising. This paper studies whether reference dependence weakens de-risking in such states. Using high-frequency cryptocurrency positions held by human and AI traders, we first validate AI traders as a low-disposition benchmark: AI traders cut losing positions aggressively, while human traders largely mute this loss-cutting response. Relative to this benchmark, human traders are significantly less responsive to adverse risk pressure specifically in loss positions. The strongest evidence comes from matched adverse shocks: among positions exposed to the same shock and matched on pre-shock characteristics, humans reduce exposure less than AI traders only when positions were already below the reference point before the shock. The gap opens immediately after the shock, persists over cumulative response horizons, and is not explained by shock definitions, mechanical exits, or any single AI trader. Ex post price-path evidence further shows that humans avoid less subsequent adverse movement in loss-adverse states, without implying uniformly worse human performance. The results show that the disposition effect is not only a static tendency to sell winners and hold losers; reference-dependent realization costs can distort risk management by weakening de-risking exactly when adverse risk materializes.

title: Toward a Manipulable Taxonomy of Product-Specific Aesthetic Dimensions
abstract:
Text-to-image generation gives designers a fast way to explore product aesthetics, but only if they
know which words reliably change how a product looks. We develop a computational method for
building product-specific taxonomies of aesthetic descriptors around three constructs: applicability
(whether a descriptor shifts a product's visual representation), prototypicality (whether the descrip-
tor already describes the category's default appearance), and orthogonality (whether a dimension
can be varied independently of the others). We measure all three through CLIP embedding shifts,
using difference vectors to remove contamination from the shared product-category term. Using
dining chairs as the focal illustration, we build the full taxonomy pipeline and then field a choice-
based conjoint study (n = 101; 2,020 choices) that reveals a sharp divergence: the descriptors that
shift a product's appearance the most are among the descriptors consumers like least. Extend-
ing the analysis to 100 product categories, we find that the taxonomy's six higher-order dimen-
sions replicate across categories, but the specific descriptor best representing a dimension changes
from category to category-generalization happens at the dimension level, not the descriptor level.
These results motivate a revision of the constructs: we recast each dimension as a transformation
axis recovered by clustering embedding residuals across products, converting applicability from an
ordinal score into a signed, continuously adjustable magnitude. Generating 20,289 images with a
CLIP-conditioned diffusion decoder, we find that a descriptor's measured applicability lands inside
the range where the manipulated product is still recognizable, about a third of the way to where it
dissolves. When two dimensions are manipulated at once, most pairs can be dialed together but
a minority interfere strongly-and the inexpensive embedding-space orthogonality screen predicts
that interference only weakly. We close with the design of planned replication studies and a discussion of future research plans.

title: Governing Human-AI Co-Creation: Capability, Opacity, and the Economics of Oversight
abstract:
Firms increasingly deploy generative AI alongside human workers, expanding workers' responsibilities from producing output to also reviewing, validating, and correcting AI-generated content. This shift makes human oversight a central mechanism of responsible AI governance. Yet human oversight is not automatically effective: AI systems can produce fluent and plausible outputs that are difficult for humans to evaluate. In many knowledge-work settings, including software development, consulting, auditing, healthcare, legal drafting, and customer service, the risk is not merely that AI makes errors, but that those errors are embedded in output that appears polished and credible. As a result, firms face a governance problem: they must decide not only whether to keep humans in the loop, but how to design the loop so that human attention is allocated effectively.

We study this problem by developing an analytical model of human-AI co-creation. In our setting, a firm deploys an AI system and relies on a human worker to both produce output and oversee AI-generated work. The firm chooses a governance policy consisting of review frequency, oversight incentives, and productive-effort incentives. The worker observes these choices and responds by choosing productive effort and oversight depth. AI capability affects the firm through two channels. First, more capable AI increases the scale and value of AI-enabled production. Second, more capable AI can make errors harder to detect because its output is more fluent, coherent, and persuasive. We call this second channel capability-induced opacity. This creates a fundamental trade-off: AI capability raises productivity, but it may also increase the burden and reduce the effectiveness of responsible oversight.

We first consider a complete-information Stackelberg game as the baseline. Specifically, the firm moves first by setting review frequency and effort-based compensation, and the worker moves second by choosing productive effort and oversight depth. This structure captures a common feature of AI-enabled work: the firm can design incentives and review policies, but the worker ultimately determines how much effort to devote to production and how carefully to scrutinize AI output. We then consider an extension in which oversight depth is hidden from the firm. In this moral-hazard extension, the firm cannot directly contract on review depth and can instead motivate oversight only through rewards for verified error detection. The comparison between these two regimes allows us to isolate how hidden oversight changes the economics of responsible AI governance.

Our analysis yields several results that are surprising relative to the common intuition that more AI capability and more human review are always beneficial. First, review frequency and oversight depth are substitutes from the worker's perspective. When the firm requires AI output to be reviewed more frequently, each review becomes less deep unless the firm adjusts incentives. However, aggregate effective oversight can still increase with review frequency when the gain in coverage dominates the decline in per-review depth. This result shows that firms face a nontrivial design choice: reviewing more outputs is not equivalent to reviewing them more carefully.

Second, the optimal governance policy depends critically on the costs of scaling review. As the organizational cost of review frequency increases, the firm reduces the fraction of AI output that is reviewed. Thus, responsible AI governance is costly to scale, especially when review requires coordination, workflow interruptions, documentation, escalation, or managerial attention. This result helps explain why firms may formally adopt human-in-the-loop policies while still relying on selective or shallow oversight in practice.

Third, higher AI capability does not always improve firm performance. When AI capability primarily increases productive output, the marginal value of oversight rises because there is more AI-enabled work to protect. However, when capability-induced opacity is sufficiently strong, more capable AI reduces the effectiveness of each unit of human review. In that case, a more capable AI system can generate greater governance burden and may even lower firm profit. This result identifies a mechanism through which a less capable but more governable AI system can dominate a more capable but opaque one.

Fourth, in the hidden-oversight extension, monitoring infrastructure becomes central to responsible AI governance. When oversight depth is not directly observable, the firm's ability to induce careful review depends on whether caught errors can be verified and rewarded. Better monitoring quality increases hidden oversight, while weak verifiability reduces the firm's ability to motivate careful review. The extension therefore shows that governance infrastructure and AI capability can be complements: firms adopting more capable AI may also need stronger systems for verification, audit trails, escalation, and feedback.

The paper contributes to the analytical literature on co-creation and the emerging literature on responsible AI operations. Unlike traditional co-creation models in which all co-creators are strategic human or organizational actors, our setting features a non-strategic but opaque technology that changes both productivity and governability. The results show that responsible AI governance is not a binary choice between human review and no human review. Its effectiveness depends on the joint design of review frequency, oversight depth, incentives, monitoring quality, and AI capability.
