title: Outsourcing Morality: How AI Labels in Marketing Communication Change Perceptions of Firm Morality
abstract:
In 2025, Aerie, a sister company of American Eagle relaunched its "100 Percent Aerie Real" pledge, publicly recommitting to never using AI to generate or alter bodies in its images. The brand's sales climbed 23% year over year following the relaunch. Equinox paired distorted AI-generated bodies with plain human portraits in its "Question Everything But Yourself" campaign, and Almond Breeze mined the same tension for comedy in a Jonas Brothers ad built around the tagline "No AI Needed." Across categories, many brands have been converging on a common strategy: publicly declaring that their content is AI-Free.

With the increase in use of generative AI in marketing communications, firms face a new disclosure dilemma. Regulatory and consumer pressure has pushed many platforms and firms toward disclosing AI-generated content (AIGC) by default. Existing research on algorithm aversion has focused on whether consumers penalize firms for using AI (Longoni et al. 2019; Castelo et al. 2019) and on the costs of disclosure itself. For example, recent work shows AI disclosures on social media erode the perceived effort behind the content and in turn reduce consumer engagement (Carney et al. 2026). This raises an important question for firms: beyond disclosing AI use, can firms benefit by declaring the absence of AI?

Across four experiments, we show that explicitly labeling firm marketing communications as AI-free, compared to disclosing AI use or providing no information about how the content is generated, increases consumers' perceptions of firm morality and, in turn, purchase intentions from the firm. This effect is driven by reduced perceptions that the firm is outsourcing its moral responsibility to a machine.

Study 1 (preregistered; n = 602) tested the main effect using an email advertisement of a fictional clothing brand. Participants on CloudResearch Connect were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: the ad was labeled as AI-generated, AI-free, or no information was given about how it was created (control). Participants then rated the firm's perceived morality using a five-item scale (α = .96). Condition significantly predicted perceived morality, F(2, 599) = 22.61, p < .001, ηp² = .07. Consumers rated the firm as more moral in the AI-free condition (M = 5.08) than in the control (M = 4.69, p < .001) or AI condition (M = 4.30, p < .001).

Study 2 (n = 453) conceptually replicated this effect to a press release by a fictional luggage brand and tested whether perceived morality drives downstream purchase intentions. Participants were randomly assigned to an AI-generated, AI-free, or control press release condition, then reported purchase intentions and perceived firm morality. Condition again affected both morality, F(2, 450) = 9.57, p < .001, ηp² = .04 and purchase intentions, F(2, 450) = 7.77, p < .001, ηp² = .03. A mediation analysis (PROCESS Model 4, 5,000 bootstrap samples) showed that perceived morality significantly mediated the effect of condition on purchase intentions for both the control-versus-AI contrast (indirect effect = .20, 95% CI [.003, .41]) and the AI-free-versus-AI contrast (indirect effect = .43, 95% CI [.23, .65]). 

Study 3 (n = 601) tested the proposed mechanism directly. Participants on Connect saw the same press release from Study 2 and additionally rated the extent to which the firm was outsourcing its moral obligations to a machine as well as the extent to which the firm's practices caused harm to people through job loss. Condition significantly affected perceived morality, F(2, 598) = 19.74, p < .001, ηp² = .06, outsourcing morality, F(2, 598) = 26.40, p < .001, ηp² = .08, and perceived harm from job loss, F(2, 598) = 61.71, p < .001, ηp² = .17. When both variables were entered as parallel mediators of condition's effect on perceived morality, only outsourcing morality emerged as a significant mediator across all three pairwise contrasts - AI vs. control (indirect effect = .11, 95% CI [.03, .21]), AI vs. AI-free (indirect effect = .14, 95% CI [.04, .27]), and control vs. AI-free (indirect effect = .04, 95% CI [.00, .10]), while the indirect effect through perceived harm from job loss was not significant. This indicates that consumers do not penalize AI-generated content primarily because they believe it was made at the expense of a human worker's employment, but because it signals that the firm is using technology to avoid taking moral responsibility.

Study 4 (n = 568) tested whether the AI-free label's benefit depends on a firm's prior moral history. Using a 2 (ad type: AI-free vs. control) × 2 (firm morality: high vs. low) between-subjects design, we found a significant Ad Type × firm morality interaction on both perceived morality, F(1, 564) = 9.38, p = .002, ηp² = .016, and purchase intentions, F(1, 562) = 4.06, p = .044, ηp² = .007. Among firms with a low prior moral history, an AI-free label significantly boosted perceived morality (3.09 vs. 3.92, p < .001) and purchase intentions (2.96 vs. 3.55, p < .001) relative to control. Among firms with a high prior moral history, the AI-free label had no significant effect on either perceived morality (5.90 vs. 6.09, p = .205) or purchase intentions (5.78 vs. 5.90, p = .449). An AI-free label helps when a firm's moral standing is otherwise low, and offers no returns once a firm has already established a strong moral reputation.

Together, these findings show that explicitly communicating that marketing content is AI-free can increase consumers' perceptions of firm morality and, in turn, their willingness to purchase from the firm. Importantly, the effect is not simply about consumers disliking AI-generated content; relative to a control condition in which firms provide no information about how their content was created, an AI-free claim provides a moral signal. This signal operates by reducing the perception that the firm is outsourcing its moral responsibility to a machine. As AI becomes increasingly common, explicitly signaling that a firm has chosen not to use AI may offer a unique way for firms to strengthen perceptions of their moral character, particularly when those perceptions are in need of repair.

title: The Economics of AI Creators
abstract:
The creator economy has traditionally been built around human creators who gradually establish public personas, attract followers through repeated interactions with consumers, and eventually monetize their influence through commercial sponsorships. Recent advances in AI reshape this process by enabling AI to function as creators in their own right rather than merely as content-generation tools. As AI creators, autonomous virtual personas that continuously produce content and interact with consumers, become increasingly prevalent on digital platforms, an important economic question emerges: How does the emergence of AI creators reshape strategic competition in the creator economy?

We study this question using a game-theoretic model of competition between a human creator and an AI creator. Before any commercial activity takes place, both creators strategically invest in developing their public personas. Persona investment represents long-term efforts devoted to building a recognizable identity through content production, interactions with followers, and consistent self-presentation. Although both creator types make the same strategic decision, the economic mechanisms behind their investments differ fundamentally. Human creators benefit from greater authenticity and stronger emotional connections with consumers, making their endorsements more persuasive. However, their commercial success remains vulnerable to unexpected persona-collapse events that may substantially reduce sponsorship opportunities after valuable commercial influence has already been established. AI creators face a different trade-off. Their synthetic personas are stable and largely immune to reputation shocks, but increasing persona realism does not always improve consumer acceptance. Consumers recognize that the creator is AI-generated, and highly realistic AI personas may nevertheless evoke technology aversion through the uncanny-valley effect. Consequently, greater persona realism eventually becomes less effective in attracting additional followers.

A key feature of the model is that it distinguishes four stages of the creator commercialization process. In Stage 1, human and AI creators choose their persona investments. In Stage 2, consumers decide which creator to follow after observing the resulting personas. In Stage 3, follower bases are translated into commercial value. Commercial value measures the creator's potential economic value before monetization and depends on both audience size and persuasive effectiveness. A creator with more followers therefore does not necessarily create more commercial value if those followers respond less strongly to sponsored recommendations. In Stage 4, commercial value is converted into realized sponsorship revenue through commercial sponsorships. At this stage, human creators remain exposed to persona-collapse risk, whereas AI creators enjoy greater commercialization stability because their synthetic personas are not subject to unexpected reputation shocks. Separating these four stages allows us to distinguish audience formation, commercial influence, and monetization, which are often treated as a single outcome in existing studies.

The analysis shows that advances in AI technology influence competition through two opposing channels. Higher AI capability allows a given level of persona investment to produce more realistic AI personas, increasing their attractiveness to consumers. At the same time, greater realism causes a growing proportion of consumers to exceed their individual tolerance thresholds (i.e., uncanny-valley effect), making the AI creator appear unsettling. As a result, additional improvements in persona realism generate diminishing returns in audience formation as increasingly strong uncanny-valley responses offset the gains from greater realism. Human creators do not face this constraint. Instead, they choose persona investments while recognizing that part of the commercial value they create may never be converted into realized sponsorship revenue because of future persona-collapse shocks. Although both creators optimize the same decision variable, their investment incentives arise from fundamentally different economic forces.

The model also demonstrates that popularity and commercial success should not be viewed as equivalent measures of creator performance. Human creators retain an important advantage in transforming followers into commercial influence because their recommendations are inherently more persuasive. At the same time, their realized sponsorship revenue remains vulnerable to unexpected persona-collapse shocks during commercialization. AI creators face the opposite trade-off. Their persuasive effectiveness is lower, but they benefit from stable personas and avoid commercialization risk. Consequently, the creator with the largest audience need not generate the greatest commercial value, while the creator with the greatest commercial value may still earn the highest realized sponsorship revenue only if that value can be successfully monetized. More broadly, the analysis suggests that human and AI creators possess different comparative advantages along the commercialization process rather than simply replacing one another. Human creators are advantaged in generating commercial influence, whereas AI creators are advantaged in preserving commercial value during commercialization. The competitive impact of AI, therefore, depends on how these advantages interact across different stages of the commercialization process instead of being determined solely by consumer attention.

To further examine commercialization, we extend the model by introducing heterogeneous advertisers that differ in their sensitivity to reputation risk. Advertisers that place greater weight on persuasive influence continue to prefer human creators despite the possibility of persona collapse. By contrast, advertisers in reputation-sensitive industries place greater value on the stability offered by AI creators. This extension suggests that AI adoption is unlikely to affect all sponsorship markets uniformly. Instead, different industries are expected to sort toward different creator types according to their tolerance for commercialization risk.

This paper contributes to the emerging literature on generative AI, digital platforms, and the creator economy in two ways. First, it models AI creators as persistent economic agents that continuously develop personas, accumulate audiences, and compete for commercial opportunities, rather than treating AI as a one-time content-generation technology. Second, it develops a framework that explicitly distinguishes persona investment, consumer following, commercial value, and commercialization as separate stages of the creator economy. This perspective shows that the economic consequences of AI cannot be understood solely through consumer attention or technological capability. They also depend on how AI reshapes persuasion, commercialization, and the distribution of economic value throughout the creator commercialization process.

title: The Selection Behind the Penalty: Strategic and Mandatory AI Disclosure in Music Streaming
abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used to assist the creation of cultural goods, and policymakers have responded by requiring that AI use be disclosed. Within roughly two years, mandatory AI-content labeling moved from proposal to law across the largest media markets: China's labeling rules took effect in 2025, the European Union's AI Act will require the disclosure of synthetic content under Article 50, and platforms from YouTube to the major music services have adopted policies of their own. The premise animating this wave is that AI involvement is a liability to be revealed: labeled AI content is observed to underperform, so a rule forcing its disclosure is presumed to tax the artists who use these tools. But when disclosure is voluntary, the observed gap between disclosed and concealed AI work blends two very different things: how listeners respond to a label, and which songs artists choose to reveal in the first place. If artists conceal precisely the songs that disclosure would cost the most, the raw gap mostly reflects that choice rather than the label's effect. Separating the two is a first-order question for theory and policy. It requires observing an artist's true AI use, including what was concealed, together with a change in disclosure independent of the artist's choice.

We study two disclosure regimes on a major music-streaming platform with an integrated generative-AI music tool. For more than two years, disclosure was voluntary: an artist who made a song with the tool could credit it to listeners or stay silent, and many stayed silent. Two features of the setting make the decomposition possible. First, we observe ground-truth AI use from the platform's back end, including songs that used AI but were never disclosed to listeners, so we see concealment directly rather than inferring it from what artists say. Second, we can hold the work fixed-the same audio, the same artist, the same song, observed both before and after a label is imposed on it. The two regimes do different jobs. In the voluntary regime we model which AI songs artists choose to credit and measure the raw conceal-versus-credit performance gap within each artist's own catalog. The mandatory regime supplies the missing counterfactual: the platform began attaching a listener-facing AI label to eligible AI songs on September 2025, but the label applied only to songs published on or after an April 2025 eligibility cutoff. Otherwise-similar concealed songs published just before the cutoff were never labeled, while those published just after were labeled at the shock. Comparing the two cohorts through the shock in a difference-in-differences design, with the song held fixed, recovers listeners' causal response to an AI label. This is the field counterpart of laboratory experiments that randomize AI disclosure on a fixed work, now with the selection margin observed rather than assumed away.

Four results follow. First, we find that artists who adopt the AI tool sharply increase their output relative to matched non-adopters. Second, disclosure is strategic rather than idiosyncratic. Crediting tracks the song and the artist in interpretable ways: songs that enter a genre new to the artist, that carry a larger production team, or in which the artist's own contribution is more visible are the ones more likely to credit the AI, while songs in the artist's habitual genres are concealed. Third, the raw voluntary gap observed is large. Within an artist's own catalog, concealed AI songs outperform credited ones by roughly 1.2 log points in plays, about a threefold difference. Fourth, the causal penalty is small relative to the raw voluntary gap. When the mandate forces disclosure onto a previously concealed song, its plays fall by only about five percent. The effect operates at discovery-fewer listeners begin the song, while completion and post-listening engagement are unchanged-and it falls unevenly, concentrated among lower- and middle-tier artists and near zero for the established. Setting the two regimes side by side, even taking the causal estimate at its largest and the voluntary gap at face value, the genuine listener response accounts for at most a few percent of the observed conceal-credit gap. The overwhelming remainder is selection. The raw voluntary comparison overstates the causal penalty of disclosure by more than an order of magnitude.

The results carry a direct policy reading and a conceptual contribution. For policy, mandatory AI labeling is debated as though it levied a heavy tax on the artists who comply, a presumption the raw disclosure gap appears to license. Our estimates suggest the tax is modest, that it operates at discovery rather than in how listeners engage with a song they have chosen to play, and that it is regressive: the cost falls on the newer and smaller artists whose audiences have the least other information, and is near zero for the established. Transparency rules should be judged against the small penalty that disclosure actually imposes, not the far larger one that artists were avoiding. Conceptually, the paper connects the economics of voluntary disclosure with the behavioral research on AI aversion. The classic prediction of disclosure theory is unraveling toward full revelation; we show why it reverses for AI authorship. Because AI use is not verifiable to listeners and the authenticity penalty it carries is real, sticky, and never good news for the discloser, silence rather than revelation is the equilibrium, and voluntary disclosure sorts songs rather than informing listeners. This complements, rather than competes with, both the laboratory studies that cleanly identify the listener response and the field studies that observe real disclosure choices: our design adds the concealment and the within-work counterfactual that a decomposition of the market penalty requires. It reframes how the disclosure penalties documented across a fast-growing literature should be read-as compounds of listener response and artist selection, not estimates of the former alone.

title: Who Pays for the Cloud? The Impact of Data Center Entry on Grocery Purchases
abstract:
In recent years, data centers have proliferated rapidly (Kearney 2024). Essential to cloud computing and artificial intelligence, data centers provide services that are consumed far beyond the communities that host them. During our 2004-2014 study period, data centers supported services like Amazon's S3 and EC2 and cloud infrastructure used by eBay (Amazon Web Services 2006; Microsoft 2010). Public debate and emerging research have largely evaluated the impact of data centers through electricity demand, utility prices, and employment (Alvarez et al. 2026; Kay, Reaser, and Taylor 2026). While important, these effects do not directly measure household response to data center entry. Household spending provides a more direct and reliable measure of household response (Dubé, Hitsch, and Rossi 2018; Scholdra et al. 2022). While data center entry can drive up costs, put pressure on households' budgets, and reduce spending, it can also create jobs and economic opportunities that increase spending.

Our paper asks three related questions: What is the effect of data center entry on local household grocery spending, including purchase frequency and basket size and composition? How do these effects evolve over time, (i.e. short-, medium-, and long-term adjustments in grocery spending)? Importantly, are the counties with the strongest response also those most likely to leverage and benefit from data center capabilities?

To answer our research questions, we combine annual establishment records from the National Establishment Time Series (NETS) with household purchase records from the 2004--2014 NielsenIQ Consumer Panel. We define entry as the first year in which a county records stable local estabilishmen classified under NAICS 518210, Data Processing, Hosting, and Related Services, between 2006 and 2014. The design includes 52 treated counties and 2,160 counties that do not record a qualifying entry. Using Callaway-Sant'Anna staggered difference-in-differences design, we estimate cohort- and time-specific treatment effects by comparing post-entry changes in treated counties with contemporaneous changes in never-treated counties. The study period gives us a clean quasi-experimental setting predating recent generative-AI-driven acceleration in data-center expansion, the current political and media salience of data centers, and the pandemic-era expansion of online grocery shopping. 

Our analysis shows several interesting results. First, we find that annual CPG spending declines by 12.3% after data center entry (SE = 0.051), which yields an average post-entry decrease of approximately $420 per household-year. Second, the decline is modest during the first three years and becomes larger and statistically significant thereafter. We provide several robustness checks, including an event study analysis shows no evidence of differential pretreatment trends in total CPG spending (p = .72). 

Our mechanism analysis further helps understand what drives the average spending declines. By decomposing spending into recorded purchase occasions and spending per occasion, we find about 27 fewer recorded occasions per household-year(decline by 16.8%), while spending per occasion does not change significantly. The recorded CPG spending decline is therefore associated with fewer recorded purchase occasions, not smaller amounts spent per occasion. Furthermore, the reduction is concentrated in lower-value purchase occasions: those under $10 fall by roughly 14 per household-year, while larger occasions change little. We find little evidence of a broad trade-down: deal purchases, coupon use, and private-label share do not change detectably. In terms of basket composition, it appears that households reduce purchases of non-food and non-discretionary categories, such as stationery, kitchen and housewares, pet and baby care, and paper products, while the purchases of storable staples such as canned goods, cereal, and frozen prepared meals do not decrease.

Finally, we ask whether places that respond most strongly also share in local economic gains. Using County Business Patterns for establishments and employment and Bureau of Economic Analysis data for per capita income, we find that in nonmetropolitan counties, annual recorded CPG spending declines by 19.8%, compared with 8.1% in metropolitan counties, while per capita income declines by 1.7% versus 1.1%. The pattern reverses for local economic expansion: metropolitan counties experience 6.1% growth in establishments and 6.4% growth in employment, compared with 1.8% and 2.2% in nonmetropolitan counties. Thus, the larger household purchasing decline appears where measured local business and employment gains are smaller. 

Overall, our research contributes in three ways. First, to our knowledge, we provide the first evidence on how data center entry affects local household consumption. Second, we contribute to the marketing research on household responses to changing economic conditions (i.e., major digital infrastructure entry) and document declines in spending driven by a reduced purchase frequency, rather than spending per occasion and product trade-down. Third, we document a mismatch between who bears the local cost of the cloud and who benefits from it; the counties and households that cut back most are not those positioned to share in data-center-related gains. Our research has several implications. For retailers and manufacturers, a decline in grocery purchases because of fewer purchase occasions has different implications relative to one driven by smaller baskets or substitution toward cheaper products; it removes the occasions on which households can be reached and converted at all. For policymakers weighing regulations, entry decisions, and host-community benefits, our results on household purchases offer a direct measure of consumer response.

title: GOVERNING AGENTIC AI WORKFLOWS: OVERSIGHT IN AGENTIC AND ASSISTIVE MODES
abstract:
Motivation. Modern AI models can perform many discrete knowledge-work tasks accurately, yet their performance often deteriorates in multi-step workflows, where planning, tool use, execution, quality control, and revision unfold over many interdependent steps. Earlier errors propagate and make subsequent mistakes more likely. Yet worker-AI engagement patterns are often unobservable: firms may not know how carefully workers verify AI-generated outputs, when they intervene, or when they invoke AI support. The central governance challenge is therefore not simply whether to keep humans in the loop, but where to position them and how to incentivize their engagement when intermediate verification is costly and difficult to observe. We study optimal checkpoint placement-the frequency of human-AI engagement-in two workflow designs: an agentic design, in which AI executes and a human checks, and an assistive design, in which a human executes and AI checks. The agentic design captures practices such as vibe coding and agentic engineering, in which workers delegate goals to AI agents and review their outputs at selected checkpoints. The assistive design captures human-led copilot workflows, in which workers retain execution and invoke tools such as GitHub Copilot or Gemini Code Assist for verification and suggestions. Because a human remains the doer and bears more of the consequences of mistakes, managers may view the assistive design as more reliable and easier to govern. The comparison is complicated by AI's jagged intelligence-the tendency of the same AI system to perform extremely well on some tasks but poorly on others that appear similar. Humans, by contrast, tend to perform more consistently across comparable tasks. Jaggedness therefore captures variation in AI reliability across tasks, rather than simply low average accuracy: systems with the same average failure rate can generate different patterns of errors. This distinction matters because role assignment determines how jagged performance enters final outcomes and how clearly those outcomes reveal hidden engagement.
Methodology. We develop an analytical framework that jointly determines checkpoint policies, human-AI role assignments, and outcome-based incentives in a multi-step workflow. A doer, either AI or human, completes N subtasks in sequence, while a checker decides how often to inspect intermediate work. Each inspection is costly but can catch errors and trigger repairs before they propagate. A check every k tasks reduces final errors, whereas less frequent checks save oversight cost but allow errors to accumulate, increasing rework and terminal errors. We first characterize the optimal checkpoint policy when engagement is observable. This first-best policy provides the target that the firm seeks to implement when checkpoint placement is hidden. Because token-based quotas are insufficient to induce the desired engagement, we focus on outcome-based contracts. Under limited liability, the worker privately chooses when to inspect AI's intermediate output in the agentic design or invoke AI support to verify her work in the assistive design. We derive contracts implementing the firm's preferred checkpoint policy when both parties are risk neutral and when the worker alone is risk-averse.
Findings. First, the operational value of oversight is non-monotone in task difficulty. The optimal checkpoint interval is U-shaped in the doer's failure rate: it is long for easy tasks, shortest at intermediate difficulty, and lengthens again as the task becomes hard. When errors are rare, frequent review adds little value. As failures become more common, shorter intervals prevent errors from propagating across downstream steps. Beyond an interior threshold, however, repeated checks and rework become too costly relative to their corrective value, so the firm checks less often and eventually moves to an end-only check. Second, moderate AI jaggedness may approximately preserve expected final performance, but it changes the distribution of final errors differently across collaboration modes. This distinction matters once the firm must contract on final outcomes, because the shape of the distribution determines how clearly performance reveals hidden engagement. Average accuracy alone is therefore insufficient to compare the two designs.
Third, when checkpoint placement is hidden, workers choose to under-check in both designs unless given an additional incentive. The agentic worker bears the checkpoint cost but does not internalize the benefit of catching AI errors. The assistive worker bears both checkpoint and rework costs and is therefore more closely aligned with the firm, but still does not internalize the full cost of undetected final errors. Despite this stronger private-cost alignment, the assistive design can be more expensive to govern. For a risk-neutral worker with limited liability and uncapped pay, a lower-tail threshold bonus can implement the agentic first best with zero information rent. The optimal contract concentrates compensation on a rare, low-error outcome that is highly informative about human checks. By contrast, outcomes under the assistive design have bounded incentive power because changing the checkpoint interval rescales the same noisy checker realization. Any nonnegative outcome contract implementing an interior first best must satisfy a payment floor determined by AI jaggedness and task difficulty. A more jagged AI and a harder task raise this floor. If it exceeds participation compensation, the firm must pay information rent or implement a different checkpoint interval. The floor disappears at the end-only-check corner, where the firm and worker prefer the same action. Worker risk aversion further makes outcome-contingent compensation costly and generates different rent profiles across the two designs.
Implications. Common managerial intuition suggests choosing the agentic design when AI execution appears technically less costly and the assistive design when human-led work appears more reliable. Our analysis shows that this intuition is incomplete. When the contract remains constant across role assignments, stronger private-cost alignment can favor the assistive design. Once the firm tailors the optimal contract to each workflow, however, this ranking can reverse because agentic outcomes may provide sharper evidence of hidden checkpoint placement and support more targeted rewards. Firms should therefore choose workflow design and incentive contracts jointly. The preferred collaboration mode depends not only on technical production cost, average accuracy, or perceived reliability, but also on error propagation, task difficulty, AI jaggedness, human risk preferences, and the cost of inducing hidden engagement. Assistive workflows' perceived reliability does not necessarily make them easier or less costly to govern in practice.
